@RestController vs @Controller?

Quick Answer

Data vs Views.

Detailed Explanation

@RestController and @Controller are both stereotype annotations in Spring MVC that mark classes as web controllers, but they serve different purposes in web application development. Understanding their differences is crucial for building appropriate web services.

@Controller:

  • Purpose: Traditional Model-View-Controller (MVC) web applications
  • Response Type: Returns view names (Strings) that are resolved to HTML templates
  • Use Case: Server-side rendered web applications using templating engines
  • Response Handling: Requires @ResponseBody for JSON/XML responses
  • Typical Stack: Thymeleaf, JSP, FreeMarker templates with server-side rendering

@RestController:

  • Purpose: RESTful web services and API development
  • Response Type: Returns data objects directly (automatically serialized to JSON/XML)
  • Use Case: Building APIs that serve data to frontend applications or other services
  • Response Handling: Built-in @ResponseBody behavior for all methods
  • Typical Stack: JSON APIs consumed by SPAs, mobile apps, or microservices

Both annotations:

  • Are discovered by @ComponentScan
  • Support @RequestMapping and its variants (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.)
  • Enable dependency injection
  • Are singletons by default
  • Support request/response handling annotations

Key architectural differences:

  • Data Flow: @Controller renders views; @RestController returns data
  • Content Negotiation: @RestController uses HTTP message converters; @Controller uses view resolvers
  • Client Types: @Controller for browsers; @RestController for programmatic clients
  • State Management: @Controller often manages session state; @RestController is typically stateless

When to use each:

  • Use @Controller: Traditional web apps, admin panels, server-side rendered pages
  • Use @RestController: REST APIs, microservices, SPAs, mobile app backends

Spring Boot's auto-configuration automatically sets up the appropriate infrastructure (Jackson for JSON, view resolvers for templates) based on dependencies and configuration.

Code Example
// Traditional MVC Controller - returns HTML views
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserMvcController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserMvcController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /users/list - Returns view name for template rendering
    @GetMapping("/list")
    public String listUsers(Model model) {
        List<User> users = userService.getAllUsers();
        model.addAttribute("users", users);
        model.addAttribute("currentTime", LocalDateTime.now());
        return "users/list";  // Returns view name (users/list.html)
    }
    
    // GET /users/profile/{id} - Returns view with user data
    @GetMapping("/profile/{id}")
    public String userProfile(@PathVariable Long id, Model model) {
        User user = userService.findById(id);
        model.addAttribute("user", user);
        return "users/profile";  // Returns view name
    }
    
    // POST /users - Handles form submission and redirects
    @PostMapping
    public String createUser(@ModelAttribute @Valid UserForm form, 
                           BindingResult result, 
                           RedirectAttributes redirectAttrs) {
        if (result.hasErrors()) {
            return "users/create";  // Return to form view on errors
        }
        
        User user = userService.createUser(form);
        redirectAttrs.addFlashAttribute("message", "User created successfully!");
        return "redirect:/users/list";  // Redirect after success
    }
    
    // GET /users/api/list - JSON endpoint in MVC controller
    @GetMapping("/api/list")
    @ResponseBody  // Explicitly marks for JSON response
    public List<UserDto> getUsersApi() {
        return userService.getAllUsers().stream()
            .map(this::convertToDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
    
    private UserDto convertToDto(User user) {
        return new UserDto(user.getId(), user.getEmail(), user.getName());
    }
}

// REST Controller - returns JSON data only
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserRestController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserRestController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /api/users - Retrieve all users as JSON
    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<List<UserDto>> getAllUsers() {
        List<UserDto> users = userService.getAllUsers().stream()
            .map(this::convertToDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(users);
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/{id} - Retrieve single user
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // POST /api/users - Create new user
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        try {
            User user = userService.createUser(request);
            UserDto response = convertToDto(user);
            
            URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
                .toUri();
            
            return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(response);
        } catch (UserAlreadyExistsException e) {
            return ResponseEntity.badRequest().build();
        }
    }
    
    // PUT /api/users/{id} - Update user
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateUserRequest request) {
        
        return userService.updateUser(id, request)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/users/{id} - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteById(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // PATCH /api/users/{id} - Partial update
    @PatchMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> patchUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @RequestBody Map<String, Object> updates) {
        
        return userService.patchUser(id, updates)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/search - Search with query parameters
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public ResponseEntity<List<UserDto>> searchUsers(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String name,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String email,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) {
        
        Page<User> userPage = userService.searchUsers(name, email, PageRequest.of(page, size));
        List<UserDto> users = userPage.getContent().stream()
            .map(this::convertToDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
        
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header("X-Total-Count", String.valueOf(userPage.getTotalElements()))
            .body(users);
    }
    
    private UserDto convertToDto(User user) {
        return new UserDto(user.getId(), user.getEmail(), user.getName(), user.getCreatedDate());
    }
}

// Supporting DTOs
public class UserDto {
    private Long id;
    private String email;
    private String name;
    private LocalDateTime createdDate;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank(message = "Email is required")
    @Email(message = "Invalid email format")
    private String email;
    
    @NotBlank(message = "Name is required")
    @Size(min = 2, max = 50, message = "Name must be between 2 and 50 characters")
    private String name;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters, validation
}

public class UpdateUserRequest {
    @Email
    private String email;
    
    @Size(min = 2, max = 50)
    private String name;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

# Content negotiation settings

spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.parameter-name=mediaType
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.json=application/json
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.xml=application/xml

# View resolver for @Controller
spring.mvc.view.prefix=/templates/

The choice between @Controller and @RestController depends on whether you're building traditional web pages or modern API-driven applications.

WebController

@RestController vs @Controller?

Quick Answer

@RestController implies @Controller + @ResponseBody.

Detailed Explanation

@RestController and @Controller are both fundamental stereotypes in Spring MVC for handling web requests, but they serve different architectural purposes in web application development. Understanding their differences is crucial for building appropriate APIs and web applications.

@Controller:

  • Purpose: Traditional MVC controller for web applications
  • Response Handling: Returns view names (Strings) resolved to HTML templates
  • Use Case: Server-side rendered applications with UI templates
  • Response Types: Primarily HTML, but can return JSON/XML with @ResponseBody
  • Integration: Works with ViewResolvers (Thymeleaf, JSP, FreeMarker)

@RestController:

  • Purpose: RESTful web services controller
  • Response Handling: Automatically serializes return values to JSON/XML
  • Use Case: Building APIs for frontend applications or microservices
  • Response Types: Pure data (JSON by default)
  • Integration: No view resolution, direct data serialization

Key Differences:

  • Default Behavior: @Controller expects views, @RestController returns data
  • Serialization: @RestController applies @ResponseBody to all methods
  • Content Negotiation: Both support, but @RestController defaults to JSON
  • Architecture: @Controller for MVC, @RestController for API-first

When to Use Each:

  • @Controller: Traditional web apps, admin panels, server-side rendering
  • @RestController: REST APIs, SPAs, mobile app backends, microservices
  • Hybrid: Some controllers may need both approaches

Common Patterns:

  • API Controllers: @RestController for /api/* endpoints
  • Web Controllers: @Controller for user-facing pages
  • Mixed Controllers: @Controller with some @ResponseBody methods

Both annotations enable dependency injection and work with Spring Security, validation, and other web features.

Code Example
// REST Controller - Returns JSON data
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
public class ProductApiController {
    
    private final ProductService productService;
    
    public ProductApiController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public List<ProductDTO> getAllProducts() {
        return productService.getAllProducts().stream()
            .map(this::convertToDTO)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductDTO> getProduct(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return productService.getProduct(id)
            .map(this::convertToDTO)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<ProductDTO> createProduct(@Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request) {
        Product product = productService.createProduct(request);
        ProductDTO dto = convertToDTO(product);
        
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder
            .fromCurrentRequest()
            .path("/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(product.getId())
            .toUri();
        
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(dto);
    }
    
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductDTO> updateProduct(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateProductRequest request) {
        return productService.updateProduct(id, request)
            .map(this::convertToDTO)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteProduct(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (productService.deleteProduct(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    private ProductDTO convertToDTO(Product product) {
        ProductDTO dto = new ProductDTO();
        dto.setId(product.getId());
        dto.setName(product.getName());
        dto.setPrice(product.getPrice());
        dto.setCategory(product.getCategory());
        return dto;
    }
}

// Traditional MVC Controller - Returns HTML views
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductWebController {
    
    private final ProductService productService;
    
    public ProductWebController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public String listProducts(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("products", productService.getAllProducts());
        return "products/list";  // Returns view name
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public String showProduct(@PathVariable Long id, Model model) {
        Product product = productService.getProduct(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException("Product not found"));
        model.addAttribute("product", product);
        return "products/detail";  // Returns view name
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/new")
    public String newProductForm(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("product", new Product());
        return "products/form";  // Returns view name
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public String createProduct(@Valid @ModelAttribute Product product, 
                               BindingResult result, RedirectAttributes redirectAttrs) {
        if (result.hasErrors()) {
            return "products/form";  // Returns view name on validation error
        }
        
        Product saved = productService.createProduct(product);
        redirectAttrs.addFlashAttribute("message", "Product created successfully");
        return "redirect:/products/" + saved.getId();  // Redirect to view
    }
    
    // Mixed approach - some methods return data, others return views
    @GetMapping("/api/search")
    @ResponseBody  // Explicit JSON response
    public List<Product> searchProducts(@RequestParam String query) {
        return productService.searchProducts(query);
    }
}

// DTOs for API
public class ProductDTO {
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private BigDecimal price;
    private String category;
    // getters/setters
}

public class CreateProductRequest {
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    @NotNull @DecimalMin("0.01")
    private BigDecimal price;
    private String category;
    // getters/setters
}

public class UpdateProductRequest {
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    @NotNull @DecimalMin("0.01")
    private BigDecimal price;
    private String category;
    // getters/setters
}

// Testing both controller types
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
public class ControllerTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;
    
    @Test
    void restControllerShouldReturnJson() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/products"))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$[0].name").exists());
    }
    
    @Test
    void webControllerShouldReturnHtml() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/products"))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.TEXT_HTML))
            .andExpect(content().string(containsString("<html>")));
    }
    
    @Test
    void mixedControllerShouldHandleBoth() throws Exception {
        // JSON response
        mockMvc.perform(get("/products/api/search").param("query", "test"))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON));
        
        // HTML response
        mockMvc.perform(get("/products"))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.TEXT_HTML));
    }
}

// Advanced configuration for content negotiation
@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    
    @Override
    public void configureContentNegotiation(ContentNegotiationConfigurer configurer) {
        configurer
            .favorParameter(true)
            .parameterName("format")
            .ignoreAcceptHeader(false)
            .useRegisteredExtensionsOnly(false)
            .defaultContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .mediaType("json", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .mediaType("xml", MediaType.APPLICATION_XML);
    }
}

// Controller supporting multiple formats
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/data")
public class ContentNegotiationController {
    
    @GetMapping
    public Data getData() {
        return new Data("example", 123);
    }
    
    // Can be accessed as:
    // /api/data (JSON)
    // /api/data?format=xml (XML)
    // Accept: application/xml header (XML)
}

public class Data {
    private String name;
    private int value;
    // getters/setters
}

// Hybrid controller pattern (less common but possible)
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/hybrid")
public class HybridController {
    
    @GetMapping("/page")
    public String showPage(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("data", getData());
        return "hybrid/page";  // Returns view
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/data")
    @ResponseBody
    public Data getData() {
        return new Data("hybrid", 456);  // Returns JSON
    }
}

The choice between @RestController and @Controller depends on the application's architecture. Use @RestController for API-centric applications and @Controller for traditional web applications with server-side rendering.

web

@RestController vs @Controller?

Quick Answer

@RestController implies @ResponseBody.

Detailed Explanation

@Controller and @RestController are both stereotypes for Spring MVC controllers, but they serve different purposes in web application development:

@Controller:

  • Used for traditional Model-View-Controller (MVC) web applications
  • Methods typically return view names (Strings) that are resolved to HTML templates
  • Can return data objects, but they need @ResponseBody to serialize to JSON/XML
  • Suitable for server-side rendered applications using templating engines like Thymeleaf, JSP, or FreeMarker
  • Supports both data and view responses from the same controller

@RestController:

  • A specialized version of @Controller designed specifically for RESTful web services
  • Automatically applies @ResponseBody to all handler methods
  • All methods return data directly (serialized to JSON by default)
  • No view resolution occurs; responses are pure data
  • Ideal for building APIs that serve JSON/XML data to frontend applications or other services

Both annotations:

  • Are scanned by @ComponentScan
  • Can use @RequestMapping and its variants (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.)
  • Support dependency injection
  • Are singletons by default

The choice depends on your application's architecture:

  • Use @Controller for web apps with server-side rendering
  • Use @RestController for REST APIs and microservices

Spring Boot's auto-configuration sets up content negotiation and JSON serialization automatically when web starters are included.

Code Example
// Traditional MVC Controller - returns views
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserMvcController {
    
    @GetMapping("/list")
    public String listUsers(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("users", userService.getAllUsers());
        return "users/list";  // Returns view name (users/list.html)
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/api/list")
    @ResponseBody  // Explicitly marks for JSON response
    public List<User> getUsersApi() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();  // Returns JSON data
    }
}

// REST Controller - returns data only
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserRestController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserRestController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public List<UserDto> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers().stream()
            .map(this::convertToDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        UserDto response = convertToDto(user);
        
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
            .path("/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
            .toUri();
        
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(response);
    }
    
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateUserRequest request) {
        
        return userService.updateUser(id, request)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // Helper method for DTO conversion
    private UserDto convertToDto(User user) {
        return new UserDto(user.getId(), user.getEmail(), user.getName());
    }
}

annotations

@Service vs @Repository?

Quick Answer

Semantic stereotypes.

Detailed Explanation

@Service and @Repository are specialized stereotype annotations in Spring that extend @Component. They provide semantic meaning and enable framework-specific features, helping organize code by layer and purpose.

@Service:

  • Purpose: Marks classes that contain business logic
  • Layer: Service/Business layer
  • Responsibilities: Orchestrates data access, applies business rules, coordinates transactions
  • Example: UserService, OrderService, PaymentService
  • Features: General component features, no special treatment

@Repository:

  • Purpose: Marks classes responsible for data access
  • Layer: Data Access/Persistence layer
  • Responsibilities: Database operations, query execution, data mapping
  • Example: UserRepository, ProductRepository, OrderRepository
  • Features: Exception translation (persistence exceptions to Spring DataAccessException)

Both annotations:

  • Extend @Component: Automatically discovered by component scanning
  • Enable DI: Can be injected into other components
  • Singleton Scope: Default scope (one instance per container)
  • Transaction Support: Can participate in Spring's transaction management

Key differences:

  • Exception Handling: @Repository translates JPA/Hibernate exceptions to Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy
  • Semantic Clarity: Makes code intent clear to developers and tools
  • AOP Integration: @Repository integrates with Spring's data access exception translation
  • Testing: Different testing approaches (service vs data layer)

Additional stereotypes:

  • @Controller/@RestController: Web layer, HTTP request handling
  • @Component: Generic component when others don't fit
  • @Configuration: Configuration classes with @Bean methods

Best practices:

  • Use Specific Stereotypes: Prefer @Service and @Repository over @Component
  • Clear Separation: Keep business logic in services, data access in repositories
  • Single Responsibility: Each component should have one clear purpose
  • Dependency Injection: Use constructor injection for required dependencies
  • Transaction Boundaries: Apply @Transactional at service layer
  • Exception Handling: Handle business exceptions in services, data exceptions in repositories

Spring Boot's component scanning automatically detects these annotations when @SpringBootApplication is used.

Code Example
// Service layer - Business logic
@Service
@Transactional  // Service layer manages transactions
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final EmailService emailService;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository, 
                      EmailService emailService,
                      PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }
    
    public User registerUser(String email, String rawPassword, String name) {
        // Business logic: validate input
        if (userRepository.existsByEmail(email)) {
            throw new UserAlreadyExistsException("Email already registered");
        }
        
        // Business logic: encode password
        String encodedPassword = passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword);
        
        // Business logic: create user
        User user = new User(email, encodedPassword, name);
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);
        
        // Business logic: send welcome email
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(saved);
        
        return saved;
    }
    
    public User authenticateUser(String email, String password) {
        User user = userRepository.findByEmail(email)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("User not found"));
        
        // Business logic: verify password
        if (!passwordEncoder.matches(password, user.getPassword())) {
            throw new InvalidCredentialsException("Invalid password");
        }
        
        return user;
    }
    
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)  // Read-only transaction for queries
    public List<User> searchUsers(String query) {
        // Business logic: search implementation
        return userRepository.findByNameContainingOrEmailContaining(query, query);
    }
}

// Repository layer - Data access
@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    
    // Spring Data JPA generates implementation

    boolean existsByEmail(String email);
    
    List<User> findByNameContainingOrEmailContaining(String name, String email);
    
    // Custom query
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.createdAt > :since")
    List<User> findRecentUsers(@Param("since") LocalDateTime since);
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/register")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> register(@Valid @RequestBody RegisterRequest request) {
        User user = userService.registerUser(request.getEmail(), request.getPassword(), request.getName());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user));
    }
    
    @PostMapping("/login")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> login(@RequestBody LoginRequest request) {
        User user = userService.authenticateUser(request.getEmail(), request.getPassword());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user));
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<UserDto> search(@RequestParam String query) {
        return userService.searchUsers(query).stream()
            .map(this::convertToDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
    
    private UserDto convertToDto(User user) {
        return new UserDto(user.getId(), user.getEmail(), user.getName());
    }
}

// Custom repository implementation (rarely needed)
@Repository
public class CustomUserRepositoryImpl implements CustomUserRepository {
    
    @PersistenceContext
    private EntityManager entityManager;
    
    @Override
    public List<User> findUsersWithComplexCriteria(String criteria) {
        // Custom JPA Criteria API implementation
        CriteriaBuilder cb = entityManager.getCriteriaBuilder();
        CriteriaQuery<User> query = cb.createQuery(User.class);
        Root<User> user = query.from(User.class);
        
        // Complex query logic
        query.where(cb.and(
            cb.like(user.get("name"), "%" + criteria + "%"),
            cb.isNotNull(user.get("email"))
        ));
        
        return entityManager.createQuery(query).getResultList();
    }
}

annotations

@SpringBootApplication?

Quick Answer

3 annotations in 1.

Detailed Explanation

The @SpringBootApplication annotation is a meta-annotation that serves as a convenient shortcut for three essential Spring Framework annotations. It encapsulates the core configuration needed to bootstrap a Spring Boot application, making it the single most important annotation in any Spring Boot project.

The three annotations it combines:

  1. @Configuration: Marks the class as a source of bean definitions for the Spring IoC container. Methods annotated with @Bean within this class will be processed to create Spring-managed beans.

  2. @EnableAutoConfiguration: Enables Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism. This tells Spring Boot to automatically configure beans based on classpath dependencies, property settings, and other factors. It's the 'magic' behind Spring Boot's convention-over-configuration approach.

  3. @ComponentScan: Instructs Spring to scan for components (classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.) in the current package and all sub-packages. This enables automatic discovery and registration of Spring beans.

Key features and capabilities:

  • Component Discovery: Automatically finds and registers beans in the annotated class's package and sub-packages
  • Auto-Configuration: Applies intelligent defaults based on classpath contents (e.g., configures DataSource if JDBC driver is present)
  • Bean Management: Enables the creation and management of Spring beans through dependency injection
  • Configuration Customization: Allows overriding of auto-configuration through properties and custom bean definitions

Advanced configuration options:

  • scanBasePackages: Specify custom packages to scan for components
  • exclude: Exclude specific auto-configuration classes
  • excludeName: Exclude beans by name
  • proxyBeanMethods: Control proxying of @Bean methods (default true for consistency)

Use cases and best practices:

  • Standard Applications: Use as-is for typical Spring Boot applications
  • Multi-Module Projects: Specify scanBasePackages to control component scanning scope
  • Custom Auto-Configuration: Exclude unwanted auto-configurations when providing custom implementations
  • Performance Tuning: Use proxyBeanMethods = false in configuration classes that don't need method interception

The annotation should typically be placed on the main application class (the one containing the main method), and Spring Boot uses this as the starting point for component scanning and auto-configuration.

Code Example
// Basic usage - most common approach
@SpringBootApplication
public class MySpringBootApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MySpringBootApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// Advanced configuration with custom scanning and exclusions
@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.example.common"},
    exclude = {
        DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class,  // Don't auto-configure database
        SecurityAutoConfiguration.class     // Don't auto-configure security
    },
    excludeName = {"myCustomBean"},  // Exclude specific bean by name
    proxyBeanMethods = false  // Disable @Bean method proxying for performance
)
public class AdvancedSpringBootApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Custom SpringApplication configuration
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(AdvancedSpringBootApplication.class);
        app.setBannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF);  // Disable startup banner
        app.setWebApplicationType(WebApplicationType.NONE);  // Non-web application
        app.setAdditionalProfiles("development");  // Set active profiles
        app.run(args);
    }
    
    // Custom bean definition
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyServiceImpl();
    }
}

// Multi-module project configuration
@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {
        "com.example.myapp.web",
        "com.example.myapp.service", 
        "com.example.myapp.repository",
        "com.example.common"  // Shared module
    }
)
public class MultiModuleApplication {
    // Scans components across multiple modules
}

// Manual equivalent (what @SpringBootApplication does automatically)
@Configuration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan
public class ManualConfiguration {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ManualConfiguration.class, args);
    }
}

CloudConfig

application.properties vs application.yml?

Quick Answer

Two standard ways to define configuration. YAML is hierarchical and cleaner to read.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot supports multiple configuration formats, with application.properties and application.yml being the most common. Each format has distinct advantages and use cases, allowing developers to choose based on their project's complexity and team preferences.

application.properties:

  • Format: Key-value pairs separated by equals signs or colons
  • Advantages: Simple, familiar syntax; safe for properties with special characters; good for simple configurations
  • Limitations: No hierarchical structure; repetition for nested properties; harder to read for complex configs
  • Best For: Simple applications, CI/CD pipelines, environment variables

application.yml (YAML):

  • Format: Hierarchical structure using indentation and colons
  • Advantages: Clean, readable structure; supports complex nested configurations; less repetition; better for documentation
  • Limitations: Sensitive to indentation; can be error-prone with spacing; not ideal for simple key-value pairs
  • Best For: Complex configurations, microservices, team collaboration

Key Differences:

  • Syntax: Properties uses dots for nesting (server.port), YAML uses indentation
  • Readability: YAML wins for complex structures, Properties for simple ones
  • Error Handling: YAML is stricter about formatting, Properties more forgiving
  • Merging: Both support profile-specific files, but YAML handles complex merges better
  • Environment Variables: Both work, but Properties syntax is more compatible

When to Use Each:

  • Properties: Small applications, legacy systems, DevOps-heavy environments
  • YAML: Large applications, microservices, configurations with deep nesting
  • Mixed: Some teams use both - Properties for simple values, YAML for complex structures

Advanced Features:

  • Profile-Specific: application-dev.properties/yml, application-prod.properties/yml
  • Multi-Document YAML: Use --- to separate multiple documents in one file
  • References: Both support ${property.name} and ${property.name:default} syntax
  • Lists: YAML supports native lists, Properties uses indexed syntax

Best Practices:

  • Consistency: Choose one format per project
  • Documentation: Use comments in both formats
  • Validation: Use @ConfigurationProperties with validation
  • Environment Separation: Use profiles for different environments
  • Secrets: Never store sensitive data in config files

Both formats are equally powerful and auto-detected by Spring Boot.

Code Example
# application.properties - Simple, flat structure
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api
spring.application.name=my-app
spring.profiles.active=dev

# Database configuration
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop

# Logging
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=INFO

# Custom properties
app.name=My Application
app.version=1.0.0
app.features.enabled=true

# Lists (indexed)
app.supported-locales[0]=en
app.supported-locales[1]=fr
app.supported-locales[2]=es

# Maps (flattened)
app.security.roles.admin=ADMIN
app.security.roles.user=USER

# application.yml - Hierarchical structure
server:
  port: 8080
  servlet:
    context-path: /api

spring:
  application:
    name: my-app
  profiles:
    active: dev
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
    username: sa
    password: ""
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop

logging:
  level:
    com.example: DEBUG
    org.springframework.web: INFO

app:
  name: My Application
  version: 1.0.0
  features:
    enabled: true
  supported-locales:
    - en
    - fr
    - es
  security:
    roles:
      admin: ADMIN
      user: USER

# Multi-document YAML (separated by ---)
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: dev

app:
  database: h2

---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod

app:
  database: postgresql
