SecurityUser

UserDetailsService interface?

Quick Answer

The core interface used to load user-specific data.

Detailed Explanation

UserDetailsService is a fundamental interface in Spring Security that provides the mechanism for loading user-specific data during the authentication process. It serves as the bridge between Spring Security's authentication framework and your application's user data store, whether it's a database, LDAP, or any other user repository.

Core Responsibility:

  • User Loading: Retrieve user details by username during authentication
  • Data Provision: Supply Spring Security with user credentials and authorities
  • Integration Point: Connects authentication with user data storage

Method Contract:

  • loadUserByUsername(String username): Returns UserDetails or throws UsernameNotFoundException
  • Exception Handling: Must throw exception when user not found
  • Thread Safety: Implementation must be thread-safe

UserDetails Interface:

  • Credentials: Password for authentication
  • Authorities: Granted permissions/roles
  • Account Status: Enabled, locked, expired flags
  • Additional Data: Custom user information

Common Implementations:

  • Database: JPA/Hibernate with custom repository
  • In-Memory: For testing and simple applications
  • LDAP: Directory server integration
  • Custom: Proprietary user stores

Integration with Authentication:

  • DaoAuthenticationProvider: Uses UserDetailsService for authentication
  • Password Encoding: Handles password verification
  • User Cache: Optional caching for performance
  • Concurrent Sessions: Session management integration

Best Practices:

  • Performance: Implement caching for production
  • Security: Never log sensitive user data
  • Validation: Validate input parameters
  • Error Handling: Use specific exception types
  • Testing: Mock implementations for unit tests

Use Cases:

  • Web Applications: Standard username/password authentication
  • APIs: Token-based authentication with user lookup
  • Enterprise: LDAP/Active Directory integration
  • Microservices: Centralized user management

UserDetailsService is essential for implementing custom authentication logic in Spring Security applications.

Code Example
// Custom UserDetailsService implementation
@Service
public class CustomUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    public CustomUserDetailsService(UserRepository userRepository, PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.userRepository = passwordEncoder;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }
    
    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) throws UsernameNotFoundException {
        // Load user from database
        User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found: " + username));
        
        // Convert to Spring Security UserDetails
        return org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User.builder()
            .username(user.getUsername())
            .password(user.getPassword())
            .disabled(!user.isEnabled())
            .accountExpired(user.isAccountExpired())
            .accountLocked(user.isAccountLocked())
            .credentialsExpired(user.isCredentialsExpired())
            .authorities(getAuthorities(user.getRoles()))
            .build();
    }
    
    private Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities(Set<Role> roles) {
        return roles.stream()
            .map(role -> new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + role.getName()))
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

// User entity
@Entity
public class User {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(unique = true, nullable = false)
    private String username;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String password;
    
    @Column(unique = true, nullable = false)
    private String email;
    
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private boolean accountExpired = false;
    private boolean accountLocked = false;
    private boolean credentialsExpired = false;
    
    @ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
    private Set<Role> roles = new HashSet<>();
    
    // getters, setters, constructors
}

// Role entity
@Entity
public class Role {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(unique = true, nullable = false)
    private String name; // ADMIN, USER, etc.
    
    // getters, setters
}

// Repository
@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByUsername(String username);
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
    boolean existsByUsername(String username);
}

// Security configuration
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {
    
    private final CustomUserDetailsService userDetailsService;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    public SecurityConfig(CustomUserDetailsService userDetailsService, PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.userDetailsService = userDetailsService;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/", "/login", "/register").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/user/**").hasAnyRole("USER", "ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .formLogin(form -> form
                .loginPage("/login")
                .defaultSuccessUrl("/dashboard")
                .failureUrl("/login?error")
                .permitAll()
            )
            .logout(logout -> logout
                .logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout")
                .permitAll()
            )
            .userDetailsService(userDetailsService); // Register custom service
        
        return http.build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration config) throws Exception {
        return config.getAuthenticationManager();
    }
}

// User service for registration
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final RoleRepository roleRepository;
    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;
    
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository, RoleRepository roleRepository, PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.roleRepository = roleRepository;
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public User registerUser(String username, String email, String rawPassword) {
        if (userRepository.existsByUsername(username)) {
            throw new UserAlreadyExistsException("Username already exists");
        }
        
        User user = new User();
        user.setUsername(username);
        user.setEmail(email);
        user.setPassword(passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword));
        
        // Assign default role
        Role userRole = roleRepository.findByName("USER")
            .orElseThrow(() -> new RoleNotFoundException("Default role not found"));
        user.getRoles().add(userRole);
        
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
    
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) {
        return userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(username);
    }
}

// In-memory UserDetailsService for testing
@Configuration
@Profile("test")
public class TestSecurityConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public UserDetailsService userDetailsService() {
        UserDetails admin = User.builder()
            .username("admin")
            .password(passwordEncoder().encode("admin"))
            .roles("ADMIN")
            .build();
        
        UserDetails user = User.builder()
            .username("user")
            .password(passwordEncoder().encode("user"))
            .roles("USER")
            .build();
        
        return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(admin, user);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

// Testing UserDetailsService
@SpringBootTest
public class UserDetailsServiceTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserDetailsService userDetailsService;
    
    @Test
    void shouldLoadUserByUsername() {
        // When
        UserDetails userDetails = userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername("testuser");
        
        // Then
        assertThat(userDetails.getUsername()).isEqualTo("testuser");
        assertThat(userDetails.getAuthorities())
            .extracting(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority)
            .contains("ROLE_USER");
        assertThat(userDetails.isEnabled()).isTrue();
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldThrowExceptionForUnknownUser() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername("unknown"))
            .isInstanceOf(UsernameNotFoundException.class)
            .hasMessageContaining("unknown");
    }
}

// Controller using authentication
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/user")
public class UserController {
    
    @GetMapping("/profile")
    public ResponseEntity<UserProfile> getProfile(@AuthenticationPrincipal UserDetails userDetails) {
        // Get current authenticated user
        String username = userDetails.getUsername();
        User user = userService.findByUsername(username);
        
        UserProfile profile = new UserProfile();
        profile.setUsername(user.getUsername());
        profile.setEmail(user.getEmail());
        profile.setRoles(user.getRoles().stream()
            .map(Role::getName)
            .collect(Collectors.toSet()));
        
        return ResponseEntity.ok(profile);
    }
    
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    @GetMapping("/admin/users")
    public List<UserSummary> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers().stream()
            .map(user -> new UserSummary(user.getUsername(), user.getEmail()))
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

// DTOs
public class UserProfile {
    private String username;
    private String email;
    private Set<String> roles;
    // getters/setters
}

public class UserSummary {
    private String username;
    private String email;
    // getters/setters
}

// Custom UserDetails for additional data
public class CustomUserDetails extends org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User {
    
    private final Long userId;
    private final String email;
    
    public CustomUserDetails(String username, String password, 
                           Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> authorities,
                           Long userId, String email) {
        super(username, password, authorities);
        this.userId = userId;
        this.email = email;
    }
    
    public Long getUserId() { return userId; }
    public String getEmail() { return email; }
}

// Updated UserDetailsService
@Service
public class CustomUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
    
    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) throws UsernameNotFoundException {
        User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found"));
        
        return new CustomUserDetails(
            user.getUsername(),
            user.getPassword(),
            getAuthorities(user.getRoles()),
            user.getId(),
            user.getEmail()
        );
    }
}

The UserDetailsService interface is crucial for integrating Spring Security with custom user data stores, providing the foundation for authentication and authorization in Spring Boot applications.

basics

Banner customization?

Quick Answer

Add banner.txt to resources.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot displays an ASCII art banner on startup. You can customize it by placing a banner.txt file in src/main/resources/ or configure it programmatically.

Banner features:

  • Text file: Place banner.txt in resources
  • Variables: Use ${variable} for dynamic content
  • Colors: ANSI color codes for colored output
  • Images: Convert images to ASCII art
  • Programmatic: Create custom banner programmatically

Variables available:

  • ${application.version}
  • ${application.formatted-version}
  • ${spring-boot.version}
  • ${spring-boot.formatted-version}
  • And any property from Environment

Best practices:

  • Keep banners reasonable in size
  • Include version information
  • Use colors sparingly for readability
  • Consider company branding
  • Can be disabled for production
Code Example
  ____             _                ____  ____  _____
 |  _ \  ___   ___| |_ ___ _ __ ___|  _ \|  _ \| ____|
 | | | |/ _ \ / __| __/ _ \ '__/ __| |_) | |_) |  _|
 | |_| | (_) | (__| ||  __/ |  \__ \  __/|  _ <| |___
 |____/  \___/ \___|\__\___|_|  |___/_|   |_| \_\_____|

 :: My Spring Boot Application ::   (v${application.version})

Colored banner:

${AnsiColor.BRIGHT_RED}
  ____             _                ____  ____  _____
 |  _ \  ___   ___| |_ ___ _ __ ___|  _ \|  _ \| ____|
 | | | |/ _ \ / __| __/ _ \ '__/ __| |_) | |_) |  _|
 | |_| | (_) | (__| ||  __/ |  \__ \  __/|  _ <| |___
 |____/  \___/ \___|\__\___|_|  |___/_|   |_| \_\_____|

 :: My Spring Boot Application ::   (v${application.version})
${AnsiColor.RESET}

Programmatic banner:

@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Application.class);
        app.setBanner(new Banner() {
            @Override
            public void printBanner(Environment environment, Class<?> sourceClass, PrintStream out) {
                out.println("=====================================");
                out.println("  Custom Spring Boot Application");
                out.println("  Version: " + environment.getProperty("app.version"));
                out.println("=====================================");
            }
        });
        app.run(args);
    }
}

Configuration in application.properties:

# Banner configuration
spring.banner.location=classpath:banner.txt
spring.banner.charset=UTF-8

# Disable banner
# spring.banner.enabled=false

# Custom application properties for banner
app.version=1.0.0
app.name=My App

Using Spring Boot CLI for banner generation:

echo "My App" | spring banner

Banner customization adds a personal touch to Spring Boot applications and can include useful information like version numbers and environment details.

servers

Default Embedded Server?

Quick Answer

Tomcat.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot includes an embedded web server within the application JAR, eliminating the need for external servlet containers. Tomcat is the default embedded server, but Jetty and Undertow are also supported alternatives.

Key benefits of embedded servers:

  • Simplified Deployment: No need to install/configure external servers
  • Portability: Application is self-contained and runnable anywhere Java is installed
  • Development Speed: Instant startup without server management
  • Cloud-Native: Perfect for containerized deployments (Docker, Kubernetes)
  • Microservices: Each service can run independently with its own server

Supported embedded servers:

  • Tomcat (default): Mature, production-ready servlet container with excellent Spring integration
  • Jetty: Lightweight, high-performance alternative with lower memory footprint
  • Undertow: Modern, non-blocking server from JBoss with excellent performance

All embedded servers support:

  • HTTP/HTTPS
  • WebSocket
  • Servlet API
  • Static resource serving
  • Request compression
  • Access logging

Configuration is done through application.properties and can be customized per environment.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml - Tomcat is included by default with spring-boot-starter-web -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <!-- Includes spring-boot-starter-tomcat -->
</dependency>

<!-- To use Jetty instead of Tomcat -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- To use Undertow instead of Tomcat -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configuration in application.properties:

# Server configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# Tomcat specific settings
server.tomcat.max-http-header-size=8192
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=20s
server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout=20s

# SSL configuration
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.jks
server.ssl.key-store-password=password
server.ssl.key-password=password
server.ssl.enabled=true

# Compression
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=text/html,text/xml,text/plain,text/css,text/javascript,application/javascript,application/json
server.compression.min-response-size=1024

# Access logging
server.tomcat.accesslog.enabled=true
server.tomcat.accesslog.pattern=%h %l %u %t "%r" %s %b
server.tomcat.accesslog.directory=logs
server.tomcat.accesslog.prefix=access_log
server.tomcat.accesslog.suffix=.log

Jetty-specific configuration:

# Jetty settings
server.jetty.max-http-header-size=8192
server.jetty.acceptors=2
server.jetty.selectors=4

Undertow-specific configuration:

# Undertow settings
server.undertow.max-http-header-size=8192
server.undertow.io-threads=4
server.undertow.worker-threads=64

Custom server configuration:

@Configuration
public class ServerConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> tomcatCustomizer() {
        return factory -> {
            factory.addConnectorCustomizers(connector -> {
                connector.setProperty("maxHttpHeaderSize", "8192");
                connector.setProperty("maxSwallowSize", "2097152"); // 2MB
            });
        };
    }
    
    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<JettyServletWebServerFactory> jettyCustomizer() {
        return factory -> {
            factory.setPort(8080);
            factory.setContextPath("/api");
        };
    }
}

Running the application:

# Development
mvn spring-boot:run

# Production
java -jar target/app.jar --server.port=8443 --server.ssl.enabled=true

Embedded servers make Spring Boot applications truly self-contained, simplifying deployment and scaling in modern architectures.

DataQuery

Derived Query Methods?

Quick Answer

Creating queries just by naming the method interface correctly.

Detailed Explanation

Derived query methods in Spring Data JPA provide a powerful way to create database queries by simply following naming conventions in repository method names. Spring Data parses these method names and automatically generates the appropriate SQL queries, eliminating the need for manual query writing in most cases.

Naming Convention Rules:

  • Keywords: findBy, readBy, queryBy, countBy, getBy, existsBy
  • Property Names: Exact property names from the entity
  • Operators: And, Or, Is, Equals, Between, LessThan, GreaterThan, etc.
  • Modifiers: IgnoreCase, AllIgnoreCase, OrderBy, Asc, Desc
  • Collections: In, NotIn, Contains, StartingWith, EndingWith

Supported Keywords:

  • Comparison: Equals, IsNot, IsNull, IsNotNull
  • Range: Between, LessThan, LessThanEqual, GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqual
  • String: Like, NotLike, StartingWith, EndingWith, Containing, IgnoreCase
  • Collection: In, NotIn, IsEmpty, IsNotEmpty
  • Boolean: IsTrue, IsFalse
  • Temporal: Before, After, IsBetween

Return Types:

  • Single Entity: Optional, T (throws exception if not found)
  • Multiple Entities: List, Iterable, Stream
  • Paged Results: Page, Slice
  • Count: long, boolean (exists)

Limitations:

  • Complexity: Very complex queries become hard to read
  • Performance: May generate suboptimal SQL
  • Maintenance: Method names can become very long
  • Refactoring: Entity property changes break method names

Best Practices:

  • Simple Queries: Use derived methods for straightforward queries
  • Complex Queries: Use @Query for complex logic
  • Naming: Keep method names readable and descriptive
  • Testing: Test generated queries for performance
  • Documentation: Document complex derived methods

Use Cases:

  • Basic CRUD: Standard finder methods
  • Search: Filtering by multiple criteria
  • Sorting: Ordered result sets
  • Pagination: Large dataset handling
  • Existence Checks: Validation logic

Derived query methods offer a balance between convenience and control in data access.

Code Example
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
public class Product {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private BigDecimal price;
    
    @Column
    private String category;
    
    @Column
    private boolean active = true;
    
    @Column
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
    
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private ProductStatus status = ProductStatus.AVAILABLE;
    
    // getters, setters, constructors
}

@Repository
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    
    // Basic finders
    List<Product> findByCategory(String category);
    Optional<Product> findByName(String name);
    List<Product> findByActiveTrue();
    
    // Comparison operators
    List<Product> findByPriceGreaterThan(BigDecimal price);
    List<Product> findByPriceBetween(BigDecimal min, BigDecimal max);
    List<Product> findByCreatedAtAfter(LocalDateTime date);
    
    // String operations
    List<Product> findByNameContaining(String keyword);
    List<Product> findByNameStartingWith(String prefix);
    List<Product> findByNameIgnoreCase(String name);
    
    // Multiple conditions
    List<Product> findByCategoryAndActive(String category, boolean active);
    List<Product> findByCategoryOrName(String category, String name);
    List<Product> findByPriceLessThanAndCategory(BigDecimal price, String category);
    
    // Collection conditions
    List<Product> findByCategoryIn(List<String> categories);
    List<Product> findByStatusNot(ProductStatus status);
    
    // Ordering
    List<Product> findByCategoryOrderByPriceAsc(String category);
    List<Product> findByActiveTrueOrderByCreatedAtDesc();
    
    // Exists and count
    boolean existsByNameAndCategory(String name, String category);
    long countByCategory(String category);
    long countByActiveTrue();
    
    // Complex queries with multiple conditions
    List<Product> findByCategoryAndPriceBetweenAndActiveTrue(
        String category, BigDecimal minPrice, BigDecimal maxPrice);
    
    // Limiting results
    Product findFirstByCategoryOrderByPriceDesc(String category);
    List<Product> findTop5ByCategoryOrderByCreatedAtDesc(String category);
    
    // Distinct results
    List<String> findDistinctCategoryByActiveTrue();
    
    // Nested properties (if Product has a Brand entity)
    // List<Product> findByBrandName(String brandName);
}

// Usage in service
@Service
public class ProductService {
    
    private final ProductRepository productRepository;
    
    public ProductService(ProductRepository productRepository) {
        this.productRepository = productRepository;
    }
    
    public List<Product> searchProducts(String category, BigDecimal minPrice, BigDecimal maxPrice) {
        if (category != null && minPrice != null && maxPrice != null) {
            return productRepository.findByCategoryAndPriceBetweenAndActiveTrue(
                category, minPrice, maxPrice);
        } else if (category != null) {
            return productRepository.findByCategory(category);
        } else if (minPrice != null && maxPrice != null) {
            return productRepository.findByPriceBetween(minPrice, maxPrice);
        } else {
            return productRepository.findByActiveTrue();
        }
    }
    
    public List<Product> getFeaturedProducts(String category) {
        return productRepository.findTop5ByCategoryOrderByCreatedAtDesc(category);
    }
    
    public boolean isProductNameAvailable(String name, String category) {
        return !productRepository.existsByNameAndCategory(name, category);
    }
    
    public Page<Product> getProductsPaged(String category, Pageable pageable) {
        if (category != null) {
            return productRepository.findByCategory(category, pageable);
        }
        return productRepository.findAll(pageable);
    }
}

// Controller with pagination and sorting
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
public class ProductController {
    
    private final ProductService productService;
    
    public ProductController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<Page<Product>> getProducts(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String category,
            @RequestParam(required = false) BigDecimal minPrice,
            @RequestParam(required = false) BigDecimal maxPrice,
            @PageableDefault(sort = "createdAt", direction = Sort.Direction.DESC) Pageable pageable) {
        
        Page<Product> products;
        if (category != null || minPrice != null || maxPrice != null) {
            List<Product> filtered = productService.searchProducts(category, minPrice, maxPrice);
            products = new PageImpl<>(filtered, pageable, filtered.size());
        } else {
            products = productService.getProductsPaged(category, pageable);
        }
        
        return ResponseEntity.ok(products);
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/featured/{category}")
    public List<Product> getFeaturedProducts(@PathVariable String category) {
        return productService.getFeaturedProducts(category);
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/categories")
    public List<String> getCategories() {
        return productRepository.findDistinctCategoryByActiveTrue();
    }
}

// Testing derived query methods
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase
public class ProductRepositoryTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private ProductRepository productRepository;
    
    @Test
    void shouldFindProductsByCategory() {
        // Given
        Product laptop = createProduct("Laptop", "Electronics", new BigDecimal("999.99"));
        Product book = createProduct("Book", "Education", new BigDecimal("29.99"));
        productRepository.saveAll(Arrays.asList(laptop, book));
        
        // When
        List<Product> electronics = productRepository.findByCategory("Electronics");
        
        // Then
        assertThat(electronics).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(electronics.get(0).getName()).isEqualTo("Laptop");
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldFindProductsInPriceRange() {
        // Given
        Product cheap = createProduct("Cheap Item", "Misc", new BigDecimal("10.00"));
        Product expensive = createProduct("Expensive Item", "Misc", new BigDecimal("100.00"));
        productRepository.saveAll(Arrays.asList(cheap, expensive));
        
        // When
        List<Product> midRange = productRepository.findByPriceBetween(
            new BigDecimal("15.00"), new BigDecimal("50.00"));
        
        // Then
        assertThat(midRange).isEmpty(); // No products in this range
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldCountProductsByCategory() {
        // Given
        productRepository.save(createProduct("Item 1", "Test", new BigDecimal("1.00")));
        productRepository.save(createProduct("Item 2", "Test", new BigDecimal("2.00")));
        
        // When
        long count = productRepository.countByCategory("Test");
        
        // Then
        assertThat(count).isEqualTo(2);
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldCheckProductExistence() {
        // Given
        productRepository.save(createProduct("Unique Name", "Test", new BigDecimal("1.00")));
        
        // When & Then
        assertThat(productRepository.existsByNameAndCategory("Unique Name", "Test")).isTrue();
        assertThat(productRepository.existsByNameAndCategory("Nonexistent", "Test")).isFalse();
    }
    
    private Product createProduct(String name, String category, BigDecimal price) {
        Product product = new Product();
        product.setName(name);
        product.setCategory(category);
        product.setPrice(price);
        product.setActive(true);
        return product;
    }
}

-- Generated SQL examples
-- findByCategory(String category)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = ?;

-- findByPriceBetween(BigDecimal min, BigDecimal max)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN ? AND ?;

-- findByCategoryAndActiveTrueOrderByPriceDesc(String category)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = ? AND active = true ORDER BY price DESC;

-- countByCategory(String category)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE category = ?;

-- existsByNameAndCategory(String name, String category)
SELECT CASE WHEN COUNT(*) > 0 THEN true ELSE false END FROM products WHERE name = ? AND category = ?;

// When derived queries become too complex, use @Query
@Repository
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    
    // Complex query using @Query
    @Query("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE " +
           "(:category IS NULL OR p.category = :category) AND " +
           "(:minPrice IS NULL OR p.price >= :minPrice) AND " +
           "(:maxPrice IS NULL OR p.price <= :maxPrice) AND " +
           "p.active = true")
    List<Product> findProductsWithFilters(
        @Param("category") String category,
        @Param("minPrice") BigDecimal minPrice,
        @Param("maxPrice") BigDecimal maxPrice);
    
    // Native query for complex operations
    @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE " +
           "MATCH(name, category) AGAINST(?1 IN NATURAL LANGUAGE MODE)", 
           nativeQuery = true)
    List<Product> searchFullText(String keyword);
}

Derived query methods provide a convenient way to create database queries without writing SQL or JPQL, but they should be used judiciously. For complex queries, @Query annotations offer more control and better performance.

controllers

Difference between @Controller and @RestController?

Quick Answer

@RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody.

Detailed Explanation

@Controller and @RestController are both stereotypes for Spring MVC controllers, but they serve different purposes in web application development:

@Controller:

  • Used for traditional Model-View-Controller (MVC) web applications
  • Methods typically return view names (Strings) that are resolved to HTML templates
  • Can return data objects, but they need @ResponseBody to serialize to JSON/XML
  • Suitable for server-side rendered applications using templating engines like Thymeleaf, JSP, or FreeMarker
  • Supports both data and view responses from the same controller

@RestController:

  • A specialized version of @Controller designed specifically for RESTful web services
  • Automatically applies @ResponseBody to all handler methods
  • All methods return data directly (serialized to JSON by default)
  • No view resolution occurs; responses are pure data
  • Ideal for building APIs that serve JSON/XML data to frontend applications or other services

Both annotations:

  • Are scanned by @ComponentScan
  • Can use @RequestMapping and its variants (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.)
  • Support dependency injection
  • Are singletons by default

The choice depends on your application's architecture:

  • Use @Controller for web apps with server-side rendering
  • Use @RestController for REST APIs and microservices

Spring Boot's auto-configuration sets up content negotiation and JSON serialization automatically when web starters are included.

Code Example
// Traditional MVC Controller - returns views
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserMvcController {
    
    @GetMapping("/list")
    public String listUsers(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("users", userService.getAllUsers());
        return "users/list";  // Returns view name (users/list.html)
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/api/list")
    @ResponseBody  // Explicitly marks for JSON response
    public List<User> getUsersApi() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();  // Returns JSON data
    }
}

// REST Controller - returns data only
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserRestController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserRestController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();  // Automatically JSON
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(user))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        return ResponseEntity.created(
            ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
                .toUri()
        ).body(user);
    }
}

// Data Transfer Object
public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank @Email
    private String email;
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    
    // getters and setters
}

In Thymeleaf template users/list.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html xmlns:th="http://www.thymeleaf.org">
<body>
    <h1>Users</h1>
    <ul>
        <li th:each="user : ${users}" th:text="${user.name}"></li>
    </ul>
</body>
</html>

The @RestController automatically configures Jackson for JSON serialization, while @Controller works with view resolvers for template rendering.

server

Does Spring Boot need an external web server?

Quick Answer

No, it typically uses an embedded server.

Detailed Explanation

Unlike traditional Java web applications that require deploying WAR files to external servlet containers like Tomcat, JBoss, or WebSphere, Spring Boot applications are self-contained and include an embedded web server within the application JAR. This fundamental shift in deployment model brings several advantages:

Embedded Servers:

  • Tomcat (default): Mature, feature-complete servlet container
  • Jetty: Lightweight, high-performance alternative
  • Undertow: Modern, non-blocking server from JBoss

Benefits:

  • Simplified Deployment: Single JAR file contains everything needed
  • Portability: No need to install/configure external server
  • Consistency: Same server in development, testing, and production
  • Cloud-Native: Perfect for containerization (Docker) and microservices
  • Fast Startup: No separate server startup time

Configuration:

  • Default port: 8080 (configurable via server.port)
  • Context path: / (configurable via server.servlet.context-path)
  • Server-specific properties available for each embedded server

Switching Servers:
You can easily switch between embedded servers by excluding the default and including the desired one in your dependencies.

Production Considerations:
While embedded servers are great for most applications, some organizations prefer external servers for:

  • Centralized server management
  • Advanced server features (clustering, session replication)
  • Legacy deployment requirements

In such cases, you can still build traditional WAR files with Spring Boot.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml - Default Tomcat (included with spring-boot-starter-web) -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Switching to Jetty:

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Switching to Undertow:

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Configuration in application.properties:

# Server port and context
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/myapp

# Tomcat-specific settings
server.tomcat.max-http-header-size=8192
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=20s

# SSL configuration
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.p12
server.ssl.key-store-password=changeit
server.ssl.keyStoreType=PKCS12

# Compression
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=text/html,text/xml,text/plain,text/css,text/javascript,application/javascript,application/json

Running the application:

# Development
mvn spring-boot:run

# Production
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

# With custom port
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar --server.port=9090

For external server deployment (WAR):

<!-- pom.xml -->
<packaging>war</packaging>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>  <!-- Provided by external server -->
</dependency>

@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp extends SpringBootServletInitializer {
    
    @Override
    protected SpringApplicationBuilder configure(SpringApplicationBuilder builder) {
        return builder.sources(MyApp.class);
    }
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

The embedded server approach has become the standard for Spring Boot applications, especially in microservices and cloud-native architectures.

basics

Embedded Server?

Quick Answer

Tomcat/Jetty inside.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot applications include an embedded web server within the application JAR, eliminating the need for external servlet containers and enabling self-contained deployment. This is a revolutionary feature that simplifies deployment and enables modern application architectures.

Key benefits of embedded servers:

  • Self-Contained Deployment: Applications are packaged with everything needed to run
  • Simplified Operations: No need to install/configure external servers
  • Portability: Run anywhere Java is installed
  • Development Speed: Instant startup without server management overhead
  • Cloud-Native: Perfect for containers, serverless, and microservices
  • Version Consistency: Server version is tied to application dependencies
  • Configuration Control: Full control over server configuration through properties

Supported embedded servers:

  • Tomcat (default): Mature, production-ready servlet container with excellent Spring integration
  • Jetty: Lightweight, high-performance alternative with lower memory footprint
  • Undertow: Modern, non-blocking server from JBoss with excellent performance for high-concurrency scenarios

All embedded servers support:

  • HTTP/HTTPS: Standard web protocols
  • WebSocket: Real-time communication
  • Servlet API: Standard Java web API
  • Static Resources: Serving CSS, JS, images
  • Request Compression: GZIP compression for responses
  • Access Logging: Request logging capabilities
  • SSL/TLS: Secure connections

Configuration is done through application.properties/application.yml and can be customized per environment. Spring Boot provides sensible defaults that work for most applications.

Embedded servers vs Traditional deployment:

  • Embedded: JAR contains server, single artifact, simple deployment
  • Traditional: WAR deployed to external Tomcat/WebLogic, separate server management

Best practices:

  • Use Default Tomcat: Unless you have specific requirements
  • Configure Appropriately: Tune thread pools, connection limits for production
  • Enable SSL: Configure HTTPS for production deployments
  • Monitor Resources: Use actuator endpoints to monitor server health
  • Log Access: Enable access logging for production troubleshooting
  • Resource Limits: Configure appropriate memory and CPU limits

Spring Boot's embedded server approach enables the 'just run it' philosophy that makes Spring Boot so productive for developers.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml - Default Tomcat embedded server -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <!-- Includes spring-boot-starter-tomcat by default -->
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- To use Jetty instead of Tomcat -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- To use Undertow instead of Tomcat -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Configuration in application.properties:

# Server configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api
server.servlet.session.timeout=30m

# Tomcat specific settings (default)
server.tomcat.max-http-header-size=8192
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=20s
server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout=20s
server.tomcat.threads.max=200
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare=10

# SSL/TLS configuration

server.ssl.key-store-password=password

# Compression

# Access logging

# Static resources

# Error handling

server.error.include-binding-errors=always

Jetty-specific configuration:

server.jetty.selectors=4

server.jetty.threads.min=10

Undertow-specific configuration:

Custom server configuration:

@Configuration
public class ServerConfig {
    
    // Tomcat customizer
    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> tomcatCustomizer() {
        return factory -> {
            factory.setPort(8080);
            factory.setContextPath("/api");
            
            factory.addConnectorCustomizers(connector -> {
                connector.setProperty("maxHttpHeaderSize", "8192");
                connector.setProperty("maxSwallowSize", "2097152"); // 2MB
                connector.setProperty("connectionTimeout", "20000");
            });
            
            factory.addAdditionalTomcatConnectors(createHttpConnector());
        };
    }
    
    private Connector createHttpConnector() {
        Connector connector = new Connector("org.apache.coyote.http11.Http11NioProtocol");
        Http11NioProtocol protocol = (Http11NioProtocol) connector.getProtocolHandler();
        connector.setPort(8080);
        connector.setSecure(false);
        connector.setRedirectPort(8443);
        return connector;
    }
    
    // Jetty customizer
    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<JettyServletWebServerFactory> jettyCustomizer() {
        return factory -> {
            factory.setPort(8080);
            factory.setContextPath("/api");
        };
    }
    
    // Undertow customizer
    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<UndertowServletWebServerFactory> undertowCustomizer() {
        return factory -> {
            factory.setPort(8080);
            factory.setContextPath("/api");
        };
    }
}

Embedded servers make Spring Boot applications truly self-contained, simplifying deployment and scaling in modern architectures while maintaining full configuration control.

packaging

How do you package a Spring Boot application?

Quick Answer

As an executable JAR file.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot applications are typically packaged as executable JAR files (fat JARs) that contain all dependencies and an embedded server, enabling 'java -jar' execution. This self-contained approach simplifies deployment compared to traditional WAR files requiring external servlet containers.

Key concepts:

  • Fat JAR: A single JAR containing the application, all dependencies, and embedded server
  • Executable JAR: Can be run directly with java -jar without external dependencies
  • Embedded Server: Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow included within the JAR
  • Classpath: All resources and classes are packaged with proper classpath isolation

Packaging options:

  • JAR (default): Executable fat JAR for standalone deployment
  • WAR: Traditional web archive for external servlet containers
  • Docker: Containerized deployment with multi-stage builds

Build tools provide plugins for packaging:

  • Maven: spring-boot-maven-plugin
  • Gradle: org.springframework.boot plugin

The packaging process:

  1. Compile source code
  2. Resolve and copy dependencies
  3. Package classes and resources
  4. Create executable JAR with proper manifest
  5. Include embedded server and auto-configuration

Benefits of fat JARs:

  • Simplified deployment
  • No external server required
  • Consistent environments
  • Easy scaling and containerization
  • Version isolation
Code Example
<!-- pom.xml for JAR packaging -->
<project>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.1.0</version>
    </parent>
    
    <packaging>jar</packaging>  <!-- Default -->
    
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <executions>
                    <execution>
                        <goals>
                            <goal>repackage</goal>  <!-- Creates executable JAR -->
                        </goals>
                    </execution>
                </executions>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

# Build executable JAR
mvn clean package

# Run the application
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

# With custom JVM options
java -Xmx512m -Xms256m -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

# With Spring profiles
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# With system properties
java -Dserver.port=9090 -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

// build.gradle
plugins {
    id 'org.springframework.boot' version '3.1.0'
    id 'io.spring.dependency-management' version '1.1.0'
    id 'java'
}

bootJar {
    archiveFileName = 'myapp.jar'
    mainClass = 'com.example.MyApplication'
    
    // Custom manifest
    manifest {
        attributes 'Start-Class': 'com.example.MyApplication'
        attributes 'Implementation-Title': 'My Spring Boot App'
        attributes 'Implementation-Version': version
    }
    
    // Exclude files from JAR
    excludes = ['application-dev.properties']
}

# Gradle build
./gradlew bootJar

# Run
java -jar build/libs/myapp.jar

<!-- WAR packaging for external servers -->
<project>
    <packaging>war</packaging>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Provided scope for embedded server -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

// For WAR deployment

    @Override
    protected SpringApplicationBuilder configure(SpringApplicationBuilder builder) {
        return builder.sources(MyApplication.class);
    }

        SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args);
    }
}

# Dockerfile for containerized deployment

COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests

EXPOSE 8080

docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp

The fat JAR approach has revolutionized Java deployment, making Spring Boot applications portable and easy to deploy across different environments.

deployment

How do you run a Spring Boot application?

Quick Answer

You can run it as a standard Java application using the main method, or using the Maven/Gradle plugin.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot applications can be run in multiple ways, providing flexibility for different development and deployment scenarios. The embedded server approach makes Spring Boot applications uniquely portable and easy to deploy.

Development Options:

  • IDE Run: Run the main method directly from your IDE
  • Maven Plugin: mvn spring-boot:run - compiles and runs in one step
  • Gradle Plugin: gradle bootRun - similar to Maven
  • Java Command: java -jar app.jar after packaging

Production Deployment:

  • Standalone JAR: Self-contained executable JAR with embedded server
  • WAR Deployment: Traditional deployment to external servlet containers
  • Containerized: Docker containers for cloud-native deployments

Key Advantages:

  • No External Server Required: Embedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow
  • Single Artifact: One JAR contains everything needed
  • Cross-Platform: Runs anywhere Java is installed
  • Easy Scaling: Simple to deploy multiple instances

Configuration Options:

  • Command-line arguments: --server.port=9090
  • Environment variables: SERVER_PORT=9090
  • System properties: -Dserver.port=9090
  • External config files

Best Practices:

  • Use profiles for different environments (dev, test, prod)
  • Externalize configuration for production
  • Use health checks for container orchestration
  • Monitor with Spring Boot Actuator
Code Example
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

json

How is JSON handling done in Spring Boot?

Quick Answer

Using the Jackson library by default.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot uses Jackson as the default JSON processing library for serializing and deserializing JSON data in REST APIs. Jackson is automatically configured and provides seamless conversion between Java objects and JSON, with sensible defaults that work for most use cases.

Key features:

  • Automatic Configuration: Jackson's ObjectMapper is auto-configured with Spring Boot conventions
  • Content Negotiation: Automatically handles JSON requests/responses based on Content-Type/Accept headers
  • Type Safety: Strong typing with generic support
  • Customization: Extensive configuration options for serialization behavior
  • Performance: High-performance JSON processing with low memory footprint

Jackson handles:

  • Object to JSON serialization
  • JSON to Object deserialization
  • Date/time formatting
  • Null value handling
  • Field naming strategies
  • Custom serializers/deserializers

Spring Boot's auto-configuration sets up Jackson with:

  • CamelCase property naming
  • ISO date formatting
  • Ignoring null values in serialization
  • Proper handling of collections and maps

For complex scenarios, Jackson can be customized through configuration properties or by providing custom ObjectMapper beans.

Alternative JSON libraries (Gson, JSON-B) can be used by excluding Jackson and including the preferred library.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // Automatic JSON serialization
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
        // Returns: [{"id":1,"name":"John","email":"john@example.com"},...]
    }
    
    // Automatic JSON deserialization
    @PostMapping
    public User createUser(@RequestBody @Valid User user) {
        return userService.save(user);
        // Accepts: {"name":"John","email":"john@example.com"}
    }
    
    // ResponseEntity with JSON
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // Custom JSON response
    @GetMapping("/{id}/summary")
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> getUserSummary(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(user -> {
                Map<String, Object> summary = new HashMap<>();
                summary.put("id", user.getId());
                summary.put("name", user.getName());
                summary.put("active", user.isActive());
                summary.put("lastLogin", user.getLastLogin());
                return ResponseEntity.ok(summary);
            })
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}

// User entity with Jackson annotations
@Entity
public class User {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    
    @NotBlank
    @Email
    private String email;
    
    private boolean active = true;
    
    @JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss")
    private LocalDateTime lastLogin;
    
    @JsonIgnore  // Exclude from JSON
    private String password;
    
    // Constructors, getters, setters
    
    // Custom JSON view
    public static class SummaryView {}
    public static class DetailView extends SummaryView {}
}

// Custom serializer
public class UserSerializer extends JsonSerializer<User> {
    
    @Override
    public void serialize(User user, JsonGenerator gen, SerializerProvider serializers) 
            throws IOException {
        
        gen.writeStartObject();
        gen.writeNumberField("id", user.getId());
        gen.writeStringField("name", user.getName());
        gen.writeStringField("email", user.getEmail());
        gen.writeBooleanField("active", user.isActive());
        gen.writeStringField("status", user.isActive() ? "ACTIVE" : "INACTIVE");
        gen.writeEndObject();
    }
}

// Custom deserializer
public class UserDeserializer extends JsonDeserializer<User> {
    
    @Override
    public User deserialize(JsonParser p, DeserializationContext ctxt) 
            throws IOException, JsonProcessingException {
        
        ObjectMapper mapper = (ObjectMapper) p.getCodec();
        JsonNode node = mapper.readTree(p);
        
        User user = new User();
        user.setName(node.get("name").asText());
        user.setEmail(node.get("email").asText());
        if (node.has("active")) {
            user.setActive(node.get("active").asBoolean());
        }
        
        return user;
    }
}

// Configuration class for custom Jackson setup
@Configuration
public class JacksonConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        
        // Custom date format
        mapper.setDateFormat(new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"));
        
        // Ignore unknown properties
        mapper.configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);
        
        // Pretty printing for development
        mapper.enable(SerializationFeature.INDENT_OUTPUT);
        
        // Custom serializers
        SimpleModule module = new SimpleModule();
        module.addSerializer(User.class, new UserSerializer());
        module.addDeserializer(User.class, new UserDeserializer());
        mapper.registerModule(module);
        
        return mapper;
    }
    
    // Alternative: Configure existing ObjectMapper
    @Bean
    public Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer jsonCustomizer() {
        return builder -> {
            builder.dateFormat(new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));
            builder.failOnUnknownProperties(false);
            builder.indentOutput(true);
        };
    }
}

# Jackson configuration in application.properties
spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false
spring.jackson.serialization.indent-output=true
spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=false
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
spring.jackson.property-naming-strategy=SNAKE_CASE
spring.jackson.date-format=yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss

# Content negotiation
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.favor-parameter=true
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.parameter-name=mediaType
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.json=application/json
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.xml=application/xml

<!-- For XML support instead of JSON -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-dataformat-xml</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Or use Gson -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.code.gson</groupId>
    <artifactId>gson</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-json</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

// Using Gson with custom configuration
@Configuration
public class GsonConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public Gson gson() {
        return new GsonBuilder()
            .setDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd")
            .excludeFieldsWithoutExposeAnnotation()
            .create();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public GsonHttpMessageConverter gsonHttpMessageConverter(Gson gson) {
        GsonHttpMessageConverter converter = new GsonHttpMessageConverter();
        converter.setGson(gson);
        return converter;
    }
}

// Testing JSON serialization
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureJsonTesters
public class UserControllerTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;
    
    @Autowired
    private JacksonTester<User> json;
    
    @Test
    public void testCreateUser() throws Exception {
        User user = new User("John", "john@example.com");
        
        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/users")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .content(json.write(user).getJson()))
            .andExpect(status().isOk())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("John"));
    }
}

Jackson's integration with Spring Boot provides robust, high-performance JSON processing that handles most use cases out of the box, with extensive customization options available when needed.

SecurityBasics

How to disable Security for a specific path?

Quick Answer

By configuring the SecurityFilterChain bean.

Detailed Explanation

Configuring selective security in Spring Boot involves creating a custom SecurityFilterChain bean that defines which paths require authentication and which are publicly accessible. This approach provides fine-grained control over application security while maintaining protection for sensitive endpoints.

SecurityFilterChain Configuration:

  • HttpSecurity: Main configuration class for web security
  • Authorization Rules: Define access patterns using request matchers
  • Permit All: Allow unrestricted access to specified paths
  • Authenticated: Require authentication for protected paths
  • Role-Based: Restrict access based on user roles/authorities

Common Public Endpoints:

  • Health Checks: /actuator/health for monitoring systems
  • Info Endpoints: /actuator/info for application metadata
  • Static Resources: CSS, JS, images for web applications
  • Login/Logout: Authentication-related pages
  • API Documentation: Swagger/OpenAPI endpoints
  • Public APIs: Endpoints that don't require authentication

Security Best Practices:

  • Principle of Least Privilege: Only expose what's necessary
  • Layered Security: Combine URL patterns with method-level security
  • CSRF Protection: Keep enabled for state-changing operations
  • HTTPS: Always use in production
  • Security Headers: Configure appropriate headers

Configuration Approaches:

  • Method-Based: Using @PreAuthorize on controller methods
  • Global Configuration: SecurityFilterChain for URL patterns
  • Combined: Both approaches for comprehensive security

Common Patterns:

  • Permit Static Resources: CSS, JS, images
  • Allow Health Checks: For load balancers and monitoring
  • Public Registration: User signup endpoints
  • API Documentation: Development and testing access

The configuration ensures that sensitive operations remain protected while allowing legitimate public access.

Code Example
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                // Public endpoints - no authentication required
                .requestMatchers("/", "/home", "/login", "/register").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/css/**", "/js/**", "/images/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health", "/actuator/info").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/swagger-ui/**", "/v3/api-docs/**").permitAll()
                
                // Admin endpoints - require ADMIN role
                .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")
                
                // All other requests require authentication
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .formLogin(form -> form
                .loginPage("/login")
                .defaultSuccessUrl("/dashboard")
                .permitAll()
            )
            .logout(logout -> logout
                .logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout")
                .permitAll()
            )
            // Enable CSRF protection (default)
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf
                .ignoringRequestMatchers("/api/public/**") // Disable for stateless APIs
            );
        
        return http.build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
public class ApiController {
    
    @GetMapping("/public/health")
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> health() {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of(
            "status", "UP",
            "timestamp", LocalDateTime.now().toString()
        ));

    @GetMapping("/public/version")

    // getters/setters

Advanced configuration with method security:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity // Enable @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, etc.
public class AdvancedSecurityConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                // Public paths
                .requestMatchers("/public/**", "/actuator/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/users/register").permitAll()
                
                // Authenticated paths
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .oauth2Login(oauth2 -> oauth2
                .loginPage("/oauth2/authorization/google")
                .defaultSuccessUrl("/dashboard")
            )
            .sessionManagement(session -> session
                .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED)
                .maximumSessions(1)
                .maxSessionsPreventsLogin(false)
            )
            .headers(headers -> headers
                .frameOptions().deny()
                .contentTypeOptions().and()
                .httpStrictTransportSecurity(hstsConfig -> hstsConfig
                    .maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)
                    .includeSubdomains(true)
                )
            );
        
        return http.build();
    }
}

@Service
public class ProductService {
    
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void deleteProduct(Long productId) {
        // Only admins can delete
    }
    
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER')")
    @PostAuthorize("returnObject.owner == authentication.name")
    public Product getProduct(Long productId) {
        // Users can view their own products
        return productRepository.findById(productId).orElse(null);
    }
    
    @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
    public List<Product> getUserProducts() {
        // Any authenticated user
        return productRepository.findByOwner(authentication.getName());
    }
}
