configuration

How to read properties?

Quick Answer

@Value annotation.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot provides multiple ways to read configuration properties from various sources (application.properties, application.yml, environment variables, command-line arguments). The @Value annotation is one of the most common methods for injecting individual property values into Spring beans.

Property sources (in order of precedence):

  1. Command-line arguments: --server.port=9090
  2. OS environment variables: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
  3. Application properties: application-{profile}.properties
  4. Application properties: application.properties
  5. @PropertySource: Custom property files
  6. Default properties: Spring Boot defaults

@Value annotation features:

  • Property Injection: Injects values from property sources into fields, constructor parameters, or method parameters
  • Default Values: Provides fallback values using : syntax (${property:default})
  • Type Conversion: Automatically converts string values to appropriate types (int, boolean, etc.)
  • SpEL Support: Allows Spring Expression Language for dynamic value resolution
  • Validation: Can be combined with validation annotations

When to use @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties:

  • Use @Value: For simple properties, external configuration values, or when you need SpEL
  • Use @ConfigurationProperties: For complex configuration objects with validation and type-safe binding

Best practices:

  • Provide Defaults: Always specify sensible default values
  • Use Profiles: Leverage profile-specific property files
  • Validate Input: Combine with Bean Validation for complex validation
  • Document Properties: Use comments in property files
  • Environment Variables: Use UPPER_CASE with underscores for env vars
  • Avoid Hardcoding: Externalize all environment-specific values

Common patterns:

  • Simple Properties: ${app.name}
  • With Defaults: ${app.timeout:30}
  • System Properties: ${java.home}
  • Environment Variables: ${JAVA_HOME}
  • SpEL Expressions: #{${app.max.size} * 2}

Spring Boot also supports YAML format for hierarchical configurations and provides @ConfigurationProperties for type-safe property binding.

Code Example
// Service using @Value for configuration
@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    // Simple property injection
    @Value("${app.email.from}")
    private String fromEmail;
    
    // Property with default value
    @Value("${app.email.enabled:true}")
    private boolean emailEnabled;
    
    // Numeric property with default
    @Value("${app.email.port:587}")
    private int smtpPort;
    
    // List property (comma-separated)
    @Value("${app.email.recipients}")
    private String[] defaultRecipients;
    
    // System property
    @Value("${java.home}")
    private String javaHome;
    
    // Environment variable
    @Value("${JAVA_HOME}")
    private String javaHomeEnv;
    
    // SpEL expression with default
    @Value("#{${app.email.timeout} ?: 5000}")
    private int timeout;
    
    // Constructor injection with @Value
    private final String smtpHost;
    
    public EmailService(@Value("${app.email.host:smtp.gmail.com}") String smtpHost) {
        this.smtpHost = smtpHost;
    }
    
    public void sendEmail(String to, String subject, String body) {
        if (!emailEnabled) {
            System.out.println("Email sending is disabled");
            return;
        }
        
        System.out.println("Sending email from: " + fromEmail);
        System.out.println("SMTP Host: " + smtpHost + ", Port: " + smtpPort);
        System.out.println("To: " + to);
        System.out.println("Subject: " + subject);
        
        // Simulate email sending
        System.out.println("Email sent successfully!");
    }
}

// Configuration class using @Value
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Value("${app.thread.pool.size:10}")
    private int threadPoolSize;
    
    @Value("${app.thread.pool.max:50}")
    private int maxPoolSize;
    
    @Bean
    public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor taskExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(threadPoolSize);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(maxPoolSize);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
        executor.setThreadNamePrefix("MyApp-");
        executor.initialize();
        return executor;
    }
}

// Using @ConfigurationProperties for complex configuration
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
@Component
public class AppProperties {
    
    private String name;
    private String version;
    private Email email = new Email();
    private ThreadPool threadPool = new ThreadPool();
    
    // Getters and setters
    
    public static class Email {
        private boolean enabled = true;
        private String from;
        private String host;
        private int port = 587;
        private int timeout = 5000;
        private String[] recipients;
        
        // Getters and setters
    }
    
    public static class ThreadPool {
        private int size = 10;
        private int max = 50;
        
        // Getters and setters
    }
}

// Service using @ConfigurationProperties
@Service
public class ConfigurableEmailService {
    
    private final AppProperties.Email emailConfig;
    
    public ConfigurableEmailService(AppProperties appProperties) {
        this.emailConfig = appProperties.getEmail();
    }
    
    public void sendEmail(String to, String subject, String body) {
        if (!emailConfig.isEnabled()) {
            return;
        }
        
        // Use configuration properties
        System.out.println("Sending from: " + emailConfig.getFrom());
        System.out.println("SMTP: " + emailConfig.getHost() + ":" + emailConfig.getPort());
    }
}

Configuration in application.properties:

# Application properties
app.name=My Spring Boot App
app.version=1.0.0

# Email configuration
app.email.enabled=true
app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com
app.email.host=smtp.gmail.com
app.email.port=587
app.email.timeout=10000
app.email.recipients=admin@myapp.com,support@myapp.com

# Thread pool configuration
app.thread.pool.size=20
app.thread.pool.max=100

# Database configuration (Spring Boot auto-configures)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

YAML equivalent (application.yml):

app:
  name: My Spring Boot App
  version: 1.0.0
  email:
    enabled: true
    from: noreply@myapp.com
    host: smtp.gmail.com
    port: 587
    timeout: 10000
    recipients:
      - admin@myapp.com
      - support@myapp.com
  thread:
    pool:
      size: 20
      max: 100

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
    username: sa
    password: ""

Profile-specific properties (application-dev.properties):

# Development-specific properties
app.email.enabled=false
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

Using properties in tests:

@SpringBootTest
@TestPropertySource(properties = {
    "app.email.enabled=false",
    "app.name=Test App"
})
public class EmailServiceTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    @Test
    public void testEmailDisabled() {
        // Test with overridden properties
        emailService.sendEmail("test@example.com", "Test", "Body");
        // Verify no email was sent
    }
}

Command-line property override:

java -jar app.jar --app.email.enabled=false --server.port=9090

@Value provides flexible property injection with support for defaults, type conversion, and SpEL expressions for dynamic configuration needs.

dev-tools

How to reload changes without restarting the server (DevTools)?

Quick Answer

By adding the spring-boot-devtools dependency, Spring Boot provides features like automatic restart and LiveReload.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot DevTools is a collection of tools designed to enhance developer productivity during application development. It provides features that make the development cycle faster and more efficient, but automatically disables itself in production to avoid performance overhead.

Key features:

  • Automatic Restart: Monitors classpath changes and automatically restarts the application when code changes. Uses two classloaders (base and restart) to make restarts much faster than cold starts.

  • LiveReload: Automatically refreshes the browser when resources change, eliminating the need to manually refresh during frontend development.

  • Property Defaults: Provides sensible development defaults for properties like template caching, which are different from production settings.

  • Remote Development: Supports remote applications with features like remote debugging and automatic restart.

  • Global Settings: Can be configured globally for all Spring Boot projects on a machine.

DevTools detects changes by monitoring the classpath and triggers restarts for:

  • Java source files
  • Properties/YAML files
  • Templates
  • Static resources

It excludes certain paths from triggering restarts (like static resources and logging config) to avoid unnecessary restarts.

DevTools also provides additional development endpoints and enhanced error pages with detailed information.

Note: DevTools should never be included in production builds as it adds overhead and potential security risks.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml - Add to dependencies -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>  <!-- Not included in fat JAR -->
</dependency>

Configuration in application.properties:

# DevTools configuration
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=true
spring.devtools.restart.additional-paths=src/main/resources
spring.devtools.restart.exclude=static/**,public/**

# LiveReload configuration
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=true
spring.devtools.livereload.port=35729

# Remote DevTools (for remote debugging)
spring.devtools.remote.secret=mysecret

Global configuration (~/.spring-boot-devtools.properties):

# Global settings for all projects
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=true
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=true

Custom restart triggers:

@Configuration
public class DevToolsConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public FileSystemWatcher fileSystemWatcher() {
        // Custom file watcher for additional paths
        FileSystemWatcher watcher = new FileSystemWatcher();
        watcher.addSourceDirectory(new File("config"));
        return watcher;
    }
}

What triggers a restart:

  • Changes to Java files in classpath
  • Changes to application.properties/yml
  • Changes to templates (Thymeleaf, etc.)
  • Changes to build files (pom.xml)

What doesn't trigger a restart:

  • Static resources (CSS, JS, images)
  • Logging configuration
  • Changes to files in target/ or build/ directories

To manually trigger restart in IDE:

  • Save a Java file
  • Use IDE's build/rebuild
  • Touch a file in monitored path

DevTools also provides enhanced error pages with stack traces, environment info, and request details when exceptions occur during development.

cli

How to run via Maven?

Quick Answer

mvn spring-boot:run.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Maven Plugin provides the spring-boot:run goal to run Spring Boot applications directly from Maven without packaging. This is convenient for development and testing.

Key features:

  • Hot reloading: Automatically restarts on code changes (with DevTools)
  • Profile support: Can specify active profiles
  • System properties: Pass JVM arguments and properties
  • Skip tests: Option to skip test execution
  • Debug mode: Enable remote debugging

The plugin also provides other goals:

  • spring-boot:repackage - Creates executable JAR
  • spring-boot:start/stop - For integration tests
  • spring-boot:build-info - Generates build information

Best practices:

  • Use for development and local testing
  • Combine with DevTools for faster development
  • Use profiles for different environments
  • Consider Gradle for larger projects
Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.0</version>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>repackage</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

Basic run command:

mvn spring-boot:run

With profiles:

mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev

With system properties:

mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.jvmArguments="-Xmx1024m -Dserver.port=9090"

Skip tests:

mvn spring-boot:run -DskipTests

Enable remote debugging:

mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.jvmArguments="-Xdebug -Xrunjdwp:transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=5005"

Using Maven wrapper:

./mvnw spring-boot:run

Alternative - package and run:

mvn clean package
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

The spring-boot:run goal is perfect for development as it provides fast startup and hot reloading capabilities.

SecurityBasics

Identify Spring Security Default Behavior.

Quick Answer

By default, adding the starter secures all endpoints with Basic Auth.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Security's default behavior when added to a Spring Boot application provides immediate security out-of-the-box through HTTP Basic Authentication. This 'secure by default' approach ensures that no endpoints are accidentally exposed without authentication. Here's a comprehensive breakdown:

Default Security Configuration:

  • Basic Authentication: Uses HTTP Basic Auth with username/password credentials sent in the Authorization header
  • Default User: Generates a user named 'user' with a randomly generated password printed to the console logs
  • Universal Protection: All HTTP endpoints are secured by default, requiring authentication for any request
  • Login Form: Provides a default HTML login form for browser-based requests at /login
  • Logout Support: Includes automatic logout functionality at /logout

Security Implications:

  • Development: The random password prevents accidental exposure during development
  • Production: Must be configured with proper users/passwords or authentication mechanisms
  • CSRF Protection: Enabled by default for state-changing operations (POST, PUT, DELETE)
  • Session Management: Uses HTTP sessions for authentication state

When to Use Default Behavior:

  • Prototyping: Quick security setup for demos and proofs-of-concept
  • Internal Tools: Simple authentication for team-internal applications
  • API Gateways: When external authentication/authorization is handled upstream

Alternatives and Best Practices:

  • Custom User Configuration: Override defaults with spring.security.user.name and spring.security.user.password
  • Database Authentication: Implement UserDetailsService for user storage
  • OAuth2/JWT: For modern web applications and APIs
  • LDAP/SSO: For enterprise environments

Common Pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to configure proper authentication in production
  • Exposing the default login form in production APIs
  • Not disabling security for public endpoints like health checks

The default behavior serves as a security baseline that developers must consciously override for their specific authentication requirements.

Code Example
// Default behavior - no configuration needed
@SpringBootApplication
public class SecureApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(SecureApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@RestController
public class HelloController {
    
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() {
        return "Hello, authenticated user!";
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/public")
    public String publicEndpoint() {
        return "This is public!";
    }
}

<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.properties - Override defaults
spring.security.user.name=admin
spring.security.user.password=secret123

# Or disable for development (NEVER in production)
spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.security.servlet.SecurityAutoConfiguration

Console output on startup:

Using generated security password: 8e557245-73e2-4286-969a-ff57fe326336

To access secured endpoints:

# Using curl with Basic Auth
curl -u user:8e557245-73e2-4286-969a-ff57fe326336 http://localhost:8080/hello

# Or with custom credentials
curl -u admin:secret123 http://localhost:8080/hello

For public endpoints, configure security:

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/public/**", "/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .httpBasic(withDefaults()); // Enable Basic Auth
        return http.build();
    }
}

For production, implement proper authentication:

@Service
public class CustomUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
    
    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) throws UsernameNotFoundException {
        // Load user from database
        return User.builder()
            .username(username)
            .password(passwordEncoder.encode("password"))
            .roles("USER")
            .build();
    }
}

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
    }
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .formLogin(withDefaults())
            .logout(logout -> logout.logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout"));
        return http.build();
    }
}
packaging

Jar vs War in Spring Boot?

Quick Answer

Jar is preferred for self-contained deployment.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot supports two packaging formats: JAR and WAR. JAR is the default and preferred format for Spring Boot applications, while WAR is used for traditional deployment to external servlet containers.

JAR advantages:

  • Self-contained: Includes embedded server (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow)
  • Simple deployment: java -jar app.jar runs anywhere with Java
  • Cloud-native: Perfect for containers, serverless, and microservices
  • Fast startup: No external container startup time
  • Portability: Single artifact with all dependencies

WAR advantages:

  • Legacy compatibility: Deploy to existing Tomcat/WebLogic/WebSphere
  • Shared resources: Multiple apps can share container resources
  • Container features: Access to container-specific features

For Spring Boot, JAR is almost always preferred unless you must deploy to an existing servlet container infrastructure.

To create WAR, change packaging in pom.xml and extend SpringBootServletInitializer.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml for JAR (default) -->
<packaging>jar</packaging>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

JAR deployment:

# Build
mvn clean package

# Run
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

# With custom properties
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar --server.port=9090 --spring.profiles.active=prod

WAR configuration:

<!-- pom.xml for WAR -->
<packaging>war</packaging>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        <scope>provided</scope>  <!-- Tomcat provided by container -->
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

WAR application class:

@SpringBootApplication
public class WarApplication extends SpringBootServletInitializer {
    
    @Override
    protected SpringApplicationBuilder configure(SpringApplicationBuilder builder) {
        return builder.sources(WarApplication.class);
    }
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(WarApplication.class, args);
    }
}

WAR deployment:

# Build
mvn clean package

# Deploy target/myapp-1.0.0.war to Tomcat webapps/
# Access at http://localhost:8080/myapp-1.0.0/

Docker with JAR:

FROM openjdk:17-jdk-slim as build

WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests

FROM openjdk:17-jre-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

JAR is the modern approach for Spring Boot applications, enabling microservices, cloud deployment, and simplified operations.

web

PathVariable vs RequestParam?

Quick Answer

URI path vs Query string.

Detailed Explanation

@PathVariable and @RequestParam are Spring MVC annotations for extracting values from HTTP requests, but they serve different purposes in RESTful API design. Understanding their differences is crucial for building clean, intuitive APIs.

@PathVariable:

  • Purpose: Extracts values from the URI path template
  • URL Structure: /users/{id}, /orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId}
  • Use Case: Resource identification, hierarchical data
  • Required: Yes by default (path variables must be present)
  • Example: /users/123 → extracts id = 123
  • REST Convention: Used for resource IDs and hierarchical paths

@RequestParam:

  • Purpose: Extracts values from query parameters
  • URL Structure: /users?id=123&status=active
  • Use Case: Optional filters, search criteria, pagination
  • Required: No by default (can be made required with required = true)
  • Example: /users?page=1&size=10&sort=name → extracts multiple parameters
  • REST Convention: Used for filtering, sorting, pagination

Key differences:

  • URL Semantics: Path variables are part of the resource identifier; query params are modifiers
  • Caching: Path variables are cache-friendly; query params may not be cached
  • Required vs Optional: Path variables are typically required; query params are optional
  • Data Type: Both support automatic type conversion
  • Default Values: Query params support defaults; path variables don't (use optional)

Best practices:

  • Use Path Variables: For resource identification (/users/{id})
  • Use Query Parameters: For filtering, sorting, pagination (?status=active&page=1)
  • Hierarchical Resources: /users/{userId}/posts/{postId}
  • Consistent Naming: Use consistent parameter names across APIs
  • Validation: Apply validation annotations to both
  • Documentation: Clearly document required vs optional parameters

Spring Boot automatically configures the necessary converters and supports various data types including custom objects.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
public class ApiController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    private final OrderService orderService;
    
    public ApiController(UserService userService, OrderService orderService) {
        this.userService = userService;
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }
    
    // PathVariable examples
    
    // GET /api/users/123 - Get user by ID
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/123/posts/456 - Hierarchical resource
    @GetMapping("/users/{userId}/posts/{postId}")
    public ResponseEntity<Post> getUserPost(
            @PathVariable Long userId, 
            @PathVariable Long postId) {
        
        return userService.findUserPost(userId, postId)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // PUT /api/users/123 - Update user
    @PutMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateUserRequest request) {
        
        return userService.updateUser(id, request)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/users/123 - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteById(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // RequestParam examples
    
    // GET /api/users?page=1&size=10&sort=name&status=active
    @GetMapping("/users")
    public Page<User> getUsers(
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String sort,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String status,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String search) {
        
        Sort sortObj = sort != null ? Sort.by(sort) : Sort.unsorted();
        Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(page, size, sortObj);
        
        return userService.findUsers(status, search, pageable);
    }
    
    // GET /api/orders?startDate=2023-01-01&endDate=2023-12-31&minAmount=100
    @GetMapping("/orders")
    public List<Order> getOrders(
            @RequestParam @DateTimeFormat(iso = DateTimeFormat.ISO.DATE) LocalDate startDate,
            @RequestParam(required = false) @DateTimeFormat(iso = DateTimeFormat.ISO.DATE) LocalDate endDate,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") BigDecimal minAmount) {
        
        return orderService.findOrders(startDate, endDate, minAmount);
    }
    
    // Mixed usage - PathVariable + RequestParam
    // GET /api/users/123/posts?published=true&page=0&size=5
    @GetMapping("/users/{userId}/posts")
    public Page<Post> getUserPosts(
            @PathVariable Long userId,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "true") boolean published,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) {
        
        Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(page, size);
        return userService.findUserPosts(userId, published, pageable);
    }
    
    // Advanced RequestParam usage
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<Product> searchProducts(
            @RequestParam Map<String, String> allParams) {
        
        // Handle dynamic parameters
        String category = allParams.get("category");
        String brand = allParams.get("brand");
        BigDecimal minPrice = allParams.containsKey("minPrice") ? 
            new BigDecimal(allParams.get("minPrice")) : null;
        
        return productService.searchProducts(category, brand, minPrice);
    }
    
    // Optional PathVariable with custom regex
    @GetMapping("/files/{filename:.+}")
    public ResponseEntity<Resource> getFile(@PathVariable String filename) {
        // Handle filenames with extensions
        return fileService.loadFile(filename);
    }
}

// Supporting classes

    @NotBlank private String name;
    @Email private String email;
    // getters/setters
}

    public Optional<User> findById(Long id) {
        // Implementation

    public Page<User> findUsers(String status, String search, Pageable pageable) {
        // Implementation with filtering

    public Optional<Post> findUserPost(Long userId, Long postId) {
        // Implementation

    }
}

public class OrderService {
    
    public List<Order> findOrders(LocalDate startDate, LocalDate endDate, BigDecimal minAmount) {
        // Implementation
        return Collections.emptyList();
    }
}

URL examples:

GET /api/users/123
GET /api/users/123/posts/456
PUT /api/users/123
DELETE /api/users/123

# RequestParam usage:
GET /api/users?page=0&size=10&sort=name&status=active

Custom parameter conversion:

@Configuration
public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    
    @Override
    public void addFormatters(FormatterRegistry registry) {
        registry.addConverter(new StringToEnumConverter());

}

public class StringToEnumConverter implements Converter<String, Status> {

}

@PathVariable and @RequestParam work together to create clean, RESTful APIs where path variables identify resources and query parameters provide filtering and pagination options.

basics

POM Starters?

Quick Answer

Dependency descriptors.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Starters are curated sets of dependencies that bundle commonly used libraries with compatible versions, eliminating the need for manual dependency management. They are one of Spring Boot's most powerful features for simplifying project setup.

Core concepts:

  • Dependency Curation: Pre-selected libraries that work well together
  • Version Management: Compatible versions managed by Spring Boot Bill of Materials (BOM)
  • Convention over Configuration: Sensible defaults for common use cases
  • Transitive Dependencies: All necessary dependencies included automatically
  • Modular Design: Include only what you need for your application

Key benefits:

  • Simplified POM: Fewer dependency declarations
  • Version Conflicts Resolved: Compatible versions guaranteed
  • Faster Setup: Quick project initialization
  • Best Practices: Industry-standard library combinations
  • Auto-Configuration: Enables Spring Boot's auto-configuration features

Common starters:

  • spring-boot-starter-web: Web development with Tomcat, Jackson, Spring MVC
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa: JPA/Hibernate data access
  • spring-boot-starter-security: Authentication and authorization
  • spring-boot-starter-test: Testing with JUnit, Mockito, Spring Test
  • spring-boot-starter-actuator: Production monitoring
  • spring-boot-starter-validation: Bean validation
  • spring-boot-starter-cache: Caching abstractions
  • spring-boot-starter-mail: Email sending

Starter naming convention:

  • spring-boot-starter-*: Official Spring Boot starters
  • *-starter: Third-party starters

Creating custom starters:

  • Follow naming convention: yourproject-starter
  • Include auto-configuration classes
  • Provide sensible defaults
  • Enable conditional configuration

Best practices:

  • Use Starters: Prefer starters over individual dependencies
  • Minimal Dependencies: Include only necessary starters
  • Version Management: Let Spring Boot manage versions
  • Custom Starters: Create for organizational common dependencies
  • Override When Needed: Can exclude and override starter dependencies

Spring Boot's parent POM provides the BOM that manages all starter versions.

Code Example
<!-- Traditional approach (many manual dependencies) -->
<project>
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.1.0</version>
    </parent>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Manual dependency management - error prone -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
            <version>6.0.9</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-web</artifactId>
            <version>6.0.9</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>2.15.2</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.tomcat.embed</groupId>
            <artifactId>tomcat-embed-core</artifactId>
            <version>10.1.11</version>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Many more with potential version conflicts -->
    </dependencies>
</project>

<!-- Spring Boot Starter approach (clean and simple) -->
<project>
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.1.0</version>
    </parent>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Single starter handles everything -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Add more starters as needed -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Database driver (not included in starters) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
            <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>

What each starter includes:

<project>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Include your common dependencies -->

}

Spring Boot starters simplify dependency management and ensure that Spring Boot applications have all necessary libraries with compatible versions, reducing configuration errors and maintenance overhead.

web

Shorthand for @RequestMapping(method=GET)?

Quick Answer

@GetMapping.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot provides convenient shortcut annotations for common HTTP methods, making controller code more readable and concise. These annotations are equivalent to @RequestMapping with specific method values.

Available shortcuts:

  • @GetMapping - for GET requests (retrieving data)
  • @PostMapping - for POST requests (creating resources)
  • @PutMapping - for PUT requests (updating resources)
  • @DeleteMapping - for DELETE requests (removing resources)
  • @PatchMapping - for PATCH requests (partial updates)

Benefits:

  • Readability: Intent is immediately clear from the annotation name
  • Type Safety: Compile-time checking prevents method typos
  • IDE Support: Better autocomplete and refactoring support
  • REST Compliance: Encourages proper HTTP method usage

Best practices:

  • Use the most specific HTTP method for each operation
  • Follow REST conventions (GET for reads, POST for creates, etc.)
  • Use @RequestMapping only when you need multiple methods on the same path
  • Combine with path variables and request parameters appropriately

These shortcuts work with all the same features as @RequestMapping, including path variables, request parameters, headers, and content negotiation.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /api/users - Retrieve all users
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/{id} - Retrieve single user
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // POST /api/users - Create new user
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
            .path("/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
            .toUri();
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(user);
    }
    
    // PUT /api/users/{id} - Full update
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> updateUser(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody UpdateUserRequest request) {
        return userService.updateUser(id, request)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // PATCH /api/users/{id} - Partial update
    @PatchMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> patchUser(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String, Object> updates) {
        return userService.patchUser(id, updates)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/users/{id} - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteById(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // Multiple methods on same path (use @RequestMapping)
    @RequestMapping(path = "/bulk", method = {RequestMethod.POST, RequestMethod.PUT})
    public ResponseEntity<BulkResult> bulkOperation(@RequestBody BulkRequest request) {
        BulkResult result = userService.processBulkOperation(request);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(result);
    }
}

// DTOs
public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank @Email private String email;
    @NotBlank @Size(min=2, max=50) private String name;
}

public class UpdateUserRequest {
    @Email private String email;
    @Size(min=2, max=50) private String name;
}

public class BulkRequest {
    private String operation;
    private List<User> users;
}

public class BulkResult {
    private int successCount;
    private int failureCount;
}

HTTP Method Guidelines:

  • GET: Safe, idempotent, cacheable - for retrieving data
  • POST: Creates new resources, not idempotent
  • PUT: Full update of existing resource, idempotent
  • PATCH: Partial update of existing resource, not necessarily idempotent
  • DELETE: Removes resource, idempotent

Using shortcuts improves code clarity and follows RESTful design principles.

concepts

Spring Boot vs Spring?

Quick Answer

Opinionated version of Spring.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot is an extension of the Spring Framework designed to simplify the bootstrapping and development of new Spring applications. While the core Spring Framework provides comprehensive infrastructure support for building enterprise applications, Spring Boot removes much of the boilerplate configuration and setup, allowing developers to focus on business logic.

Key differences and advantages:

  • Convention over Configuration: Spring Boot provides sensible defaults for configuration, reducing the need for explicit setup
  • Embedded Servers: Includes Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow out-of-the-box, eliminating the need for external servlet containers
  • Auto-Configuration: Automatically configures beans based on classpath dependencies and properties
  • Starters: Curated dependency sets that bundle commonly used libraries with compatible versions
  • Production-Ready Features: Built-in support for metrics, health checks, and monitoring via Actuator
  • Standalone Applications: Creates executable JARs that can run with java -jar

Spring Boot doesn't replace Spring but enhances it by making common patterns easier to implement. Traditional Spring applications require extensive XML configuration or Java config classes, while Spring Boot applications can be created with minimal configuration.

Use cases for Spring Boot:

  • Microservices development
  • RESTful web services
  • Batch processing applications
  • Cloud-native applications
  • Rapid prototyping

Best practices:

  • Use Spring Boot for new applications unless you need fine-grained control over Spring configuration
  • Leverage auto-configuration but override when necessary
  • Use starters to manage dependencies
  • Take advantage of embedded servers for development and simple deployments
  • Use Spring Boot Actuator for production monitoring
Code Example
// Traditional Spring MVC Application (lots of configuration)
@Configuration
@EnableWebMvc
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example")
@PropertySource("classpath:application.properties")
public class TraditionalSpringConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public ViewResolver viewResolver() {
        InternalResourceViewResolver resolver = new InternalResourceViewResolver();
        resolver.setPrefix("/WEB-INF/views/");
        resolver.setSuffix(".jsp");
        return resolver;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        DriverManagerDataSource dataSource = new DriverManagerDataSource();
        dataSource.setDriverClassName("com.mysql.jdbc.Driver");
        dataSource.setUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/myapp");
        dataSource.setUsername("user");
        dataSource.setPassword("password");
        return dataSource;
    }
    
    // Many more bean definitions...
}

// Spring Boot equivalent (minimal configuration)
@SpringBootApplication
public class SpringBootApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(SpringBootApp.class, args);
    }
}

Configuration in application.properties:

# Spring Boot auto-configures based on these properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/myapp
spring.datasource.username=user
spring.datasource.password=password

# Embedded server configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# View resolver (if needed)
spring.mvc.view.prefix=/WEB-INF/views/
spring.mvc.view.suffix=.jsp

Maven dependencies comparison:

    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
        <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>

    </dependency>

</dependencies>

<!-- Spring Boot (single starter handles everything) -->

    </dependency>

    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>mysql</groupId>
        <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>

Running the applications:

# Traditional Spring: Deploy WAR to Tomcat
# Requires external servlet container setup

# Spring Boot: Simple execution
mvn spring-boot:run
# or
java -jar target/app.jar

Spring Boot follows the principle of 'Convention over Configuration', providing sensible defaults while allowing customization when needed. This makes it ideal for rapid application development while maintaining the power and flexibility of the Spring ecosystem.

CloudActuator

usage of /actuator/health endpoint?

Quick Answer

Returns the health status of the application (UP/DOWN).

Detailed Explanation

The /actuator/health endpoint is a critical component of Spring Boot Actuator that provides health monitoring capabilities for applications. It performs automated checks on various system components to determine overall application health, making it essential for production deployments, monitoring systems, and orchestration platforms.

Health Indicators:

  • Database: Checks database connectivity and basic queries
  • Disk Space: Monitors available disk space
  • Ping: Basic liveness check
  • Custom: Application-specific health checks
  • Composite: Aggregates multiple health indicators

Health States:

  • UP: All checks pass, application is healthy
  • DOWN: One or more critical checks fail
  • OUT_OF_SERVICE: Application is out of service (maintenance mode)
  • UNKNOWN: Health status cannot be determined

Response Structure:

  • Basic: Simple status for load balancers
  • Detailed: Full health information with component details
  • Custom: Application-specific health data

Configuration Options:

  • Exposure: Control which endpoints are accessible
  • Security: Protect sensitive health information
  • Custom Indicators: Add application-specific checks
  • Grouping: Organize health checks into groups

Use Cases:

  • Load Balancers: Health checks for traffic routing
  • Monitoring Systems: Integration with Prometheus, Grafana
  • Kubernetes: Readiness and liveness probes
  • CI/CD: Deployment verification
  • Alerting: Automated notifications on health failures

Best Practices:

  • Security: Don't expose detailed health in production
  • Performance: Keep health checks lightweight
  • Dependencies: Include all critical external dependencies
  • Timeouts: Configure appropriate timeouts
  • Caching: Avoid expensive operations in health checks

The endpoint serves as the foundation for application observability and reliability in distributed systems.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.properties
# Expose health endpoint
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info

# Show detailed health information (be careful in production)
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized

# Health check timeouts
management.health.diskspace.threshold=10MB
management.health.db.enabled=true

# Custom health check properties
app.health.custom.enabled=true
app.health.custom.threshold=100

// Basic health check response
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/actuator/health")
public class HealthController {
    
    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<Health> health() {
        // This is handled automatically by Spring Boot
        return null; // Spring Boot provides the implementation
    }
}

// Sample health response (basic)
{
    "status": "UP"
}

// Sample health response (detailed)
{
    "status": "UP",
    "components": {
        "db": {
            "status": "UP",
            "details": {
                "database": "H2",
                "validationQuery": "SELECT 1"
            }
        },
        "diskSpace": {
            "status": "UP",
            "details": {
                "total": 500068036608,
                "free": 200263000000,
                "threshold": 10485760,
                "exists": true
            }
        },
        "ping": {
            "status": "UP"
        }
    }
}

Creating custom health indicators:

@Component
public class CustomHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    
    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try {
            // Perform custom health check
            int activeConnections = checkActiveConnections();
            int maxConnections = getMaxConnections();
            
            if (activeConnections > maxConnections * 0.9) {
                return Health.down()
                    .withDetail("activeConnections", activeConnections)
                    .withDetail("maxConnections", maxConnections)
                    .withDetail("error", "Connection pool nearly exhausted")
                    .build();
            }
            
            return Health.up()
                .withDetail("activeConnections", activeConnections)
                .withDetail("maxConnections", maxConnections)
                .build();
                
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return Health.down(e)
                .withDetail("error", e.getMessage())
                .build();
        }
    }
    
    private int checkActiveConnections() {
        // Implementation to check connection pool
        return 15; // Example value
    }
    
    private int getMaxConnections() {
        return 20; // Example value
    }
}

@Component
public class ExternalServiceHealthIndicator implements ReactiveHealthIndicator {
    
    private final WebClient webClient;
    
    public ExternalServiceHealthIndicator(WebClient.Builder webClientBuilder) {
        this.webClient = webClientBuilder.build();
    }
    
    @Override
    public Mono<Health> health() {
        return webClient.get()
            .uri("http://external-service/health")
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(String.class)
            .map(response -> Health.up().withDetail("externalService", "available").build())
            .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Health.down()
                .withDetail("externalService", "unavailable")
                .withDetail("error", e.getMessage())
                .build()))
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
            .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Health.unknown()
                .withDetail("externalService", "timeout")
                .build()));
    }
}

@Configuration
public class HealthConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public HealthIndicator dbHealthIndicator(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new DataSourceHealthIndicator(dataSource);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public HealthIndicator diskSpaceHealthIndicator() {
        DiskSpaceHealthIndicator indicator = new DiskSpaceHealthIndicator();
        indicator.setThreshold(DataSize.ofMegabytes(10)); // 10MB threshold
        return indicator;
    }
}

// Health groups for different environments
@Configuration
public class HealthGroupConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.health.group.liveness.enabled", havingValue = "true")
    public HealthIndicator livenessHealthIndicator() {
        return () -> Health.up().build(); // Simple liveness check
    }
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "app.health.group.readiness.enabled", havingValue = "true")
    public HealthIndicator readinessHealthIndicator(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new DataSourceHealthIndicator(dataSource);
    }
}

# Health groups configuration
management.endpoint.health.group.liveness.include=liveness
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readiness,db

# Enable health groups
app.health.group.liveness.enabled=true
app.health.group.readiness.enabled=true

Testing health endpoints:

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase
public class HealthEndpointTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private TestRestTemplate restTemplate;
    
    @Test
    void healthEndpointShouldReturnUp() {
        ResponseEntity<String> response = restTemplate.getForEntity("/actuator/health", String.class);
        
        assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK);
        assertThat(response.getBody()).contains("\"status\":\"UP\"");
    }
    
    @Test
    void healthEndpointShouldReturnDetailedInfo() {
        HttpHeaders headers = new HttpHeaders();
        headers.set("Authorization", "Basic " + Base64.getEncoder()
            .encodeToString("admin:password".getBytes()));
        
        HttpEntity<?> entity = new HttpEntity<>(headers);
        ResponseEntity<String> response = restTemplate.exchange(
            "/actuator/health", HttpMethod.GET, entity, String.class);
        
        assertThat(response.getBody()).contains("components");
        assertThat(response.getBody()).contains("db");
        assertThat(response.getBody()).contains("diskSpace");
    }
}

starters

What are Spring Boot Starters?

Quick Answer

Dependency descriptors that bundle related libraries.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Starters are curated sets of dependencies that simplify the build configuration by bundling together commonly used libraries for specific functionalities. They eliminate the need to manually manage version compatibility between different libraries, as all dependencies within a starter are guaranteed to work together.

Key characteristics:

  • Convention over Configuration: Each starter follows Spring Boot's philosophy of providing sensible defaults
  • Transitive Dependencies: They include not just the main libraries but also all necessary transitive dependencies
  • Version Management: The Spring Boot Bill of Materials (BOM) ensures all starter dependencies use compatible versions
  • Modular: You can include only the starters you need for your application

Common starters include:

  • spring-boot-starter-web: For web applications (includes Spring MVC, Tomcat, Jackson)
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa: For JPA-based data access (includes Hibernate, Spring Data JPA)
  • spring-boot-starter-security: For authentication and authorization
  • spring-boot-starter-test: For testing (includes JUnit, Mockito, Spring Test)
  • spring-boot-starter-actuator: For production monitoring

Starters also enable auto-configuration; when you add a starter, Spring Boot automatically configures the associated beans and settings. For example, adding spring-boot-starter-web automatically configures a DispatcherServlet, JSON converters, and an embedded Tomcat server.

You can create custom starters for your organization's common dependencies, following the naming convention yourproject-starter.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependencies>
    <!-- Web starter includes: Spring MVC, Tomcat, Jackson, Spring Web -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Data JPA starter includes: Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, JDBC -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- H2 database for development/testing -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
        <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Without starters, you would need to manually specify each dependency:

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
        <version>5.3.23</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-web</artifactId>
        <version>5.3.23</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
        <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
        <version>2.13.4</version>
    </dependency>
    <!-- And many more with version conflicts possible -->
</dependencies>

The BOM ensures version compatibility:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>2.7.5</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
