annotations

What does @Autowired do?

Quick Answer

It marks a constructor, field, or setter method to be autowired by Spring's dependency injection.

Detailed Explanation

@Autowired is a core annotation in Spring that enables automatic dependency injection. It tells the Spring IoC container to automatically wire (inject) a matching bean into the annotated field, constructor, or setter method. This is a key part of Spring's dependency injection mechanism.

Injection types:

  • Field Injection: Direct injection into private fields (most common but least testable)
  • Constructor Injection: Injection through constructor parameters (preferred by Spring team)
  • Setter Injection: Injection through setter methods

How it works:

  1. Spring scans for beans in the application context
  2. When it encounters @Autowired, it looks for a bean of the required type
  3. If multiple beans of the same type exist, it can use @Qualifier to specify which one
  4. If no matching bean is found, it throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException

The annotation can be made optional with required = false, in which case injection will be skipped if no bean is found.

Spring Boot's auto-configuration creates many beans automatically, so @Autowired often 'just works' without explicit bean definitions.

Best practices:

  • Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies
  • Use field injection sparingly (mainly for optional dependencies)
  • Avoid circular dependencies
  • Use @Qualifier when multiple beans of same type exist
Code Example
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    // Field injection (not recommended for required dependencies)
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection (recommended)
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired  // Can be omitted in Spring 4.3+ for single constructors
    public UserService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    // Setter injection (for optional dependencies)
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    public User createUser(CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = new User(request.getEmail(), request.getName());
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);
        
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(saved);
        
        if (auditService != null) {
            auditService.logUserCreation(saved);
        }
        
        return saved;
    }
}

// When multiple implementations exist
@Service
@Qualifier("emailService")
public class SmtpEmailService implements EmailService {
    // SMTP implementation
}

@Service
@Qualifier("mockEmailService")
public class MockEmailService implements EmailService {
    // Mock implementation for testing
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("emailService")  // Specify which implementation to use
    public NotificationService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
}

With @ConfigurationProperties:

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.notification")
@Component
public class NotificationProperties {
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private String fromEmail;
    // getters/setters
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    @Autowired
    private NotificationProperties properties;  // Injects configured properties
    
    // Use properties.getFromEmail(), etc.
}

In application.properties:

app.notification.enabled=true
app.notification.from-email=noreply@myapp.com

Spring Boot auto-configures many beans, so @Autowired works for:

  • DataSource (from spring-boot-starter-data-jpa)
  • JdbcTemplate
  • EntityManager
  • ObjectMapper (Jackson)
  • RestTemplate
  • And many more...
annotations

What does @SpringBootApplication do?

Quick Answer

It is a convenience annotation that combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan.

Detailed Explanation

The @SpringBootApplication annotation is a meta-annotation that serves as a shortcut for three essential Spring annotations, making it the cornerstone of any Spring Boot application. Here's what each component does:

  • @Configuration: Indicates that the class can be used by the Spring IoC container as a source of bean definitions. Methods annotated with @Bean within this class will be processed to create Spring beans.

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Tells Spring Boot to start adding beans based on classpath settings, property settings, and other factors. This is where the 'magic' of auto-configuration happens - Spring Boot automatically configures beans for features like data sources, message converters, and security based on what's available.

  • @ComponentScan: Instructs Spring to scan for components (classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.) in the current package and all sub-packages. This is how Spring discovers and registers your application's beans.

By using @SpringBootApplication, you enable all these features with a single annotation, placed typically on the main application class. This annotation also enables other features like @EnableWebMvc if Spring MVC is on the classpath, but only if you haven't already configured it manually.

The annotation has attributes you can customize:

  • scanBasePackages: Specify packages to scan for components
  • exclude: Exclude specific auto-configuration classes
  • excludeName: Exclude by bean names

This single annotation replaces what would otherwise require multiple annotations and extensive XML configuration in traditional Spring applications.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.example.common"},  // Custom scan packages
    exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class}  // Exclude specific auto-configs
)
public class Application {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
    
    // This method creates a bean that can be injected elsewhere
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyServiceImpl();
    }
}

Without @SpringBootApplication, you would need:

@Configuration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan
public class Application {
    // Same main method
}

The annotation is typically placed on the class that contains the main method, and Spring Boot uses this as the starting point for component scanning.

annotations

What does @SpringBootApplication do?

Quick Answer

It enables auto-configuration, component scanning, and configuration.

Detailed Explanation

@SpringBootApplication is a meta-annotation that serves as a convenient shortcut for three essential Spring annotations: @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan, and @Configuration. It marks the main class of a Spring Boot application and enables all the core features needed to bootstrap and run the application.

The three component annotations:

  • @Configuration: Indicates that the class can be used by the Spring IoC container as a source of bean definitions. Methods annotated with @Bean within this class will be processed to create Spring beans.

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Tells Spring Boot to start adding beans based on classpath settings, property settings, and other factors. This enables the 'magic' of auto-configuration, where Spring Boot automatically configures beans for features like data sources, message converters, and security based on what's available on the classpath.

  • @ComponentScan: Instructs Spring to scan for components (classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.) in the current package and all sub-packages. This is how Spring discovers and registers your application's beans automatically.

Additional features enabled by @SpringBootApplication:

  • Enables @EnableWebMvc if Spring MVC is on the classpath
  • Configures default error pages
  • Sets up logging and metrics
  • Enables component scanning with default filters

The annotation can be customized with attributes:

  • scanBasePackages: Specify packages to scan for components
  • exclude: Exclude specific auto-configuration classes
  • excludeName: Exclude by bean names
  • proxyBeanMethods: Control proxying of @Bean methods

This single annotation replaces what would otherwise require multiple annotations and extensive XML configuration in traditional Spring applications, making Spring Boot applications much simpler to create and maintain.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.example.common"},  // Custom scan packages
    exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class},                   // Exclude specific auto-configs
    proxyBeanMethods = false                                         // Disable @Bean method proxying for performance
)
public class Application {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Bootstrap the entire Spring application
        // - Creates ApplicationContext
        // - Scans for components
        // - Applies auto-configuration
        // - Starts embedded server
        // - Runs CommandLineRunners
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
    
    // @Configuration allows @Bean methods
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyServiceImpl();
    }
    
    // Custom bean with dependencies
    @Bean
    public DataProcessor dataProcessor(MyService myService, 
                                     @Value("${app.batch.size:100}") int batchSize) {
        return new DataProcessor(myService, batchSize);
    }
}

// Example service components that get auto-scanned
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection works automatically
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    public User createUser(String name, String email) {
        User user = new User(name, email);
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}

@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    // Spring Data JPA provides implementation automatically
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    // Auto-scanned and dependency injected
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public User createUser(@RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        return userService.createUser(request.getName(), request.getEmail());
    }
}

// Without @SpringBootApplication, you would need:
@Configuration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.myapp"})
public class Application {
    // Same main method
}

// For testing, you can use @SpringBootTest
@SpringBootTest
public class ApplicationTests {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService;
    
    @Test
    public void contextLoads() {
        assertThat(userService).isNotNull();
    }
    
    @Test
    public void testUserCreation() {
        User user = userService.createUser("John", "john@example.com");
        assertThat(user.getId()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(user.getName()).isEqualTo("John");
    }
}

// Configuration properties binding
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
@Component
public class AppConfig {
    
    private String name;
    private int batchSize = 100;
    
    // getters/setters
}

// In application.properties
app.name=My Application
app.batch-size=200

// CommandLineRunner for startup tasks
@Component
public class StartupRunner implements CommandLineRunner {
    
    @Override
    public void run(String... args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Application started successfully!");
        // Perform initialization tasks
    }
}

// ApplicationRunner alternative
@Component
public class AppStartupRunner implements ApplicationRunner {
    
    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("Application arguments: " + Arrays.toString(args.getSourceArgs()));
    }
}

The @SpringBootApplication annotation is the cornerstone of every Spring Boot application, enabling all the framework's powerful features with minimal configuration.

annotations

What does @SpringBootApplication do?

Quick Answer

Combines 3 annotations.

Detailed Explanation

The @SpringBootApplication annotation is a meta-annotation that serves as a shortcut for three essential Spring annotations, making it the cornerstone of any Spring Boot application. Here's what each component does:

  • @Configuration: Indicates that the class can be used by the Spring IoC container as a source of bean definitions. Methods annotated with @Bean within this class will be processed to create Spring beans.

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Tells Spring Boot to start adding beans based on classpath settings, property settings, and other factors. This is where the 'magic' of auto-configuration happens - Spring Boot automatically configures beans for features like data sources, message converters, and security based on what's available.

  • @ComponentScan: Instructs Spring to scan for components (classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.) in the current package and all sub-packages. This is how Spring discovers and registers your application's beans.

By using @SpringBootApplication, you enable all these features with a single annotation, placed typically on the main application class. This annotation also enables other features like @EnableWebMvc if Spring MVC is on the classpath, but only if you haven't already configured it manually.

The annotation has attributes you can customize:

  • scanBasePackages: Specify packages to scan for components
  • exclude: Exclude specific auto-configuration classes
  • excludeName: Exclude by bean names

This single annotation replaces what would otherwise require multiple annotations and extensive XML configuration in traditional Spring applications.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.example.common"},  // Custom scan packages
    exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class}  // Exclude specific auto-configs
)
public class Application {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
    
    // This method creates a bean that can be injected elsewhere
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyServiceImpl();
    }
}

// Without @SpringBootApplication, you would need:
@Configuration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan
public class Application {
    // Same main method
}

The annotation is typically placed on the class that contains the main method, and Spring Boot uses this as the starting point for component scanning. It automatically scans the package of the annotated class and all sub-packages.

Advanced configuration:

@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {"com.example.web", "com.example.service"},
    exclude = {
        DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class,  // Don't auto-configure database
        SecurityAutoConfiguration.class     // Don't auto-configure security
    },
    excludeName = {"myCustomBean"}  // Exclude specific bean by name
)
public class MyApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Custom SpringApplication configuration
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(MyApplication.class);
        app.setBannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF);  // Disable banner
        app.setWebApplicationType(WebApplicationType.NONE);  // Non-web application
        app.run(args);
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Profile("dev")  // Only create this bean in dev profile
    public DataSource devDataSource() {
        return new EmbeddedDatabaseBuilder()
            .setType(EmbeddedDatabaseType.H2)
            .build();
    }
    
    @Bean
    @Profile("prod")  // Only create this bean in prod profile
    public DataSource prodDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url("jdbc:mysql://prod-db:3306/myapp")
            .username("${DB_USER}")
            .password("${DB_PASSWORD}")
            .build();
    }
}

The @SpringBootApplication annotation is the entry point that enables Spring Boot's auto-configuration magic, component scanning, and bean management, allowing developers to create powerful applications with minimal configuration.

boot

What does SpringApplication.run() do?

Quick Answer

Bootstraps the application.

Detailed Explanation

SpringApplication.run() is the entry point that bootstraps a Spring Boot application. It creates the ApplicationContext, performs component scanning, applies auto-configuration, starts the embedded server, and runs any CommandLineRunners or ApplicationRunners.

What it does:

  1. Creates ApplicationContext: Sets up the Spring container
  2. Component Scanning: Finds and registers beans with stereotypes
  3. Auto-Configuration: Applies configuration based on classpath
  4. Embedded Server: Starts Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow if web starter present
  5. Runs Runners: Executes CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner beans
  6. Handles Shutdown: Registers shutdown hooks for graceful termination

The method returns a ConfigurableApplicationContext that can be used to access beans programmatically.

Spring Boot provides several ways to run applications:

  • SpringApplication.run() - standard approach
  • SpringApplicationBuilder - fluent API for complex setups
  • SpringApplication.exit() - for programmatic shutdown

The main class should be annotated with @SpringBootApplication and contain the main method.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Standard way to run
        SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// Alternative approaches
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Using SpringApplication for more control
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(MyApplication.class);
        app.setBannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF);  // Disable banner
        app.setWebApplicationType(WebApplicationType.NONE);  // Non-web app
        app.setAdditionalProfiles("dev");  // Set active profiles
        
        ConfigurableApplicationContext context = app.run(args);
        
        // Access beans programmatically
        MyService service = context.getBean(MyService.class);
        service.doSomething();
    }
}

// Using SpringApplicationBuilder (fluent API)
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new SpringApplicationBuilder(MyApplication.class)
            .bannerMode(Banner.Mode.CONSOLE)
            .profiles("dev")
            .properties("server.port=9090")
            .run(args);
    }
}

// CommandLineRunner for startup tasks
@Component
public class StartupRunner implements CommandLineRunner {
    
    @Override
    public void run(String... args) throws Exception {
        logger.info("Application started with args: {}", Arrays.toString(args));
        // Perform startup tasks
    }
}

// ApplicationRunner (similar but with ApplicationArguments)
@Component
public class AppRunner implements ApplicationRunner {
    
    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) throws Exception {
        logger.info("Application started!");
        
        // Access different types of arguments
        logger.info("Option args: {}", args.getOptionNames());
        logger.info("Non-option args: {}", args.getNonOptionArgs());
        
        // Check for specific flags
        if (args.containsOption("init-data")) {
            initializeSampleData();
        }
        
        if (args.containsOption("validate")) {
            performValidation();
        }
    }
}

Configuration options:

# Application properties
spring.main.banner-mode=console
spring.main.web-application-type=servlet
spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true
spring.main.allow-circular-references=false

# Command line arguments
# --spring.profiles.active=prod
# --server.port=8443

The SpringApplication.run() method is the heart of Spring Boot, handling all the complex setup and initialization automatically.

dependency-injection

What is @Autowired?

Quick Answer

Dependency Injection.

Detailed Explanation

@Autowired is a core Spring Framework annotation that enables automatic dependency injection (DI), a fundamental concept in Spring and Spring Boot applications. It tells the Spring IoC (Inversion of Control) container to automatically inject a matching bean into the annotated field, constructor, or setter method, eliminating the need for manual instantiation and wiring of dependencies.

How dependency injection works:

  1. Bean Discovery: Spring scans for classes annotated with component stereotypes (@Component, @Service, etc.)
  2. Type Matching: When @Autowired is encountered, Spring looks for beans of the required type
  3. Injection: The matching bean is automatically injected into the annotated dependency
  4. Singleton Management: Spring manages bean lifecycle and ensures singletons are reused

Injection types and their use cases:

  • Constructor Injection (recommended): Dependencies are provided through constructor parameters. Preferred because it makes dependencies explicit, enables immutable objects, and is testable.

  • Field Injection: Direct injection into private fields. Most common but makes testing harder and hides dependencies.

  • Setter Injection: Injection through setter methods. Useful for optional dependencies that can be changed at runtime.

Resolution strategies:

  • By Type: Default behavior - matches beans by class type
  • By Name: Uses field/method name when multiple beans of same type exist
  • @Qualifier: Explicitly specifies which bean to inject when multiple candidates exist
  • @Primary: Marks a bean as primary candidate for injection

Best practices for dependency injection:

  • Prefer Constructor Injection: Makes dependencies explicit and enables immutable objects
  • Use Field Injection Sparingly: Only for optional dependencies in test-friendly code
  • Avoid Circular Dependencies: Design your components to prevent circular references
  • Use @Qualifier for Clarity: When multiple implementations exist, explicitly specify which to use
  • Keep Components Focused: Each component should have a single responsibility
  • Test with Mocks: DI makes it easy to inject mock dependencies for unit testing

Common pitfalls to avoid:

  • Circular Dependencies: When A depends on B and B depends on A
  • Multiple Candidates: When Spring can't decide which bean to inject
  • Missing Beans: When no suitable bean is found for injection
  • Performance Issues: Creating too many beans or complex dependency graphs

Spring Boot enhances DI with auto-configuration, automatically providing beans for common frameworks (DataSource, JdbcTemplate, ObjectMapper, etc.) based on classpath dependencies.

Code Example
// Service layer - business logic
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    // Field injection (not recommended for required dependencies)
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection (recommended approach)
    private final EmailService emailService;
    private final AuditService auditService;
    
    @Autowired  // Can be omitted in Spring 4.3+ for single constructors
    public UserService(EmailService emailService, AuditService auditService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    // Setter injection (for optional dependencies)
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setNotificationService(NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    public User createUser(CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = new User(request.getEmail(), request.getName());
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);
        
        // Use injected email service
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(saved);
        
        // Optional dependency - check before use
        if (notificationService != null) {
            notificationService.notifyUserCreation(saved);
        }
        
        return saved;
    }
}

// Repository layer - data access
@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    // Spring Data JPA provides implementation automatically
}

// Email service implementations
@Service
@Qualifier("smtpEmailService")
public class SmtpEmailService implements EmailService {
    
    @Override
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User user) {
        // SMTP implementation
        System.out.println("Sending welcome email via SMTP to: " + user.getEmail());
    }
}

@Service
@Qualifier("mockEmailService")
public class MockEmailService implements EmailService {
    
    @Override
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User user) {
        // Mock implementation for testing
        System.out.println("Mock: Would send email to: " + user.getEmail());
    }
}

// Controller using specific implementation
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    @Autowired
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody @Valid CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(user);
    }
}

// Configuration class with @Autowired
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Autowired
    private Environment environment;
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url(environment.getProperty("spring.datasource.url"))
            .username(environment.getProperty("spring.datasource.username"))
            .password(environment.getProperty("spring.datasource.password"))
            .build();
    }
}

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# Custom properties
app.email.enabled=true
app.notification.enabled=false

Testing with mocked dependencies:

@SpringBootTest
public class UserServiceTest {
    
    @Mock
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Mock
    private EmailService emailService;
    
    @InjectMocks
    private UserService userService;
    
    @Test
    public void testCreateUser() {
        // Arrange
        CreateUserRequest request = new CreateUserRequest("john@example.com", "John Doe");
        User savedUser = new User(1L, "john@example.com", "John Doe");
        
        when(userRepository.save(any(User.class))).thenReturn(savedUser);
        
        // Act
        User result = userService.createUser(request);
        
        // Assert
        assertEquals(savedUser, result);
        verify(emailService).sendWelcomeEmail(savedUser);
    }
}

@Autowired enables loose coupling and testability by allowing Spring to manage object creation and dependency resolution automatically.

dependency-injection

What is @Autowired?

Quick Answer

It marks a dependency, constructor, or setter to be auto-injected by Spring's dependency injection facilities.

Detailed Explanation

@Autowired is a core annotation in Spring Framework that enables automatic dependency injection. It tells the Spring IoC (Inversion of Control) container to automatically wire (inject) a matching bean into the annotated field, constructor, or setter method. This is the foundation of Spring's dependency injection mechanism, promoting loose coupling and testability.

Injection types:

  1. Constructor Injection (recommended): Dependencies are provided through constructor parameters. Spring calls the constructor with matching beans from the context.

  2. Field Injection: Dependencies are injected directly into private fields. This is the most common but least testable approach.

  3. Setter Injection: Dependencies are injected through setter methods, allowing for optional dependencies.

How Spring resolves dependencies:

  • By Type: Looks for beans of the exact required type
  • By Name: Uses the field/method name if multiple beans of same type exist
  • By Qualifier: Uses @Qualifier annotation to specify which bean to inject
  • By Collection: Can inject all beans of a type into a Collection or Map

The annotation supports:

  • required = false: Makes injection optional (no exception if bean not found)
  • @Qualifier: Specifies which bean to inject when multiple candidates exist
  • @Primary: Marks a bean as the primary choice for injection

Best practices:

  • Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies (immutable, testable)
  • Use setter/field injection only for optional dependencies
  • Avoid circular dependencies
  • Use @Qualifier to disambiguate when multiple beans of same type exist
  • Avoid circular dependencies
  • Use @Required for setter injection (though deprecated in favor of constructor)

Spring Boot's auto-configuration creates many beans automatically, making @Autowired work seamlessly for common components like DataSource, JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, etc.

Code Example
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    // Field injection (not recommended for required dependencies)
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection (recommended approach)
    private final EmailService emailService;
    private final AuditService auditService;
    
    @Autowired  // Optional in Spring 4.3+ for single constructors
    public UserService(EmailService emailService, 
                      @Autowired(required = false) AuditService auditService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    // Setter injection (for optional dependencies)
    private NotificationService notificationService;
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setNotificationService(NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    public User createUser(CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = new User(request.getEmail(), request.getName());
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);
        
        // Required dependency - always available
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(saved);
        
        // Optional dependency - check before use
        if (auditService != null) {
            auditService.logUserCreation(saved);
        }
        
        if (notificationService != null) {
            notificationService.notifyAdmin(saved);
        }
        
        return saved;
    }
}

// When multiple implementations exist
interface EmailService {
    void sendWelcomeEmail(User user);
}

@Service
@Qualifier("smtpEmailService")
public class SmtpEmailService implements EmailService {
    // Implementation using SMTP
}

@Service  
@Qualifier("mockEmailService")
public class MockEmailService implements EmailService {
    // Mock implementation for testing
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("smtpEmailService")  // Specify which implementation
    public NotificationService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
}

// Injecting collections of beans
@Service
public class PluginManager {
    
    private final List<DataProcessor> processors;
    private final Map<String, DataProcessor> processorMap;
    
    @Autowired
    public PluginManager(List<DataProcessor> processors, 
                        Map<String, DataProcessor> processorMap) {
        this.processors = processors;
        this.processorMap = processorMap;
    }
    
    public void processData(String data) {
        processors.forEach(processor -> processor.process(data));
    }
}

public class DatabaseService {
    
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource;  // From spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
    
    @Autowired
    private JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;  // Auto-configured
    
    @Autowired
    private ObjectMapper objectMapper;  // Jackson ObjectMapper
    
    @Autowired
    private RestTemplate restTemplate;  // For HTTP calls
}

The @Autowired annotation eliminates the need for manual bean lookup and wiring, allowing developers to focus on business logic while Spring handles the infrastructure.

di

What is @Autowired?

Quick Answer

Marks a dependency for injection.

Detailed Explanation

@Autowired is a core annotation in Spring that enables automatic dependency injection. It tells the Spring IoC container to automatically wire (inject) a matching bean into the annotated field, constructor, or setter method. This is a key part of Spring's dependency injection mechanism.

Injection types:

  • Field Injection: Direct injection into private fields (most common but least testable)
  • Constructor Injection: Injection through constructor parameters (preferred by Spring team)
  • Setter Injection: Injection through setter methods

How it works:

  1. Spring scans for beans in the application context
  2. When it encounters @Autowired, it looks for a bean of the required type
  3. If multiple beans of the same type exist, it can use @Qualifier to specify which one
  4. If no matching bean is found, it throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException

The annotation can be made optional with required = false, in which case injection will be skipped if no bean is found.

Spring Boot's auto-configuration heavily relies on DI to provide ready-to-use beans for common functionalities.

Best practices:

  • Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies
  • Use field injection sparingly (mainly for optional dependencies)
  • Avoid circular dependencies
  • Use @Qualifier when multiple beans of same type exist
Code Example
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    // Field injection (not recommended for required dependencies)
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection (recommended)
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired  // Can be omitted in Spring 4.3+ for single constructors
    public UserService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    // Setter injection (for optional dependencies)
    private AuditService auditService;
    
    @Autowired(required = false)
    public void setAuditService(AuditService auditService) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
    }
    
    public User createUser(CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = new User(request.getEmail(), request.getName());
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);
        
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(saved);
        
        if (auditService != null) {
            auditService.logUserCreation(saved);
        }
        
        return saved;
    }
}

// When multiple implementations exist
@Service
@Qualifier("emailService")
public class SmtpEmailService implements EmailService {
    // SMTP implementation
}

@Service
@Qualifier("mockEmailService")
public class MockEmailService implements EmailService {
    // Mock implementation for testing
}

@Service
public class NotificationService {
    
    private final EmailService emailService;
    
    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("emailService")  // Specify which implementation to use
    public NotificationService(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
}

  • JdbcTemplate
  • EntityManager
  • ObjectMapper (Jackson)
  • RestTemplate
  • And many more...
di

What is @Component?

Quick Answer

Generic stereotype for a Spring-managed bean.

Detailed Explanation

@Component is a fundamental stereotype annotation in Spring that marks a class as a Spring-managed bean. It's the generic form of component annotation, and more specific stereotypes like @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are meta-annotations that extend @Component.

Key characteristics:

  • Component Scanning: Classes annotated with @Component are automatically detected during classpath scanning
  • Bean Registration: Spring registers these classes as beans in the application context
  • Dependency Injection: Beans can be injected into other components using @Autowired
  • Singleton Scope: By default, components are singletons within the container

Specialized stereotypes:

  • @Service: For business logic classes
  • @Repository: For data access classes (includes exception translation)
  • @Controller/@RestController: For web controllers

Best practices:

  • Use the most specific stereotype when possible
  • Prefer constructor injection over field injection
  • Use meaningful class names
  • Keep components focused on single responsibilities
  • Use @Component for generic components that don't fit other stereotypes

Spring Boot's @ComponentScan automatically scans for these annotations when @SpringBootApplication is used.

Code Example
// Generic component
@Component
public class UtilityService {
    
    public String formatDate(LocalDate date) {
        return date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE);
    }
    
    public boolean isValidEmail(String email) {
        return email != null && email.contains("@");
    }
}

// Service layer - business logic
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    private final UtilityService utilityService;  // Injected component
    
    @Autowired
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository, UtilityService utilityService) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.utilityService = utilityService;
    }
    
    public User createUser(String email, String name) {
        if (!utilityService.isValidEmail(email)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email");
        }
        
        User user = new User(email, name);
        user.setCreatedDate(utilityService.formatDate(LocalDate.now()));
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}

// Repository layer - data access
@Repository
public class UserRepository {
    
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    
    @Autowired
    public UserRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }
    
    public User save(User user) {
        // Database operations
        return user;
    }
}

// Controller layer - web handling
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    @Autowired
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request.getEmail(), request.getName());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(user);
    }
}

public class AppConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public ObjectMapper objectMapper() {
        ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
        mapper.registerModule(new JavaTimeModule());
        return mapper;
    }
}

        System.out.println("Application started successfully!");
    }
}

Stereotype annotations help organize code by layer and enable automatic component discovery and wiring.

mappings

What is @RequestMapping?

Quick Answer

It maps HTTP requests to handler methods of MVC and REST controllers.

Detailed Explanation

@RequestMapping is a fundamental annotation in Spring MVC that maps HTTP requests to specific handler methods in controller classes. It serves as the bridge between HTTP requests and your application's business logic.

Key Features:

  • URL Mapping: Maps requests based on URL patterns
  • HTTP Methods: Restricts mapping to specific HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.)
  • Request Parameters: Can map based on request parameters or headers
  • Content Types: Supports content negotiation (produces/consumes)
  • Inheritance: Can be used at class level (base path) and method level

Mapping Levels:

  • Class Level: Defines a base path for all methods in the controller
  • Method Level: Defines specific paths and HTTP methods for individual endpoints

Specialized Variants (introduced in Spring 4.3):

  • @GetMapping - for GET requests
  • @PostMapping - for POST requests
  • @PutMapping - for PUT requests
  • @DeleteMapping - for DELETE requests
  • @PatchMapping - for PATCH requests

These variants are preferred over @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET) for better readability.

Path Variables: Use {variable} in the path and @PathVariable to extract values from the URL.

Request Parameters: Use @RequestParam for query parameters.

Request Body: Use @RequestBody for JSON/XML request bodies.

Spring Boot's auto-configuration sets up the necessary infrastructure for request mapping to work out of the box.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")  // Class-level mapping - base path
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /api/users - Get all users
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/{id} - Get user by ID
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUserById(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/search?name=john&age=25 - Search with parameters
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<User> searchUsers(
            @RequestParam String name,
            @RequestParam(required = false) Integer age) {
        return userService.searchUsers(name, age);
    }
    
    // POST /api/users - Create new user
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder
            .fromCurrentRequest()
            .path("/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
            .toUri();
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(user);
    }
    
    // PUT /api/users/{id} - Update user
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id,
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateUserRequest request) {
        return userService.updateUser(id, request)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/users/{id} - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteUser(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/{id}/posts - Nested resources
    @GetMapping("/{id}/posts")
    public List<Post> getUserPosts(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.getUserPosts(id);
    }
}

// Request/Response DTOs
public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank @Email
    private String email;
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    
    // getters/setters
}

public class UpdateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    
    // getters/setters
}

Advanced mapping examples:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1")
public class AdvancedController {
    
    // Multiple HTTP methods for same path
    @RequestMapping(value = "/resource", method = {RequestMethod.GET, RequestMethod.POST})
    public String handleResource() {
        return "Handled GET or POST";
    }
    
    // Content negotiation
    @GetMapping(
        value = "/data",
        produces = {"application/json", "application/xml"}
    )
    public Data getData() {
        return new Data();
    }
    
    // Header-based mapping
    @GetMapping(value = "/admin", headers = "X-API-Key")
    public String adminEndpoint() {
        return "Admin access";
    }
    
    // Matrix variables (Spring 3.2+)
    @GetMapping("/books/{id}")
    public Book getBook(
            @PathVariable Long id,
            @MatrixVariable(required = false) String format) {
        // URL: /books/123;format=pdf
        return bookService.getBook(id, format);
    }
}

The @RequestMapping system is highly flexible and supports complex routing scenarios, making it easy to build RESTful APIs with clean, intuitive URL structures.

annotations

What is @RequestMapping?

Quick Answer

It maps HTTP requests to handler methods of MVC and REST controllers.

Detailed Explanation

@RequestMapping is a fundamental annotation in Spring MVC that maps HTTP requests to specific handler methods in controller classes. It provides flexible routing capabilities and can be applied at both class and method levels to define URL patterns, HTTP methods, content types, and other request characteristics.

Key features:

  • URL Mapping: Defines the URL path that the method handles
  • HTTP Methods: Specifies which HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.) the method accepts
  • Content Negotiation: Controls request/response content types via consumes and produces
  • Request Parameters: Can map based on query parameters, headers, and cookies
  • Path Variables: Extracts values from URL path segments
  • Request Body: Binds request body to method parameters

Best practices:

  • Use specific HTTP method annotations (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.) for clarity
  • Prefer path variables over request parameters for resource identification
  • Use consumes and produces for API versioning and content negotiation
  • Combine class-level and method-level mappings for clean URL hierarchies
  • Use @RequestMapping at class level for common path prefixes

The annotation supports:

  • Ant-style path patterns (/users/*/profile)
  • Regular expressions in paths
  • Matrix variables
  • Custom request conditions

Spring Boot provides convenient shortcut annotations like @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping that are equivalent to @RequestMapping with specific method values.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/users")  // Class-level mapping - base path for all methods
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users - Get all users
    @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
    
    // Equivalent using shortcut annotation
    @GetMapping  // Same as @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)
    public List<User> getUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users/{id} - Get user by ID
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // POST /api/v1/users - Create new user
    @PostMapping(
        consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,  // Only accept JSON
        produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE   // Only produce JSON
    )
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody @Valid User user) {
        User saved = userService.save(user);
        return ResponseEntity.created(
            ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(saved.getId())
                .toUri()
        ).body(saved);
    }
    
    // PUT /api/v1/users/{id} - Update user
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @RequestBody @Valid User user) {
        return userService.updateUser(id, user)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/v1/users/{id} - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteById(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users/search - Search with query parameters
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<User> searchUsers(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String name,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String email,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) {
        
        return userService.searchUsers(name, email, PageRequest.of(page, size));
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users/{id}/posts - Nested resources
    @GetMapping("/{userId}/posts")
    public List<Post> getUserPosts(@PathVariable Long userId) {
        return userService.getUserPosts(userId);
    }
    
    // Advanced mapping with headers and content type
    @PostMapping(
        path = "/import",
        consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
        produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
        headers = "X-API-Version=1"  // Require specific header
    )
    public ResponseEntity<ImportResult> importUsers(
            @RequestBody List<User> users,
            @RequestHeader("Authorization") String authToken) {
        
        ImportResult result = userService.importUsers(users, authToken);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(result);
    }
    
    // Mapping with multiple HTTP methods
    @RequestMapping(
        path = "/bulk",
        method = {RequestMethod.POST, RequestMethod.PUT}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<BulkResult> bulkOperation(@RequestBody BulkRequest request) {
        BulkResult result = userService.processBulkOperation(request);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(result);
    }
}

    private String name;

    // Constructor, getters, setters, validation annotations
}

    // Constructor, getters, setters

spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.parameter-name=mediaType
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.json=application/json
spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.media-types.xml=application/xml

Path patterns support:

  • ? - matches one character
  • * - matches zero or more characters within a path segment
  • ** - matches zero or more path segments

Examples:

  • /users/*/profile - matches /users/123/profile
  • /users/** - matches /users/123/posts/456
  • /files/{filename:.+} - matches any filename with extension
web

What is @RequestMapping?

Quick Answer

Maps HTTP requests to handler methods.

Detailed Explanation

@RequestMapping is a fundamental annotation in Spring MVC that maps HTTP requests to specific handler methods in controller classes. It provides flexible routing capabilities and can be applied at both class and method levels to define URL patterns, HTTP methods, content types, and other request characteristics.

Key features:

  • URL Mapping: Defines the URL path that the method handles
  • HTTP Methods: Specifies which HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.) the method accepts
  • Content Negotiation: Controls request/response content types via consumes and produces
  • Request Parameters: Can map based on query parameters, headers, and cookies
  • Path Variables: Extracts values from URL path segments
  • Request Body: Binds request body to method parameters

Best practices:

  • Use specific HTTP method annotations (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.) for clarity
  • Prefer path variables over request parameters for resource identification
  • Use consumes and produces for API versioning and content negotiation
  • Combine class-level and method-level mappings for clean URL hierarchies
  • Use @RequestMapping at class level for common path prefixes

The annotation supports:

  • Ant-style path patterns (/users/*/profile)
  • Regular expressions in paths
  • Matrix variables
  • Custom request conditions

Spring Boot provides convenient shortcut annotations like @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping that are equivalent to @RequestMapping with specific method values.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/users")  // Class-level mapping - base path for all methods
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users - Get all users
    @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
    
    // Equivalent using shortcut annotation
    @GetMapping  // Same as @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)
    public List<User> getUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users/{id} - Get user by ID
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // POST /api/v1/users - Create new user
    @PostMapping(
        consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,  // Only accept JSON
        produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE   // Only produce JSON
    )
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody @Valid User user) {
        User saved = userService.save(user);
        return ResponseEntity.created(
            ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(saved.getId())
                .toUri()
        ).body(saved);
    }
    
    // PUT /api/v1/users/{id} - Update user
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @RequestBody @Valid User user) {
        return userService.updateUser(id, user)
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/v1/users/{id} - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteById(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users/search - Search with query parameters
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<User> searchUsers(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String name,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String email,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) {
        
        return userService.searchUsers(name, email, PageRequest.of(page, size));
    }
    
    // GET /api/v1/users/{id}/posts - Nested resources
    @GetMapping("/{userId}/posts")
    public List<Post> getUserPosts(@PathVariable Long userId) {
        return userService.getUserPosts(userId);
    }
    
    // Advanced mapping with headers and content type
    @PostMapping(
        path = "/import",
        consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
        produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE,
        headers = "X-API-Version=1"  // Require specific header
    )
    public ResponseEntity<ImportResult> importUsers(
            @RequestBody List<User> users,
            @RequestHeader("Authorization") String authToken) {
        
        ImportResult result = userService.importUsers(users, authToken);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(result);
    }
    
    // Mapping with multiple HTTP methods
    @RequestMapping(
        path = "/bulk",
        method = {RequestMethod.POST, RequestMethod.PUT}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<BulkResult> bulkOperation(@RequestBody BulkRequest request) {
        BulkResult result = userService.processBulkOperation(request);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(result);
    }
}

// Supporting classes

    private String name;
    private String email;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters, validation annotations
}

public class ImportResult {
    private int successCount;
    private int failureCount;
    private List<String> errors;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

    private List<User> users;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

annotations

What is @RestController?

Quick Answer

A convenience annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody.

Detailed Explanation

@RestController is a specialized version of the @Controller annotation designed specifically for building RESTful web services in Spring Boot. It combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, automatically serializing method return values to JSON (or XML) and writing them directly to the HTTP response body. This eliminates the need for manual @ResponseBody annotations on every handler method.

Key characteristics:

  • RESTful Focus: Unlike @Controller which is designed for MVC applications that return views, @RestController is optimized for APIs that return data
  • Automatic Serialization: Return values are automatically converted to JSON using Jackson by default
  • No View Resolution: Responses are pure data; no template rendering occurs
  • Content Negotiation: Supports multiple response formats (JSON, XML) based on client Accept headers
  • HTTP Status Codes: Methods can return ResponseEntity for full control over status codes and headers

When to use @RestController:

  • Building REST APIs
  • Microservices communication
  • AJAX endpoints in single-page applications
  • Mobile app backends
  • Third-party API integrations

Best practices:

  • Use meaningful HTTP status codes
  • Implement proper error handling
  • Include HATEOAS links for discoverable APIs
  • Use DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) for request/response payloads
  • Validate input with Bean Validation annotations

@RestController is part of Spring MVC and requires a web starter dependency to function.

Code Example
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserRestController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    // Constructor injection - no @Autowired needed in Spring 4.3+
    public UserRestController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    // GET /api/users - Retrieve all users
    @GetMapping
    public List<UserDto> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers().stream()
            .map(this::convertToDto)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
    
    // GET /api/users/{id} - Retrieve single user
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // POST /api/users - Create new user
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        UserDto response = convertToDto(user);
        
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
            .path("/{id}")
            .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
            .toUri();
        
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(response);
    }
    
    // PUT /api/users/{id} - Update existing user
    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> updateUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @Valid @RequestBody UpdateUserRequest request) {
        
        return userService.updateUser(id, request)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // DELETE /api/users/{id} - Delete user
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        if (userService.deleteById(id)) {
            return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
        }
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
    
    // PATCH /api/users/{id} - Partial update
    @PatchMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDto> patchUser(
            @PathVariable Long id, 
            @RequestBody Map<String, Object> updates) {
        
        return userService.patchUser(id, updates)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(convertToDto(user)))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    // Helper method for DTO conversion
    private UserDto convertToDto(User user) {
        return new UserDto(user.getId(), user.getEmail(), user.getName());
    }
}

// Data Transfer Objects
public class UserDto {
    private Long id;
    private String email;
    private String name;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank(message = "Email is required")
    @Email(message = "Invalid email format")
    private String email;
    
    @NotBlank(message = "Name is required")
    @Size(min = 2, max = 50, message = "Name must be between 2 and 50 characters")
    private String name;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

public class UpdateUserRequest {
    @Email
    private String email;
    
    @Size(min = 2, max = 50)
    private String name;
    
    // Constructor, getters, setters
}

spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null

# Content negotiation
