spring.mvc.contentnegotiation.parameter-name=mediaType

For XML support, add dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-dataformat-xml</artifactId>
</dependency>

The controller automatically handles:

  • JSON serialization/deserialization
  • HTTP method routing
  • Request parameter binding
  • Validation and error responses
  • Content negotiation
  • CORS if configured
DataTransactions

What is @Transactional?

Quick Answer

Ensures that a method runs within a database transaction.

Detailed Explanation

@Transactional is a crucial annotation in Spring that provides declarative transaction management, ensuring data consistency and integrity in database operations. It creates a transactional context around method execution, automatically handling commit and rollback scenarios.

Core Concepts:

  • ACID Properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
  • Declarative: No manual transaction code required
  • Automatic Rollback: On unchecked exceptions
  • Propagation: Controls transaction behavior across method calls
  • Isolation: Manages concurrent transaction visibility
  • Timeout: Prevents long-running transactions
  • Read-Only: Optimization for read operations

Transaction Lifecycle:

  1. Begin: Transaction starts when method enters
  2. Execute: Business logic runs within transaction
  3. Commit: Changes saved if no exceptions
  4. Rollback: Changes reverted on errors

Propagation Behaviors:

  • REQUIRED (default): Join existing or create new
  • REQUIRES_NEW: Always create new transaction
  • SUPPORTS: Join if exists, execute non-transactional if not
  • MANDATORY: Must join existing, fail if none
  • NEVER: Must execute non-transactional, fail if transaction exists
  • NOT_SUPPORTED: Suspend existing and execute non-transactional

Isolation Levels:

  • DEFAULT: Database default
  • READ_UNCOMMITTED: Dirty reads possible
  • READ_COMMITTED: No dirty reads
  • REPEATABLE_READ: No dirty or non-repeatable reads
  • SERIALIZABLE: No phantom reads, strictest

Best Practices:

  • Service Layer: Apply at service methods, not repositories
  • Public Methods: Only works on public methods
  • Checked Exceptions: Don't rollback by default
  • Performance: Use read-only for queries
  • Testing: Test both success and failure scenarios

Common Use Cases:

  • Data Integrity: Multi-table operations
  • Consistency: Related database changes
  • Error Handling: Automatic cleanup on failures
  • Performance: Batch operations

The annotation simplifies transaction management while providing powerful configuration options.

Code Example
@Service
public class OrderService {
    
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;
    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;
    
    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository, 
                        InventoryService inventoryService,
                        PaymentService paymentService,
                        NotificationService notificationService) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }
    
    // Default transaction - REQUIRED propagation
    @Transactional
    public Order createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        // Reserve inventory
        inventoryService.reserveItems(request.getItems());
        
        // Process payment
        PaymentResult payment = paymentService.processPayment(request.getPayment());
        
        // Create order
        Order order = new Order(request.getCustomerId(), request.getItems(), payment.getId());
        Order saved = orderRepository.save(order);
        
        // Send notification (will be rolled back if any previous step fails)
        notificationService.sendOrderConfirmation(saved);
        
        return saved;
    }
    
    // Read-only transaction for queries
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<Order> getCustomerOrders(Long customerId) {
        return orderRepository.findByCustomerId(customerId);
    }
    
    // Requires new transaction - independent of caller
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void processRefund(Long orderId) {
        Order order = orderRepository.findById(orderId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException("Order not found"));
        
        // Refund payment
        paymentService.refundPayment(order.getPaymentId());
        
        // Update order status
        order.setStatus(OrderStatus.REFUNDED);
        orderRepository.save(order);
        
        // Send refund notification
        notificationService.sendRefundNotification(order);
    }
    
    // Custom rollback rules
    @Transactional(rollbackFor = {PaymentException.class, InventoryException.class})
    public void processComplexOrder(ComplexOrderRequest request) {
        try {
            // Complex business logic that might throw custom exceptions
            validateOrder(request);
            createOrder(request);
            updateCustomerLoyalty(request.getCustomerId());
        } catch (ValidationException e) {
            // Don't rollback for validation errors
            throw e;
        }
    }
    
    // No rollback for checked exceptions
    @Transactional(dontRollbackOn = {NotificationException.class})
    public void updateOrderWithNotification(Long orderId, UpdateOrderRequest request) {
        Order order = orderRepository.findById(orderId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException("Order not found"));
        
        order.update(request);
        orderRepository.save(order);
        
        try {
            notificationService.sendUpdateNotification(order);
        } catch (NotificationException e) {
            // Log but don't rollback
            logger.warn("Failed to send notification", e);
        }
    }
}

// Custom exceptions
public class PaymentException extends RuntimeException {
    public PaymentException(String message) { super(message); }
}

public class InventoryException extends RuntimeException {
    public InventoryException(String message) { super(message); }
}

public class ValidationException extends RuntimeException {
    public ValidationException(String message) { super(message); }
}

public class NotificationException extends Exception {
    public NotificationException(String message) { super(message); }
}

@Repository
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(Long customerId);
    
    @Modifying
    @Transactional
    @Query("UPDATE Order o SET o.status = :status WHERE o.id = :id")
    int updateOrderStatus(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("status") OrderStatus status);
}

@Entity
public class Order {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;
    
    private Long customerId;
    
    @OneToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
    private List<OrderItem> items;
    
    private Long paymentId;
    
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PENDING;
    
    // getters, setters, constructors
    
    public void update(UpdateOrderRequest request) {
        // Update logic
    }
}

Testing transactional behavior:

@SpringBootTest
public class OrderServiceTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderService orderService;
    
    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository orderRepository;
    
    @Autowired
    private InventoryService inventoryService;
    
    @Test
    void shouldRollbackOnPaymentFailure() {
        // Given
        CreateOrderRequest request = createOrderRequest();
        doThrow(new PaymentException("Payment failed"))
            .when(inventoryService).reserveItems(any());
        
        // When & Then
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> orderService.createOrder(request))
            .isInstanceOf(PaymentException.class);
        
        // Verify rollback - no order should be saved
        assertThat(orderRepository.count()).isZero();
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldCommitOnSuccess() {
        // Given
        CreateOrderRequest request = createOrderRequest();
        
        // When
        Order order = orderService.createOrder(request);
        
        // Then
        assertThat(order.getId()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(orderRepository.findById(order.getId())).isPresent();
    }
    
    @Test
    void refundShouldRunInSeparateTransaction() {
        // Test REQUIRES_NEW propagation
        // Create order in one transaction
        Order order = orderService.createOrder(createOrderRequest());
        
        // Refund in separate transaction - should succeed even if first transaction fails
        assertThatCode(() -> orderService.processRefund(order.getId()))
            .doesNotThrowAnyException();
    }
}

Configuration for transaction management:

# application.properties
spring.transaction.default-timeout=30
spring.transaction.rollback-on-commit-failure=true

# JPA transaction settings
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true

@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
public class TransactionConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        JpaTransactionManager transactionManager = new JpaTransactionManager();
        transactionManager.setEntityManagerFactory(emf);
        return transactionManager;
    }
    
    // Custom transaction attributes
    @Bean
    public TransactionAttributeSource transactionAttributeSource() {
        return new AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource();
    }
}

Programmatic transaction management (alternative to declarative):

@Service
public class ProgrammaticTransactionService {
    
    @Autowired
    private PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager;
    
    public void executeInTransaction() {
        DefaultTransactionDefinition def = new DefaultTransactionDefinition();
        def.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRED);
        def.setIsolationLevel(TransactionDefinition.ISOLATION_READ_COMMITTED);
        def.setTimeout(30);
        
        TransactionStatus status = transactionManager.getTransaction(def);
        try {
            // Business logic
            businessOperation();
            transactionManager.commit(status);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            transactionManager.rollback(status);
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

The @Transactional annotation provides a clean, declarative way to manage transactions, ensuring data consistency while keeping business logic focused and readable.

configuration

What is @Value?

Quick Answer

Injects values from properties files.

Detailed Explanation

@Value is a Spring annotation that injects values from property sources (like application.properties) into fields, constructor parameters, or method parameters. It supports Spring Expression Language (SpEL) for dynamic value resolution.

Key features:

  • Property injection: Injects values from application.properties/yml
  • SpEL support: Allows expressions like ${property.name} and #{expression}
  • Default values: Provides fallback values with : syntax
  • Type conversion: Automatically converts strings to appropriate types
  • Dynamic refresh: Can be refreshed at runtime with @RefreshScope

Common use cases:

  • Configuration values
  • Environment-specific settings
  • Dynamic property resolution
  • Computed values using SpEL

Best practices:

  • Use for simple values and external configuration
  • Prefer @ConfigurationProperties for complex configuration objects
  • Provide sensible defaults
  • Use SpEL for computed values
  • Consider @RefreshScope for dynamic configuration
Code Example
@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    // Simple property injection
    @Value("${app.email.from}")
    private String fromEmail;
    
    // Property with default value
    @Value("${app.email.enabled:true}")
    private boolean emailEnabled;
    
    // Numeric property with default
    @Value("${app.email.port:587}")
    private int smtpPort;
    
    // List property
    @Value("${app.email.recipients}")
    private String[] defaultRecipients;
    
    // SpEL expression
    @Value("#{${app.email.timeout} ?: 5000}")
    private int timeout;
    
    // System property
    @Value("${java.home}")
    private String javaHome;
    
    // Environment variable
    @Value("${JAVA_HOME}")
    private String javaHomeEnv;
    
    // Constructor injection
    private final String smtpHost;
    
    public EmailService(@Value("${app.email.host:smtp.gmail.com}") String smtpHost) {
        this.smtpHost = smtpHost;
    }
    
    public void sendEmail(String to, String subject, String body) {
        if (!emailEnabled) {
            return;
        }
        
        // Use injected values
        System.out.println("Sending email from " + fromEmail + " to " + to);
        System.out.println("Using SMTP host: " + smtpHost + " port: " + smtpPort);
    }
}

// Configuration class using @Value
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    
    @Value("${app.thread.pool.size:10}")
    private int threadPoolSize;
    
    @Bean
    public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor taskExecutor() {
        ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
        executor.setCorePoolSize(threadPoolSize);
        executor.setMaxPoolSize(threadPoolSize * 2);
        executor.setQueueCapacity(100);
        return executor;
    }
}

In application.properties:

# Email configuration
app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com
app.email.enabled=true
app.email.host=smtp.gmail.com
app.email.port=587
app.email.timeout=10000
app.email.recipients=admin@myapp.com,support@myapp.com

# Thread pool configuration
app.thread.pool.size=20

Advanced SpEL examples:

@Component
public class SpELExamples {
    
    // System properties
    @Value("#{systemProperties['user.home']}")
    private String userHome;
    
    // Environment variables
    @Value("#{environment['JAVA_HOME']}")
    private String javaHome;
    
    // Mathematical operations
    @Value("#{${app.max.size} * 2}")
    private int doubledMaxSize;
    
    // String operations
    @Value("#{'${app.name}'.toUpperCase()}")
    private String appNameUpper;
    
    // Conditional expressions
    @Value("#{${app.debug} ? 'DEBUG' : 'INFO'}")
    private String logLevel;
    
    // Collection access
    @Value("#{${app.servers}.split(',')[0]}")
    private String primaryServer;
}

Using @RefreshScope for dynamic updates:

@Configuration
@RefreshScope
public class DynamicConfig {
    
    @Value("${app.dynamic.value}")
    private String dynamicValue;
    
    // This value can be changed at runtime via actuator refresh endpoint
}

@Value provides flexible property injection with SpEL support for dynamic configuration needs.

configuration

What is application.properties?

Quick Answer

The default configuration file for Spring Boot applications.

Detailed Explanation

application.properties (or its YAML equivalent application.yml) is the primary mechanism for externalizing configuration in Spring Boot applications. It allows you to define properties that can be changed without recompiling the code, enabling different configurations for different environments (development, testing, production).

Key features:

  • External Configuration: Properties can be overridden by environment variables, system properties, command-line arguments, or external property files
  • Profile-Specific: You can have application-dev.properties, application-prod.properties, etc., activated by spring.profiles.active
  • Hierarchical Loading: Properties are loaded in a specific order, with later sources overriding earlier ones
  • Type-Safe Binding: Spring Boot automatically binds properties to @ConfigurationProperties classes
  • Validation: Properties can be validated using Bean Validation annotations

Common categories of properties:

  • Server: server.port, server.servlet.context-path
  • Database: spring.datasource.url, spring.datasource.username
  • Logging: logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
  • Security: spring.security.user.name, spring.security.user.password
  • Custom Application: Your own properties like app.email.from

Spring Boot also supports YAML format for more complex hierarchical configurations, and properties can reference each other using ${property.name} syntax.

The file is typically placed in src/main/resources/ and is automatically picked up by Spring Boot's auto-configuration.

Code Example
# Server configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# Database configuration
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# JPA/Hibernate configuration
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# Logging configuration
logging.level.com.example.myapp=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=INFO
logging.file.name=app.log

# Custom application properties
app.name=My Spring Boot App
app.version=1.0.0
app.email.enabled=true
app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com

# Profile activation
spring.profiles.active=dev

YAML equivalent (application.yml):

server:
  port: 8080
  servlet:
    context-path: /api

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
    driver-class-name: org.h2.Driver
    username: sa
    password: ""
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop
    show-sql: true

logging:
  level:
    com.example.myapp: DEBUG
    org.springframework.web: INFO
  file:
    name: app.log

app:
  name: My Spring Boot App
  version: 1.0.0
  email:
    enabled: true
    from: noreply@myapp.com

spring:
  profiles:
    active: dev

Using properties in code:

@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    @Value("${app.email.from}")
    private String fromEmail;
    
    @Value("${app.email.enabled:false}")
    private boolean emailEnabled;
    
    // Or using @ConfigurationProperties
}

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
@Component
public class AppProperties {
    private String name;
    private String version;
    private Email email = new Email();
    
    public static class Email {
        private boolean enabled;
        private String from;
        // getters/setters
    }
    // getters/setters
}

Profile-specific files:

  • application-dev.properties (activated with --spring.profiles.active=dev)
  • application-prod.properties

Command line override: java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090 --app.name="Production App"

configuration

What is application.properties?

Quick Answer

The default configuration file for Spring Boot.

Detailed Explanation

application.properties (and its YAML counterpart application.yml) is the primary mechanism for externalizing configuration in Spring Boot applications. It allows developers to configure application behavior, database connections, logging levels, and custom properties without modifying source code. This enables different configurations for development, testing, and production environments.

Key features:

  • External Configuration: Properties can be overridden by environment variables, system properties, command-line arguments, or external property files
  • Hierarchical Loading: Properties are loaded in a specific order, with later sources taking precedence
  • Profile-Specific: Use application-dev.properties, application-prod.properties for environment-specific settings
  • Type-Safe Binding: Properties automatically bind to @ConfigurationProperties classes
  • Validation: Properties can be validated using Bean Validation annotations
  • Placeholder Resolution: Properties can reference each other using ${property.name} syntax

Loading order (last wins):

  1. Default properties (from Spring Boot)
  2. @PropertySource annotations
  3. application.properties/yml in classpath
  4. Profile-specific files (application-{profile}.properties/yml)
  5. External files (outside JAR)
  6. Environment variables
  7. System properties
  8. Command-line arguments

Common configuration categories:

  • Server: Port, context path, SSL
  • Database: URL, credentials, connection pooling
  • Logging: Levels, file output, format
  • Security: Authentication, authorization
  • Custom Application: Business logic settings

Spring Boot supports both Properties and YAML formats, with YAML being preferred for complex hierarchical configurations.

Code Example
# Server Configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api
server.servlet.session.timeout=30m
server.error.include-message=always
server.error.include-binding-errors=always

# Database Configuration
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5

# JPA/Hibernate Configuration
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.use_sql_comments=true

# Logging Configuration
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.example.myapp=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
logging.level.org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql.BasicBinder=TRACE
logging.file.name=application.log
logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-file-size=10MB
logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-history=30

# Security Configuration
spring.security.user.name=admin
spring.security.user.password=secret
spring.security.user.roles=ADMIN

# Custom Application Properties
app.name=My Spring Boot Application
app.version=1.0.0
app.description=${app.name} v${app.version}
app.features.enabled=true
app.cache.size=1000
app.email.enabled=true
app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com
app.email.host=smtp.gmail.com
app.email.port=587
app.email.username=myapp@gmail.com
app.email.password=app-password

# Actuator Configuration
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
management.info.env.enabled=true
management.metrics.export.jmx.enabled=true

# Externalized Configuration
app.external.config.path=/etc/myapp/config.properties

# Profile Activation
spring.profiles.active=dev

YAML equivalent (application.yml):

server:
  port: 8080
  servlet:
    context-path: /api
    session:
      timeout: 30m
  error:
    include-message: always
    include-binding-errors: always

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
    driver-class-name: org.h2.Driver
    username: sa
    password: ""
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      minimum-idle: 5
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop
    show-sql: true
    properties:
      hibernate:
        format_sql: true
        use_sql_comments: true

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example.myapp: DEBUG
    org.springframework.web: DEBUG
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG
    "org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql.BasicBinder": TRACE
  file:
    name: application.log
  logback:
    rollingpolicy:
      max-file-size: 10MB
      max-history: 30

app:
  name: My Spring Boot Application
  version: 1.0.0
  description: ${app.name} v${app.version}
  features:
    enabled: true
  cache:
    size: 1000
  email:
    enabled: true
    from: noreply@myapp.com
    host: smtp.gmail.com
    port: 587
    username: myapp@gmail.com
    password: app-password

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
  info:
    env:
      enabled: true
  metrics:
    export:
      jmx:
        enabled: true

spring:
  profiles:
    active: dev

Profile-specific files:

  • application-dev.properties (for development)
  • application-test.properties (for testing)
  • application-prod.properties (for production)

Example application-prod.properties:

server.port=8443
spring.profiles.active=prod

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/myapp
spring.datasource.username=${DB_USER}
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

logging.level.root=WARN
logging.level.com.example.myapp=INFO

app.cache.size=10000

Using properties in code:

@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    @Value("${app.email.from}")
    private String fromEmail;
    
    @Value("${app.email.enabled:false}")
    private boolean emailEnabled;
    
    @Value("${app.description}")
    private String appDescription;
}

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
@Component
public class AppProperties {
    
    private String name;
    private String version;
    private Features features;
    private Cache cache;
    private Email email;
    
    // Getters and setters
    
    public static class Features {
        private boolean enabled;
        // getters/setters
    }
    
    public static class Cache {
        private int size;
        // getters/setters
    }
    
    public static class Email {
        private boolean enabled;
        private String from;
        private String host;
        private int port;
        private String username;
        private String password;
        // getters/setters
    }
}

Command-line overrides:

java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090 --app.name="Production App" --spring.profiles.active=prod

Environment variables:

export SERVER_PORT=9090
export APP_EMAIL_PASSWORD=mypassword

External configuration files:

java -jar app.jar --spring.config.location=file:/etc/myapp/application.properties

The configuration system allows applications to be deployed to different environments without code changes, making them highly portable and maintainable.

lifecycle

What is CommandLineRunner?

Quick Answer

Interface to run code after startup.

Detailed Explanation

CommandLineRunner is a Spring Boot interface that allows you to execute code after the application context has been loaded and before the application starts accepting requests. It's commonly used for initialization tasks, data seeding, or startup validation.

Key features:

  • Execution timing: Runs after Spring context initialization but before the application is fully ready
  • Multiple runners: Multiple beans can implement CommandLineRunner and will execute in order
  • Access to args: Receives command-line arguments passed to the application
  • Exception handling: Exceptions in run() will prevent application startup

Use cases:

  • Database initialization or data seeding
  • Cache warming
  • External service connectivity checks
  • Startup logging and validation
  • Background task initialization

ApplicationRunner is similar but provides structured access to arguments.

Best practices:

  • Keep startup tasks lightweight
  • Handle exceptions properly
  • Use @Order to control execution sequence
  • Consider @PostConstruct for simpler initialization
  • Avoid long-running operations that delay startup
Code Example
@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}

// Simple CommandLineRunner
@Component
public class StartupRunner implements CommandLineRunner {
    
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(StartupRunner.class);
    
    @Override
    public void run(String... args) throws Exception {
        logger.info("Application started with args: {}", Arrays.toString(args));
        
        // Perform startup tasks
        initializeData();
        validateConfiguration();
    }
    
    private void initializeData() {
        // Initialize database, caches, etc.
        logger.info("Initializing application data...");
    }
    
    private void validateConfiguration() {
        // Validate external dependencies
        logger.info("Validating configuration...");
    }
}

// Multiple runners with ordering
@Component
@Order(1)  // Execute first
public class DatabaseInitializer implements CommandLineRunner {
    
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource;
    
    @Override
    public void run(String... args) throws Exception {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            // Initialize database schema
            logger.info("Database initialized successfully");
        }
    }
}

@Component
@Order(2)  // Execute second
public class CacheWarmer implements CommandLineRunner {
    
    @Autowired
    private CacheService cacheService;
    
    @Override
    public void run(String... args) throws Exception {
        cacheService.warmCache();
        logger.info("Cache warmed successfully");
    }
}

// Using ApplicationRunner for structured arguments
@Component
public class ArgsProcessor implements ApplicationRunner {
    
    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) throws Exception {
        logger.info("Application started!");
        
        // Access different types of arguments
        logger.info("Option args: {}", args.getOptionNames());
        logger.info("Non-option args: {}", args.getNonOptionArgs());
        
        // Check for specific flags
        if (args.containsOption("init-data")) {
            initializeSampleData();
        }
        
        if (args.containsOption("validate")) {
            performValidation();
        }
    }
    
    private void initializeSampleData() {
        // Initialize sample data
    }
    
    private void performValidation() {
        // Perform validation
    }
}

Running with arguments:

# Pass arguments to CommandLineRunner
java -jar app.jar --init-data --validate arg1 arg2

Alternative to CommandLineRunner:

@Component
public class PostConstructExample {
    
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        // Simpler initialization
        // Runs after dependency injection
    }
}

CommandLineRunner is ideal for startup tasks that need to run after the application context is fully initialized.

DataJPA

What is JpaRepository?

Quick Answer

It is a Spring Data interface that provides standard CRUD operations + paging + sorting.

Detailed Explanation

JpaRepository is a core interface in Spring Data JPA that provides a comprehensive set of database operations out-of-the-box, eliminating the need for boilerplate CRUD code. It extends CrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository, offering both basic and advanced data access patterns.

Core Features:

  • CRUD Operations: save(), findById(), findAll(), delete(), deleteById(), existsById()
  • Batch Operations: saveAll(), deleteAll(), deleteAllInBatch()
  • Counting: count() for total records
  • Fluent API: deleteAllInBatch() for efficient bulk operations

Advanced Capabilities:

  • Pagination: findAll(Pageable) for memory-efficient large dataset handling
  • Sorting: findAll(Sort) for ordered results
  • Query Methods: Automatic query generation from method names
  • Custom Queries: @Query annotations for complex SQL/JPQL
  • Specifications: Dynamic query building with JpaSpecificationExecutor

Inheritance Hierarchy:

  • Repository (base interface)
  • CrudRepository (basic CRUD)
  • PagingAndSortingRepository (pagination + sorting)
  • JpaRepository (JPA-specific features)

Performance Considerations:

  • Lazy Loading: Relationships are loaded on-demand by default
  • Batch Operations: Use deleteAllInBatch() for large deletions to avoid N+1 queries
  • Query Optimization: Custom @Query methods can use JOIN FETCH for eager loading
  • Indexing: Ensure proper database indexes for query performance

Best Practices:

  • Interface Segregation: Create specific repositories for different aggregates
  • Query Methods: Use derived queries for simple cases, @Query for complex ones
  • DTO Projections: Use interface projections to avoid loading full entities
  • Transaction Boundaries: Repository methods are typically @Transactional
  • Testing: Use @DataJpaTest for repository unit tests

Common Use Cases:

  • Basic CRUD: Standard entity management
  • Search Functionality: Derived query methods for filtering
  • Admin Interfaces: Paginated listings with sorting
  • Data Import/Export: Batch operations for data migration
  • Audit Trails: Versioned entities with @Version

JpaRepository works seamlessly with Spring Boot's auto-configuration, requiring only the entity class and repository interface definition.

Code Example
// Entity
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
public class Product {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private BigDecimal price;
    
    @Column
    private String category;
    
    @Column
    private boolean active = true;
    
    @CreationTimestamp
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
    
    @UpdateTimestamp
    private LocalDateTime updatedAt;
    
    // getters, setters, constructors
}

// Repository Interface
@Repository
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    
    // Derived query methods - Spring Data generates implementation
    List<Product> findByCategory(String category);
    List<Product> findByActiveTrue();
    List<Product> findByPriceBetween(BigDecimal min, BigDecimal max);
    List<Product> findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String name);
    
    // Custom queries with @Query
    @Query("SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.price > :minPrice AND p.category = :category")
    List<Product> findExpensiveProductsInCategory(@Param("minPrice") BigDecimal minPrice, 
                                                 @Param("category") String category);
    
    // Native SQL queries
    @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE created_at > :since", nativeQuery = true)
    List<Product> findRecentProducts(@Param("since") LocalDateTime since);
    
    // Pagination and sorting
    Page<Product> findByCategoryOrderByPriceDesc(String category, Pageable pageable);
    
    // Exists queries for validation
    boolean existsByNameAndCategory(String name, String category);
    
    // Count queries
    long countByCategory(String category);
    
    // Delete queries
    void deleteByCategory(String category);
}

// Service using the repository
@Service
@Transactional
public class ProductService {
    
    private final ProductRepository productRepository;
    
    public ProductService(ProductRepository productRepository) {
        this.productRepository = productRepository;
    }
    
    // Basic CRUD
    public Product createProduct(Product product) {
        return productRepository.save(product);
    }
    
    public Optional<Product> getProduct(Long id) {
        return productRepository.findById(id);
    }
    
    public List<Product> getAllProducts() {
        return productRepository.findAll();
    }
    
    // Search with pagination
    public Page<Product> searchProducts(String category, Pageable pageable) {
        return productRepository.findByCategoryOrderByPriceDesc(category, pageable);
    }
    
    // Custom query usage
    public List<Product> findPremiumProducts(String category) {
        return productRepository.findExpensiveProductsInCategory(
            new BigDecimal("100.00"), category);
    }
    
    // Batch operations
    public void deactivateCategory(String category) {
        List<Product> products = productRepository.findByCategory(category);
        products.forEach(p -> p.setActive(false));
        productRepository.saveAll(products);
    }
    
    // Validation
    public boolean isProductNameUnique(String name, String category) {
        return !productRepository.existsByNameAndCategory(name, category);
    }
}

// Controller
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
public class ProductController {
    
    private final ProductService productService;
    
    public ProductController(ProductService productService) {
        this.productService = productService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public Page<Product> getProducts(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String category,
            @PageableDefault(sort = "createdAt", direction = Sort.Direction.DESC) Pageable pageable) {
        if (category != null) {
            return productService.searchProducts(category, pageable);
        }
        return new PageImpl<>(productService.getAllProducts());
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/premium/{category}")
    public List<Product> getPremiumProducts(@PathVariable String category) {
        return productService.findPremiumProducts(category);
    }
}

<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
    <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

# application.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:productdb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

Usage examples:

// In a test or main method
@SpringBootApplication
public class JpaDemoApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(JpaDemoApplication.class, args);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo) {
        return args -> {
            // Create sample data
            repo.save(new Product("Laptop", new BigDecimal("999.99"), "Electronics"));
            repo.save(new Product("Book", new BigDecimal("29.99"), "Education"));
            
            // Query data
            System.out.println("All products:");
            repo.findAll().forEach(System.out::println);
            
            System.out.println("Electronics:");
            repo.findByCategory("Electronics").forEach(System.out::println);
            
            // Pagination
            Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(0, 10, Sort.by("price").descending());
            Page<Product> page = repo.findAll(pageable);
            System.out.println("Page: " + page.getContent());
        };
    }
}
concepts

What is a Starter POM?

Quick Answer

A set of convenient dependency descriptors.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Starters are curated dependency descriptors that bundle together commonly used libraries for specific functionalities. They eliminate the need to manually manage version compatibility between interdependent libraries, as all dependencies within a starter are guaranteed to work together through Spring Boot's Bill of Materials (BOM).

Key characteristics:

  • Dependency Curation: Each starter includes all necessary libraries for a specific use case
  • Version Management: The Spring Boot BOM ensures compatible versions across all starters
  • Transitive Dependencies: Includes not just direct dependencies but also required transitive ones
  • Convention over Configuration: Follows Spring Boot's sensible defaults philosophy
  • Modular Design: Include only the starters needed for your application

Starters are named with the pattern spring-boot-starter-* and provide:

  • Core functionality (web, data, security)
  • Integration capabilities (JMS, AMQP, mail)
  • Development tools (test, actuator)
  • Third-party integrations (cloud platforms, databases)

The BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) manages versions for over 100 dependencies, ensuring compatibility and reducing version conflicts.

Custom starters can be created for organizational common dependencies using the naming convention yourcompany-starter-*.

Starters automatically trigger relevant auto-configuration when added to the classpath.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<project>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.1.0</version>
    </parent>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Web Development Starter -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Data Access Starter -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Database Driver -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
            <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Security Starter -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Testing Starter -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Actuator for Monitoring -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Mail Integration -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-mail</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Caching Support -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        
        <!-- Validation -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>

What each starter includes:

spring-boot-starter-web:

  • Spring MVC for web development
  • Tomcat as embedded servlet container
  • Jackson for JSON processing
  • Spring Web for RESTful services

spring-boot-starter-data-jpa:

  • Spring Data JPA
  • Hibernate as JPA implementation
  • JDBC API
  • Transaction management

spring-boot-starter-security:

spring-boot-starter-test:

  • Mockito
  • AssertJ
  • JSON Path
  • Hamcrest

spring-boot-starter-actuator:

  • Health checks
  • Metrics collection
  • Application info
  • Environment details

Without starters (manual dependency management):

<dependencies>

</dependencies>

Gradle equivalent:

plugins {

<!-- Custom starter POM -->

Starters simplify dependency management and ensure that Spring Boot applications have all necessary libraries with compatible versions, reducing configuration errors and maintenance overhead.

configuration

What is a Starter?

Quick Answer

A dependency descriptor.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Starters are curated sets of dependencies that bundle together commonly used libraries for specific functionalities. They eliminate the need to manually manage version compatibility between different libraries, as all dependencies within a starter are guaranteed to work together.

Key characteristics:

  • Convention over Configuration: Each starter follows Spring Boot's philosophy of providing sensible defaults
  • Transitive Dependencies: They include not just the main libraries but also all necessary transitive dependencies
  • Version Management: The Spring Boot Bill of Materials (BOM) ensures all starter dependencies use compatible versions
  • Modular: You can include only the starters you need for your application

Common starters include:

  • spring-boot-starter-web: For web applications (includes Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON processing, and Tomcat as the embedded server)
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jpa: For JPA-based data access (includes Hibernate, Spring Data JPA)
  • spring-boot-starter-security: For authentication and authorization
  • spring-boot-starter-test: For testing (includes JUnit, Mockito, Spring Test)
  • spring-boot-starter-actuator: For production monitoring

Starters also enable auto-configuration; when you add a starter, Spring Boot automatically configures the associated beans and settings. For example, adding spring-boot-starter-web automatically configures a DispatcherServlet, JSON converters, and an embedded Tomcat server.

You can create custom starters for your organization's common dependencies, following the naming convention yourproject-starter.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependencies>
    <!-- Web starter includes: Spring MVC, Tomcat, Jackson, Spring Web -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Data JPA starter includes: Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, JDBC -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- H2 database for development/testing -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
        <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Without starters, you would need to manually specify each dependency:

<dependencies>
    <!-- Manual web dependencies - error-prone -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
        <version>5.3.23</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-web</artifactId>
        <version>5.3.23</version>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
        <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
        <version>2.13.4</version>
    </dependency>
    <!-- And many more with version conflicts possible -->
</dependencies>

The BOM ensures version compatibility:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>2.7.5</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

Creating a custom starter:

<!-- Custom starter POM -->
<project>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>example-starter</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    
    <dependencies>
        <!-- Include your common dependencies -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.example</groupId>
            <artifactId>common-library</artifactId>
            <version>1.0.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>

@AutoConfigureAfter(DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
public class ExampleAutoConfiguration {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    public ExampleService exampleService() {
        return new ExampleService();
    }
}

In META-INF/spring.factories:

org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=\

Starters simplify dependency management and ensure that Spring Boot applications have all necessary libraries with compatible versions, reducing configuration errors and maintenance overhead.

server

What is an Embedded Server?

Quick Answer

A web server (like Tomcat, Jetty) that runs inside the application JAR.

Detailed Explanation

An embedded server in Spring Boot is a web server that runs within the application process itself, rather than requiring deployment to an external servlet container. This is a key innovation that simplifies deployment and enables Spring Boot's 'just run' philosophy.

Supported embedded servers:

  • Tomcat (default): Mature, production-ready servlet container
  • Jetty: Lightweight, high-performance alternative
  • Undertow: Modern, non-blocking server from JBoss
  • Netty: Asynchronous, event-driven networking framework

Key benefits:

  • Simplified Deployment: No need to install/configure external servers
  • Portability: Application is self-contained and runnable anywhere Java is installed
  • Development Speed: Instant startup without server management
  • Cloud-Native: Perfect for containerized deployments (Docker, Kubernetes)
  • Microservices: Each service can run independently with its own server
  • Hot Reloading: Faster development cycles with DevTools

Embedded servers include:

  • HTTP/HTTPS support
  • WebSocket capabilities
  • Servlet API compatibility
  • Static resource serving
  • Request/response filtering

Configuration is externalized through application.properties, allowing different settings per environment.

For production deployments, embedded servers can be configured for:

  • SSL/TLS termination
  • Connection pooling
  • Request compression
  • Access logging
  • Health monitoring

Spring Boot also supports traditional WAR deployment for legacy environments requiring external servers.

Embedded servers revolutionized Java web development by eliminating the complexity of server management and enabling the microservices architecture that powers modern cloud applications.

Code Example
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

server.port=8080

@SpringBootApplication
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}
auto-configuration

What is Auto-Configuration?

Quick Answer

It is a mechanism that automatically configures your Spring application based on the jar dependencies that you have added.

Detailed Explanation

Auto-Configuration is one of Spring Boot's most powerful features that eliminates the need for manual bean configuration in most cases. It works by intelligently analyzing the classpath and automatically configuring beans based on the libraries present, following the principle of 'convention over configuration'.

How it Works:

  • Spring Boot scans the classpath for specific libraries and frameworks
  • Based on what's found, it automatically creates and configures beans
  • It uses conditional annotations to determine when to apply configurations
  • Configurations can be overridden by explicit bean definitions

Key Benefits:

  • Reduced Boilerplate: No need to manually configure common beans like DataSource, EntityManager, or ObjectMapper
  • Intelligent Defaults: Sensible defaults that work out-of-the-box
  • Conditional Configuration: Only configures what's needed based on dependencies
  • Extensible: You can create custom auto-configurations for your libraries

Common Auto-Configurations:

  • Database: Configures DataSource, JdbcTemplate, EntityManager for JPA
  • Web: Sets up DispatcherServlet, JSON converters, embedded server
  • Security: Configures basic authentication and authorization
  • Messaging: Auto-configures JMS, RabbitMQ, or Kafka beans
  • Caching: Sets up caching providers like Redis, EhCache, or Caffeine

Conditional Annotations:

  • @ConditionalOnClass: Only if a class is present on classpath
  • @ConditionalOnMissingBean: Only if no bean of that type exists
  • @ConditionalOnProperty: Based on configuration properties
  • @ConditionalOnWebApplication: Only in web applications

Best Practices:

  • Let Spring Boot handle common configurations
  • Override only when necessary with explicit @Bean methods
  • Use @ConditionalOnProperty for optional features
  • Test configurations with @SpringBootTest

Auto-configuration makes Spring Boot applications extremely productive while remaining flexible for customization.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

// With spring-boot-starter-data-jpa on classpath, these are auto-configured:
// - DataSource bean (using H2 if no other DB configured)
// - EntityManagerFactory
// - TransactionManager
// - JpaRepository implementations

@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    // Spring Data JPA auto-implements this interface
    List<User> findByEmail(String email);
}

@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    // Constructor injection - UserRepository is auto-configured
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    public List<User> getUsersByEmail(String email) {
        return userRepository.findByEmail(email);
    }
}

With spring-boot-starter-web:

@RestController
public class HelloController {
    
    // ObjectMapper is auto-configured for JSON serialization
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public Map<String, String> hello() {
        return Map.of("message", "Hello World");
    }
}

Custom auto-configuration:

@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(MyLibrary.class)
@ConditionalOnMissingBean
@EnableConfigurationProperties(MyProperties.class)
public class MyAutoConfiguration {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "my.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
    public MyService myService(MyProperties properties) {
        return new MyService(properties);
    }
}

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "my")
public class MyProperties {
    private boolean enabled = true;
    private String url;
    // getters/setters
}

In application.properties:

# Enable/disable auto-configuration
my.enabled=true
my.url=http://example.com

To exclude auto-configurations:

@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class})
public class MyApp {
    // Custom DataSource configuration
}

Auto-configuration dramatically reduces configuration code while maintaining flexibility for customization.

concepts

What is Auto-Configuration?

Quick Answer

Spring automatically configures beans based on classpath.

Detailed Explanation

Auto-configuration is a core Spring Boot feature that automatically configures beans and settings based on the dependencies present on the classpath. It eliminates the need for explicit configuration by applying sensible defaults when certain conditions are met.

How it works:

  1. Classpath scanning: Spring Boot scans for JARs and classes
  2. Conditional configuration: Beans are created only when specific conditions are met
  3. Convention over configuration: Uses sensible defaults that work for most cases
  4. Override capability: Defaults can be customized or completely overridden

Key components:

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Enables auto-configuration (included in @SpringBootApplication)
  • @ConditionalOnClass: Creates beans only if classes are present
  • @ConditionalOnMissingBean: Creates beans only if no other bean exists
  • @ConditionalOnProperty: Creates beans based on property values

Common auto-configurations:

  • DataSource (when JDBC driver present)
  • JPA/Hibernate (when spring-boot-starter-data-jpa present)
  • Web MVC (when spring-boot-starter-web present)
  • Security (when spring-boot-starter-security present)

Benefits:

  • Reduced configuration: Most applications need minimal setup
  • Convention over configuration: Sensible defaults work out-of-the-box
  • Flexibility: Can override or disable specific auto-configurations
  • Extensibility: Custom auto-configurations can be created

Debugging auto-configuration:

  • Use --debug flag to see what auto-configuration is applied
  • Check conditional reports in logs
  • Exclude unwanted auto-configurations
Code Example
// Example of how auto-configuration works
// When spring-boot-starter-web is added, these beans are auto-configured:

@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass({Servlet.class, DispatcherServlet.class})
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(value = DispatcherServlet.class, name = DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration.DEFAULT_DISPATCHER_SERVLET_BEAN_NAME)
@AutoConfigureOrder(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
@AutoConfigureAfter(ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration.class)
public class DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnBean(MultipartResolver.class)
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(name = DispatcherServlet.MULTIP_RESOLVER_BEAN_NAME)
    public MultipartResolver multipartResolver(MultipartResolver resolver) {
        return resolver;
    }
    
    // More auto-configured beans...
}

// When spring-boot-starter-data-jpa is added:
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass({LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean.class, EntityManager.class})
@EnableConfigurationProperties(JpaProperties.class)
@AutoConfigureAfter({HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration.class})
public class JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "spring.data.jpa.repositories", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
    public JpaRepositoryFactoryBean<?> jpaRepositoryFactoryBean() {
        return new JpaRepositoryFactoryBean<>();
    }
}

// Custom auto-configuration example
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(RedisConnectionFactory.class)
@AutoConfigureAfter(RedisAutoConfiguration.class)
public class CustomRedisAutoConfiguration {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    public RedisTemplate<String, Object> redisTemplate(RedisConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
        RedisTemplate<String, Object> template = new RedisTemplate<>();
        template.setConnectionFactory(connectionFactory);
        template.setKeySerializer(new StringRedisSerializer());
        template.setValueSerializer(new Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer<>(Object.class));
        return template;
    }
}

Configuration in application.properties:

# Control auto-configuration
# Exclude specific auto-configurations
spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration

# Debug auto-configuration
logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG

Running with debug:

java -jar app.jar --debug

This will show detailed logs of which auto-configurations were applied, skipped, or failed.

Auto-configuration makes Spring Boot applications work with minimal configuration by automatically setting up beans based on classpath contents and properties. It's the 'magic' that makes Spring Boot so productive for developers.

dependency-injection

What is Dependency Injection (DI)?

Quick Answer

A design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from an external source.

Detailed Explanation

Dependency Injection is a fundamental design pattern in Spring (and Spring Boot) that implements Inversion of Control (IoC). Instead of objects creating their own dependencies (which leads to tight coupling), dependencies are 'injected' from outside, typically by the Spring IoC container. This promotes:

  • Loose Coupling: Classes don't need to know how to create their dependencies
  • Testability: Dependencies can be easily mocked or stubbed in unit tests
  • Maintainability: Changes to dependency implementations don't affect dependent classes
  • Reusability: Components can be reused in different contexts with different dependencies

In Spring Boot, DI is achieved through:

  1. Constructor Injection (preferred): Dependencies are provided through the constructor
  2. Setter Injection: Dependencies are set via setter methods
  3. Field Injection: Dependencies are injected directly into fields (less preferred due to testing difficulties)

The Spring container manages the lifecycle of beans and automatically wires dependencies based on types, names, or qualifiers. Spring Boot's auto-configuration heavily relies on DI to provide ready-to-use beans for common functionalities.

DI is not just about injecting services; it also includes configuration values, data sources, and any other beans that a class might need to function properly.

Code Example
// Service layer - depends on repository
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;  // Dependency
    private final EmailService emailService;      // Another dependency
    
    // Constructor injection - Spring will provide the dependencies
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository, EmailService emailService) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }
    
    public User createUser(String email, String name) {
        User user = new User(email, name);
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);  // Use injected repository
        emailService.sendWelcomeEmail(saved);     // Use injected email service
        return saved;
    }
}

// Repository layer
@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    // Spring Data JPA provides implementation automatically
}

// Email service
@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    @Value("${app.email.from}")  // Configuration injection
    private String fromEmail;
    
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User user) {
        // Implementation would send email
        System.out.println("Sending welcome email to " + user.getEmail());
    }
}

In application.properties:

app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com

This example shows how Spring Boot automatically wires all dependencies, including configuration values, without any explicit configuration.

Quick Answer

Objects get their dependencies from outside.

Detailed Explanation

Dependency Injection is a fundamental design pattern in Spring (and Spring Boot) that implements Inversion of Control (IoC). Instead of objects creating their own dependencies (which leads to tight coupling), dependencies are 'injected' from outside, typically by the Spring IoC container. This promotes:

The Spring container manages the lifecycle of beans and automatically wires dependencies based on types, names, or qualifiers. Spring Boot's auto-configuration heavily relies on DI to provide ready-to-use beans for common functionalities.

DI is not just about injecting services; it also includes configuration values, data sources, and any other beans that a class might need to function properly.

Code Example

    // Spring Data JPA provides implementation automatically
}

// Email service
@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    @Value("${app.email.from}")  // Configuration injection
    private String fromEmail;
    
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(User user) {

    }

In application.properties:

app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com
