server

What is Embedded Server in Spring Boot?

Quick Answer

An embedded server means the servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow) is part of the application JAR, not an external software installed on the machine.

Detailed Explanation

Unlike traditional Java web applications that require deploying WAR files to external servlet containers like Tomcat, JBoss, or WebSphere, Spring Boot applications are self-contained and include an embedded web server within the application JAR. This fundamental shift in deployment model brings several advantages:

Embedded Servers:

  • Tomcat (default): Mature, feature-complete servlet container
  • Jetty: Lightweight, high-performance alternative
  • Undertow: Modern, non-blocking server from JBoss

Benefits:

  • Simplified Deployment: Single JAR file contains everything needed
  • Portability: No need to install/configure external server
  • Consistency: Same server in development, testing, and production
  • Cloud-Native: Perfect for containerization (Docker) and microservices
  • Fast Startup: No separate server startup time

Configuration:

  • Default port: 8080 (configurable via server.port)
  • Context path: / (configurable via server.servlet.context-path)
  • Server-specific properties available for each embedded server

Switching Servers:
You can easily switch between embedded servers by excluding the default and including the desired one in your dependencies.

Production Considerations:
While embedded servers are great for most applications, some organizations prefer external servers for:

  • Centralized server management
  • Advanced server features (clustering, session replication)
  • Legacy deployment requirements

In such cases, you can still build traditional WAR files with Spring Boot.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml - Default Tomcat (included with spring-boot-starter-web) -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Switching to Jetty:

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Switching to Undertow:

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Configuration in application.properties:

# Server port and context
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/myapp

# Tomcat-specific settings
server.tomcat.max-http-header-size=8192
server.tomcat.max-swallow-size=2MB
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=20s

# SSL configuration
server.ssl.key-store=classpath:keystore.p12
server.ssl.key-store-password=changeit
server.ssl.keyStoreType=PKCS12

# Compression
server.compression.enabled=true
server.compression.mime-types=text/html,text/xml,text/plain,text/css,text/javascript,application/javascript,application/json

Running the application:

# Development
mvn spring-boot:run

# Production
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

# With custom port
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar --server.port=9090

For external server deployment (WAR):

<!-- pom.xml -->
<packaging>war</packaging>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>  <!-- Provided by external server -->
</dependency>

@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp extends SpringBootServletInitializer {
    
    @Override
    protected SpringApplicationBuilder configure(SpringApplicationBuilder builder) {
        return builder.sources(MyApp.class);
    }
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

The embedded server approach has become the standard for Spring Boot applications, especially in microservices and cloud-native architectures.

DataH2

What is H2 Database?

Quick Answer

A fast in-memory SQL database often used for testing/development in Spring Boot.

Detailed Explanation

H2 is a lightweight, open-source relational database written in Java that serves as an excellent choice for development, testing, and embedded scenarios in Spring Boot applications. Its in-memory nature and zero-configuration setup make it particularly valuable during development cycles.

Key Characteristics:

  • In-Memory Database: Data stored in RAM, extremely fast for read/write operations
  • Embedded Mode: Runs within the same JVM as the application, no separate process
  • SQL Compliance: Supports standard SQL with some extensions
  • Multiple Modes: In-memory, file-based, or server mode
  • Web Console: Built-in web interface for database inspection and queries
  • Cross-Platform: Pure Java implementation

Use Cases:

  • Development: Rapid prototyping without external database setup
  • Testing: Unit and integration tests with isolated database state
  • Demos: Self-contained applications for presentations
  • Embedded Systems: Applications needing portable database functionality
  • CI/CD: Fast test execution in continuous integration pipelines

Modes of Operation:

  • In-Memory: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb - Data lost when application stops
  • File-Based: jdbc:h2:~/testdb - Persistent storage to file system
  • Server Mode: jdbc:h2:tcp://localhost:9092/testdb - Multi-application access

Spring Boot Integration:

  • Auto-Configuration: Automatically configured when H2 is on classpath
  • Console Access: Web console enabled via spring.h2.console.enabled=true
  • Default Credentials: Username 'sa', empty password
  • DDL Auto: Works with Hibernate's schema generation

Performance Advantages:

  • Speed: Millisecond response times for most operations
  • Resource Light: Minimal memory and CPU footprint
  • Concurrent Access: Supports multiple connections
  • ACID Compliance: Full transactional support

Limitations and Considerations:

  • Data Persistence: In-memory data lost on application restart
  • Production Unsuitable: Not designed for high-concurrency production use
  • Feature Set: Lacks some advanced enterprise database features
  • Memory Constraints: Limited by available RAM

Best Practices:

  • Test Isolation: Use unique database names for different test classes
  • Data Loading: Use schema.sql and data.sql for test data setup
  • Console Security: Disable console in production environments
  • Migration Path: Design schema to be compatible with production databases
  • Connection Pooling: Configure HikariCP for optimal performance

H2 serves as a bridge between development speed and production database compatibility, allowing teams to develop rapidly while maintaining database abstraction.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
    <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

# application.properties - Basic H2 configuration
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# H2 Console (for development)
spring.h2.console.enabled=true
spring.h2.console.path=/h2-console
spring.h2.console.settings.web-allow-others=false

# JPA/Hibernate configuration
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

// Entity example
@Entity
public class User {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
    
    @CreationTimestamp
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
    
    // getters, setters, constructors
}

@Repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
}

@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public User createUser(String email, String name) {
        if (userRepository.findByEmail(email).isPresent()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Email already exists");
        }
        return userRepository.save(new User(email, name));
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request.getEmail(), request.getName());
        return ResponseEntity.created(
            ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
                .toUri()
        ).body(user);
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userRepository.findAll();
    }
}

public class CreateUserRequest {
    private String email;
    private String name;
    // getters/setters
}

-- schema.sql (optional - for custom schema)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS user (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- data.sql (optional - for initial data)
INSERT INTO user (email, name) VALUES
('john@example.com', 'John Doe'),
('jane@example.com', 'Jane Smith');

Accessing H2 Console:

  • URL: http://localhost:8080/h2-console
  • JDBC URL: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
  • Username: sa
  • Password: (leave empty)

Advanced configuration:

# File-based H2 database (persistent)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:file:~/myappdb;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE

# Server mode H2 (accessible from external tools)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:tcp://localhost:9092/testdb

# H2 with MySQL compatibility mode
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb;MODE=MySQL

# Connection pool configuration
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=20000

Testing with H2:

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
public class UserServiceTest {
    
    @Autowired
    private UserService userService;
    
    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;
    
    @Test
    void shouldCreateUser() {
        User user = userService.createUser("test@example.com", "Test User");
        assertThat(user.getId()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(user.getEmail()).isEqualTo("test@example.com");
    }
    
    @Test
    void shouldNotCreateDuplicateEmail() {
        userService.createUser("duplicate@example.com", "User 1");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> 
            userService.createUser("duplicate@example.com", "User 2")
        ).isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }
}

Multiple database configurations:

@Configuration
@Profile("test")
public class TestDatabaseConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Primary
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return new EmbeddedDatabaseBuilder()
            .setType(EmbeddedDatabaseType.H2)
            .addScript("schema.sql")
            .addScript("test-data.sql")
            .build();
    }
}

@Configuration
@Profile("prod")
public class ProductionDatabaseConfig {
    
    @Bean
    @Primary
    @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "spring.datasource")
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }
}

H2 with Flyway/Liquibase for migrations:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

spring.flyway.enabled=true
spring.flyway.locations=classpath:db/migration

-- V1__Create_user_table.sql
CREATE TABLE user (
    id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

The H2 database provides a perfect development companion, offering speed and convenience while maintaining SQL compatibility with production databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL.

actuator

What is Spring Actuator?

Quick Answer

A sub-project of Spring Boot that provides production-ready features to help you monitor and manage your application.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Actuator is a powerful sub-project that provides production-ready features for monitoring and managing Spring Boot applications. It exposes various endpoints that provide insights into the application's internal state, performance metrics, and operational information.

Key Features:

  • Health Checks: /actuator/health - Shows application health status and dependencies
  • Application Info: /actuator/info - Displays custom application information
  • Metrics: /actuator/metrics - Provides various metrics about the application
  • Environment: /actuator/env - Shows environment properties and configuration
  • Beans: /actuator/beans - Lists all Spring beans in the application context
  • Mappings: /actuator/mappings - Shows all HTTP request mappings
  • Configuration: /actuator/configprops - Displays configuration properties
  • Logging: /actuator/loggers - Allows dynamic logging level changes

Security Considerations:

  • Endpoints are sensitive and should be secured in production
  • Use Spring Security to protect actuator endpoints
  • Configure which endpoints are exposed

Integration with Monitoring Tools:

  • Micrometer: For metrics collection and export to various monitoring systems
  • Prometheus: Popular monitoring and alerting toolkit
  • Grafana: For creating dashboards from metrics
  • ELK Stack: Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana for log aggregation

Custom Endpoints:
You can create custom actuator endpoints for application-specific monitoring.

Best Practices:

  • Secure endpoints in production
  • Use appropriate logging levels
  • Monitor key metrics regularly
  • Set up alerts for critical health checks
  • Use structured logging for better observability
Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- For security -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configuration in application.properties:

# Actuator configuration
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/actuator

# Health check details
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized

# Custom info
info.app.name=My Spring Boot App
info.app.version=1.0.0
info.app.java.version=17

# Metrics configuration
management.metrics.export.prometheus.enabled=true

@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

// Custom health indicator
@Component
public class CustomHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    
    @Override
    public Health health() {
        // Custom health check logic
        boolean databaseUp = checkDatabaseConnection();
        
        if (databaseUp) {
            return Health.up()
                .withDetail("database", "Available")
                .build();
        } else {
            return Health.down()
                .withDetail("database", "Unavailable")
                .build();
        }
    }
    
    private boolean checkDatabaseConnection() {
        // Implementation
        return true;
    }
}

// Custom info contributor
@Component
public class CustomInfoContributor implements InfoContributor {
    
    @Override
    public void contribute(Info.Builder builder) {
        builder.withDetail("custom", Map.of(
            "build-time", "2023-12-01",
            "features", List.of("feature1", "feature2")
        ));
    }
}

// Custom actuator endpoint
@Component
@Endpoint(id = "custom")
public class CustomEndpoint {
    
    @ReadOperation
    public Map<String, Object> custom() {
        return Map.of(
            "status", "OK",
            "timestamp", System.currentTimeMillis()
        );
    }
}

Security configuration:

@Configuration
public class ActuatorSecurityConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(authz -> authz
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
        
        return http.build();
    }
}

Available endpoints (when exposed):

  • GET /actuator/health - Application health status
  • GET /actuator/info - Application information
  • GET /actuator/metrics - Available metrics
  • GET /actuator/metrics/{name} - Specific metric value
  • GET /actuator/env - Environment properties
  • GET /actuator/beans - Spring beans
  • GET /actuator/mappings - Request mappings
  • GET /actuator/configprops - Configuration properties
  • GET /actuator/loggers - Logger configuration
  • POST /actuator/loggers/{name} - Change log level

With Micrometer for advanced metrics:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>

@RestController
public class SampleController {
    
    private final Counter requestCounter;
    private final Timer requestTimer;
    
    public SampleController(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.requestCounter = Counter.builder("http_requests_total")
            .description("Total HTTP requests")
            .register(registry);
        
        this.requestTimer = Timer.builder("http_request_duration")
            .description("HTTP request duration")
            .register(registry);
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/api/data")
    public ResponseEntity<String> getData() {
        return requestTimer.recordCallable(() -> {
            requestCounter.increment();
            // Business logic
            return ResponseEntity.ok("Data");
        });
    }
}

Actuator transforms Spring Boot applications from black boxes into transparent, observable systems that are much easier to monitor and maintain in production environments.

tools

What is Spring Boot Actuator?

Quick Answer

Production-ready features.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready features for monitoring and managing Spring Boot applications. It exposes various endpoints that provide insights into the application's health, metrics, configuration, and more.

Key features:

  • Health Checks: /actuator/health - shows application health status
  • Application Info: /actuator/info - displays custom application information
  • Metrics: /actuator/metrics - provides various metrics and statistics
  • Environment: /actuator/env - shows environment properties and configuration
  • Beans: /actuator/beans - lists all Spring beans in the application context
  • Mappings: /actuator/mappings - shows all HTTP request mappings
  • Configuration: /actuator/configprops - displays configuration properties
  • Logging: /actuator/loggers - allows dynamic logging level changes

Security considerations:

  • Endpoints are sensitive and should be secured in production
  • Use Spring Security to restrict access
  • Configure which endpoints are exposed

Actuator integrates with monitoring systems like Prometheus, Grafana, and application servers for comprehensive observability.

Best practices:

  • Secure actuator endpoints in production
  • Customize health checks for application-specific requirements
  • Use metrics for performance monitoring
  • Integrate with external monitoring tools
Code Example
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configuration in application.properties:

# Actuator configuration
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,env
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
management.endpoint.metrics.enabled=true
management.info.env.enabled=true

# Custom application info
info.app.name=My Spring Boot App
info.app.version=1.0.0
info.app.java.version=${java.version}

Custom health indicator:

@Component
public class DatabaseHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    
    @Autowired
    private DataSource dataSource;
    
    @Override
    public Health health() {
        try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            // Test database connection
            return Health.up().build();
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            return Health.down(ex).build();
        }
    }
}

Custom info contributor:

@Component
public class AppInfoContributor implements InfoContributor {
    
    @Override
    public void contribute(Info.Builder builder) {
        builder.withDetail("database", Map.of(
            "type", "H2",
            "version", "2.1.214"
        ));
    }
}

Security configuration:

@Configuration
public class ActuatorSecurityConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {
    
    @Override
    protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeRequests()
            .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("health")).permitAll()
            .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()).hasRole("ADMIN")
            .and()
            .httpBasic();
    }
}

Available endpoints:

  • GET /actuator/health - Application health status
  • GET /actuator/info - Application information
  • GET /actuator/metrics - Available metrics
  • GET /actuator/metrics/{name} - Specific metric value
  • GET /actuator/env - Environment properties
  • GET /actuator/beans - Spring beans
  • GET /actuator/mappings - Request mappings
  • GET /actuator/configprops - Configuration properties
  • GET /actuator/loggers - Logger configuration
  • POST /actuator/loggers/{name} - Change log level

Actuator endpoints provide essential monitoring and management capabilities for production applications.

dev-tools

What is Spring Boot DevTools?

Quick Answer

A module that improves the development experience.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot DevTools is a collection of tools designed to enhance developer productivity during application development. It provides features that make the development cycle faster and more efficient, but automatically disables itself in production to avoid performance overhead.

Key features:

  • Automatic Restart: Monitors classpath changes and automatically restarts the application when code changes. Uses two classloaders (base and restart) to make restarts much faster than cold starts.

  • LiveReload: Automatically refreshes the browser when resources change, eliminating the need to manually refresh during frontend development.

  • Property Defaults: Provides sensible development defaults for properties like template caching, which are different from production settings.

  • Remote Development: Supports remote applications with features like remote debugging and automatic restart.

  • Global Settings: Can be configured globally for all Spring Boot projects on a machine.

DevTools detects changes by monitoring the classpath and triggers restarts for:

  • Java source files
  • Properties/YAML files
  • Templates
  • Static resources

It excludes certain paths from triggering restarts (like static resources and logging config) to avoid unnecessary restarts.

DevTools also provides additional development endpoints and enhanced error pages with detailed information.

Note: DevTools should never be included in production builds as it adds overhead and potential security risks.

Code Example
<!-- pom.xml - Add to dependencies -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>  <!-- Not included in fat JAR -->
</dependency>

Configuration in application.properties:

# DevTools configuration
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=true
spring.devtools.restart.additional-paths=src/main/resources
spring.devtools.restart.exclude=static/**,public/**

# LiveReload configuration
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=true
spring.devtools.livereload.port=35729

# Remote DevTools (for remote debugging)
spring.devtools.remote.secret=mysecret

Global configuration (~/.spring-boot-devtools.properties):

# Global settings for all projects
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=true
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=true

Custom restart triggers:

@Configuration
public class DevToolsConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public FileSystemWatcher fileSystemWatcher() {
        // Custom file watcher for additional paths
        FileSystemWatcher watcher = new FileSystemWatcher();
        watcher.addSourceDirectory(new File("config"));
        return watcher;
    }
}

What triggers a restart:

  • Changes to Java files in classpath
  • Changes to application.properties/yml
  • Changes to templates (Thymeleaf, etc.)
  • Changes to build files (pom.xml)

What doesn't trigger a restart:

  • Static resources (CSS, JS, images)
  • Logging configuration
  • Changes to files in target/ or build/ directories

To manually trigger restart in IDE:

  • Save a Java file
  • Use IDE's build/rebuild
  • Touch a file in monitored path

DevTools also provides enhanced error pages with stack traces, environment info, and request details when exceptions occur during development.

basics

What is Spring Boot?

Quick Answer

An extension of the Spring Framework that simplifies setup and development.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot is a powerful framework designed to simplify the creation of production-ready applications based on the Spring Framework. It adopts an opinionated approach, making assumptions about how you want to configure your application based on common best practices, which significantly reduces the amount of boilerplate code and configuration required. Key components include:

  • Starters: These are dependency descriptors that bundle together all the necessary libraries for specific functionalities. For example, adding 'spring-boot-starter-web' brings in Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON processing, and Tomcat as the embedded server, ensuring version compatibility.

  • Auto-Configuration: Spring Boot automatically configures your application based on the dependencies present on the classpath. If you have HSQLDB on the classpath, it will auto-configure an in-memory database without any explicit configuration.

  • Embedded Servers: Unlike traditional Spring applications that require deploying to an external servlet container, Spring Boot includes an embedded web server (Tomcat by default, but Jetty or Undertow can be used) within the application JAR. This enables 'java -jar' execution and simplifies deployment, especially in cloud environments or containers.

  • Production-Ready Features: Includes built-in support for metrics, health checks, externalized configuration, and logging, making it easier to monitor and manage applications in production.

  • Convention over Configuration: Spring Boot follows the principle of sensible defaults, allowing developers to override only what they need to customize, rather than configuring everything from scratch.

Overall, Spring Boot allows developers to focus on writing business logic while handling the infrastructure concerns automatically, leading to faster development cycles and more maintainable code.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication  // Meta-annotation combining @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // This single line bootstraps the entire Spring application
        // It creates the ApplicationContext, scans for components, applies auto-configuration,
        // starts the embedded server, and runs any CommandLineRunners
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

To run this application:

# Compile and package
mvn clean package

# Run the JAR
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

The application will start on port 8080 by default, and you can access it at http://localhost:8080.

basics

What is Spring Boot?

Quick Answer

RAPID Spring development.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot is a powerful extension of the Spring Framework designed to simplify and accelerate the development of production-ready Spring applications. It eliminates much of the boilerplate configuration and setup required in traditional Spring applications, allowing developers to focus on business logic rather than infrastructure concerns.

Core concepts and philosophy:

  • Convention over Configuration: Spring Boot provides sensible defaults for configuration, reducing the need for explicit setup while still allowing customization when needed
  • Standalone Applications: Creates self-contained applications that can run with a simple java -jar command, including embedded web servers
  • Opinionated Defaults: Makes decisions about technology stack and configuration based on common use cases and best practices
  • Production-Ready: Includes features like health checks, metrics, and monitoring out-of-the-box

Key features that differentiate Spring Boot:

  • Auto-Configuration: Automatically configures beans and settings based on classpath dependencies and properties
  • Starters: Curated dependency sets that bundle commonly used libraries with compatible versions
  • Embedded Servers: Includes Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow servers within the application JAR
  • Actuator: Provides production-ready features for monitoring and managing applications
  • CLI Tools: Command-line tools for rapid prototyping and development

Use cases where Spring Boot excels:

  • Microservices Development: Lightweight, independently deployable services
  • RESTful Web Services: Building APIs with minimal configuration
  • Batch Processing: Large-scale data processing applications
  • Cloud-Native Applications: Applications designed for cloud platforms
  • Rapid Prototyping: Quick development of proof-of-concepts and MVPs
  • Enterprise Applications: Large-scale applications with complex requirements

Best practices for Spring Boot development:

  • Use Starters: Leverage Spring Boot starters to manage dependencies
  • Follow Convention: Use default configurations unless you have specific requirements
  • Externalize Configuration: Use application.properties/yml for environment-specific settings
  • Use Profiles: Separate configuration for different environments (dev, test, prod)
  • Monitor with Actuator: Enable health checks and metrics for production applications
  • Keep Dependencies Updated: Regularly update Spring Boot and dependencies for security and features
  • Use DevTools: Enhance development experience with automatic restarts and live reload

Spring Boot vs Traditional Spring:

  • Configuration: Spring Boot requires minimal configuration; traditional Spring requires extensive XML or Java config
  • Deployment: Spring Boot creates executable JARs; traditional Spring often requires external containers
  • Development Speed: Spring Boot allows faster development with auto-configuration and defaults
  • Learning Curve: Spring Boot is easier for beginners due to convention over configuration

Spring Boot doesn't replace Spring but enhances it by making common patterns easier to implement while maintaining the full power and flexibility of the Spring ecosystem.

Code Example
// Traditional Spring MVC Application (extensive configuration required)
@Configuration
@EnableWebMvc
@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example.traditional")
@PropertySource("classpath:application.properties")
public class TraditionalSpringConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public ViewResolver viewResolver() {
        InternalResourceViewResolver resolver = new InternalResourceViewResolver();
        resolver.setPrefix("/WEB-INF/views/");
        resolver.setSuffix(".jsp");
        return resolver;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        DriverManagerDataSource dataSource = new DriverManagerDataSource();
        dataSource.setDriverClassName("org.h2.Driver");
        dataSource.setUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb");
        dataSource.setUsername("sa");
        dataSource.setPassword("");
        return dataSource;
    }
    
    @Bean
    public JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate(DataSource dataSource) {
        return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource);
    }
    
    @Bean
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean entityManagerFactory() {
        LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean emf = new LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean();
        emf.setDataSource(dataSource());
        emf.setPackagesToScan("com.example.traditional.entity");
        emf.setJpaVendorAdapter(new HibernateJpaVendorAdapter());
        return emf;
    }
    
    // Many more bean definitions required...
}

// Spring Boot equivalent (minimal configuration)
@SpringBootApplication
public class SpringBootApplication {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(SpringBootApplication.class, args);
    }
}

// Optional: Custom configuration bean
@Configuration
public class CustomConfig {
    
    @Bean
    public CommandLineRunner demoCommand(UserRepository userRepository) {
        return args -> {
            // Demo data initialization
            User user = new User("John", "Doe", "john@example.com");
            userRepository.save(user);
            System.out.println("Demo user created: " + user);
        };
    }
}

Configuration in application.properties:

# Spring Boot auto-configures based on these minimal properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# JPA/Hibernate configuration (optional - Spring Boot provides defaults)
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# Server configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# Logging
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG

Maven dependencies (Spring Boot approach):

<dependencies>

    <dependency>

        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Data JPA starter brings in Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, JDBC -->

    </dependency>

    </dependency>
    
    <!-- Testing starter -->

        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Running the Spring Boot application:

# Development mode (with hot reload if DevTools is included)
mvn spring-boot:run

# Production mode
mvn clean package
java -jar target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar

# With custom profiles
java -jar target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=production

REST Controller example:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    public UserController(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userRepository.findAll();
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody @Valid CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = new User(request.getFirstName(), request.getLastName(), request.getEmail());
        User saved = userRepository.save(user);
        return ResponseEntity.created(
            ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(saved.getId())
                .toUri()
        ).body(saved);
    }
}

Spring Boot follows the principle of 'Convention over Configuration', providing sensible defaults while allowing customization when needed. This makes it ideal for rapid application development while maintaining the power and flexibility of the Spring ecosystem.

basics

What is Spring Boot?

Quick Answer

An extension of the Spring Framework that simplifies setup and development.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Boot is a powerful framework designed to simplify the creation of production-ready applications based on the Spring Framework. It adopts an opinionated approach, making assumptions about how you want to configure your application based on common best practices, which significantly reduces the amount of boilerplate code and configuration required. Key components include:

  • Starters: These are dependency descriptors that bundle together all the necessary libraries for specific functionalities. For example, adding 'spring-boot-starter-web' brings in Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON processing, and Tomcat as the embedded server, ensuring version compatibility.

  • Auto-Configuration: Spring Boot automatically configures your application based on the dependencies present on the classpath. If you have HSQLDB on the classpath, it will auto-configure an in-memory database without any explicit configuration.

  • Embedded Servers: Unlike traditional Spring applications that require deploying to an external servlet container, Spring Boot includes an embedded web server (Tomcat by default, but Jetty or Undertow can be used) within the application JAR. This enables 'java -jar' execution and simplifies deployment, especially in cloud environments.

  • Production-Ready Features: Includes built-in support for metrics, health checks, externalized configuration, and logging, making it easier to monitor and manage applications in production.

  • Convention over Configuration: Spring Boot follows the principle of sensible defaults, allowing developers to override only what they need to customize, rather than configuring everything from scratch.

Overall, Spring Boot allows developers to focus on writing business logic while handling the infrastructure concerns automatically, leading to faster development cycles and more maintainable code.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication  // Meta-annotation combining @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // This single line bootstraps the entire Spring application
        // It creates the ApplicationContext, scans for components, applies auto-configuration,
        // starts the embedded server, and runs any CommandLineRunners
        SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args);
    }
}

To run this application:

# Compile and package
mvn clean package

# Run the JAR
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.0.jar

The application will start on port 8080 by default, and you can access it at http://localhost:8080.

data

What is Spring Data JPA?

Quick Answer

Data Access Layer.

Detailed Explanation

Spring Data JPA is a powerful abstraction layer built on top of JPA (Java Persistence API) and Hibernate that dramatically simplifies data access in Spring Boot applications. It eliminates boilerplate code by providing automatic implementation of repository interfaces and offering advanced querying capabilities.

Core concepts and benefits:

  • Repository Abstraction: Define data access interfaces, Spring provides implementations automatically
  • Query Methods: Generate queries from method names (findByEmail, findByNameContaining, etc.)
  • @Query Annotations: Custom JPQL/HQL/SQL queries with method parameters
  • Pagination & Sorting: Built-in support for Pageable and Sort parameters
  • Auditing: Automatic timestamping and user tracking with @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate
  • Custom Repository: Extend functionality with custom implementations
  • Specifications: Dynamic query building with JPA Criteria API

Key components:

  • Repository Interfaces: Extend JpaRepository, CrudRepository, or PagingAndSortingRepository
  • Entity Classes: JPA-annotated domain objects
  • Query Methods: Method name-based query generation
  • @Query: Custom query annotations
  • EntityManager: Direct JPA access when needed

Repository hierarchy:

  • Repository: Basic interface with find/save methods
  • CrudRepository: Adds CRUD operations
  • PagingAndSortingRepository: Adds pagination and sorting
  • JpaRepository: JPA-specific methods and features

Query method naming conventions:

  • findBy<Field>: Find by field value
  • findBy<Field>And<Field>: Multiple conditions with AND
  • findBy<Field>Or<Field>: Multiple conditions with OR
  • findBy<Field>OrderBy<Field>: With sorting
  • findBy<Field>Containing: LIKE queries
  • findBy<Field>Between: Range queries
  • countBy<Field>: Count queries
  • deleteBy<Field>: Delete queries

Best practices:

  • Use JpaRepository: Provides comprehensive functionality
  • Naming Conventions: Follow Spring Data naming rules for queries
  • @Query for Complex: Use @Query for complex or optimized queries
  • Pagination: Always use Pageable for large datasets
  • DTO Projections: Use interfaces or classes for selective field retrieval
  • N+1 Problem: Be aware of lazy loading issues
  • Indexing: Add database indexes for frequently queried fields
  • Transactions: Use @Transactional for data modification operations

Spring Boot auto-configures JPA when spring-boot-starter-data-jpa is present, setting up EntityManager, transaction management, and Hibernate.

Code Example
// Entity class
@Entity
@Table(name = "users")
public class User {
    
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    
    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;
    
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
    
    @Column(name = "created_at")
    @CreatedDate
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
    
    @Column(name = "updated_at")
    @LastModifiedDate
    private LocalDateTime updatedAt;
    
    // Constructors, getters, setters
}

// Basic repository interface
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    
    // Query method - Spring generates implementation
    List<User> findByEmail(String email);
    
    // Multiple conditions
    List<User> findByNameContainingAndEmail(String name, String email);
    
    // With sorting
    List<User> findByNameOrderByCreatedAtDesc(String name);
    
    // Exists check
    boolean existsByEmail(String email);
    
    // Count query
    long countByCreatedAtAfter(LocalDateTime date);
    
    // Delete query
    void deleteByEmail(String email);
    
    // Custom query with @Query
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email LIKE %:domain%")
    List<User> findUsersByEmailDomain(@Param("domain") String domain);
    
    // Native SQL query
    @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE created_at > :date", nativeQuery = true)
    List<User> findRecentUsers(@Param("date") LocalDateTime date);
    
    // Query with pagination
    Page<User> findByNameContaining(String name, Pageable pageable);
    
    // Custom query with joins
    @Query("SELECT u FROM User u JOIN u.posts p WHERE p.published = true")
    List<User> findUsersWithPublishedPosts();
}

// Custom repository with additional methods
public interface CustomUserRepository {
    List<User> findUsersWithCustomCriteria(String criteria);
}

@Repository
public class CustomUserRepositoryImpl implements CustomUserRepository {
    
    @PersistenceContext
    private EntityManager entityManager;
    
    @Override
    public List<User> findUsersWithCustomCriteria(String criteria) {
        CriteriaBuilder cb = entityManager.getCriteriaBuilder();
        CriteriaQuery<User> query = cb.createQuery(User.class);
        Root<User> user = query.from(User.class);
        
        query.where(cb.like(user.get("name"), "%" + criteria + "%"));
        
        return entityManager.createQuery(query).getResultList();
    }
}

// Combined repository
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long>, CustomUserRepository {
    // Inherits all methods from JpaRepository and CustomUserRepository
}

// Service using repository
@Service
public class UserService {
    
    private final UserRepository userRepository;
    
    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
    
    public List<User> searchUsers(String name, String email, int page, int size) {
        Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by("name"));
        
        if (name != null && email != null) {
            return userRepository.findByNameContainingAndEmail(name, email);
        } else if (name != null) {
            return userRepository.findByNameContaining(name, pageable).getContent();
        } else if (email != null) {
            return userRepository.findByEmail(email);
        } else {
            return userRepository.findAll(pageable).getContent();
        }
    }
    
    @Transactional
    public User createUser(String email, String name) {
        if (userRepository.existsByEmail(email)) {
            throw new UserAlreadyExistsException("User with email already exists");
        }
        
        User user = new User(email, name);
        return userRepository.save(user);
    }
}

// Controller using service
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<User> searchUsers(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String name,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String email,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) {
        
        return userService.searchUsers(name, email, page, size);
    }
}

Configuration in application.properties:

# JPA/Hibernate configuration
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

# Connection pooling
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# Optional: Enable JPA auditing
spring.jpa.auditing.enabled=true

DTO projection example:

// Interface-based projection
public interface UserSummary {
    String getName();
    String getEmail();
    LocalDateTime getCreatedAt();
}

// Repository method
@Query("SELECT u.name as name, u.email as email, u.createdAt as createdAt FROM User u")
List<UserSummary> findAllSummaries();

// Class-based projection
public class UserDto {
    private String name;
    private String email;
    
    public UserDto(String name, String email) {
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
    }
    
    // Getters
}

@Query("SELECT new com.example.UserDto(u.name, u.email) FROM User u")
List<UserDto> findAllDtos();

Specifications for dynamic queries:

public class UserSpecifications {
    
    public static Specification<User> hasName(String name) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> 
            name == null ? null : cb.like(root.get("name"), "%" + name + "%");
    }
    
    public static Specification<User> hasEmail(String email) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> 
            email == null ? null : cb.equal(root.get("email"), email);
    }
}

// Usage in repository
List<User> findAll(Specification<User> spec);

// Usage in service
List<User> users = userRepository.findAll(
    where(UserSpecifications.hasName(name))
    .and(UserSpecifications.hasEmail(email))
);

Spring Data JPA dramatically reduces boilerplate code while providing powerful querying capabilities and automatic implementation generation.

annotations

What is the @SpringBootApplication annotation?

Quick Answer

It is a convenience annotation that combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan.

Detailed Explanation

The @SpringBootApplication annotation is a meta-annotation that serves as a shortcut for three essential Spring annotations, making it the cornerstone of any Spring Boot application. Here's what each component does:

  • @Configuration: Indicates that the class can be used by the Spring IoC container as a source of bean definitions. Methods annotated with @Bean within this class will be processed to create Spring beans.

  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: Tells Spring Boot to start adding beans based on classpath settings, property settings, and other factors. This is where the 'magic' of auto-configuration happens - Spring Boot automatically configures beans for features like data sources, message converters, and security based on what's available.

  • @ComponentScan: Instructs Spring to scan for components (classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.) in the current package and all sub-packages. This is how Spring discovers and registers your application's beans.

By using @SpringBootApplication, you enable all these features with a single annotation, placed typically on the main application class. This annotation also enables other features like @EnableWebMvc if Spring MVC is on the classpath, but only if you haven't already configured it manually.

The annotation has attributes you can customize:

  • scanBasePackages: Specify packages to scan for components
  • exclude: Exclude specific auto-configuration classes
  • excludeName: Exclude by bean names

This single annotation replaces what would otherwise require multiple annotations and extensive XML configuration in traditional Spring applications.

Code Example
@SpringBootApplication(
    scanBasePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.example.common"},  // Custom scan packages
    exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class}  // Exclude specific auto-configs
)
public class Application {
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
    
    // This method creates a bean that can be injected elsewhere
    @Bean
    public MyService myService() {
        return new MyServiceImpl();
    }
}

// Without @SpringBootApplication, you would need:
@Configuration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan
public class Application {
    // Same main method
}

The annotation is typically placed on the class that contains the main method, and Spring Boot uses this as the starting point for component scanning.

controllers

What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?

Quick Answer

@RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody.

Detailed Explanation

@Controller and @RestController are both stereotypes for Spring MVC controllers, but they serve different purposes in web application development:

@Controller:

  • Used for traditional Model-View-Controller (MVC) web applications
  • Methods typically return view names (Strings) that are resolved to HTML templates
  • Can return data objects, but they need @ResponseBody to serialize to JSON/XML
  • Suitable for server-side rendered applications using templating engines like Thymeleaf, JSP, or FreeMarker
  • Supports both data and view responses from the same controller

@RestController:

  • A specialized version of @Controller designed specifically for RESTful web services
  • Automatically applies @ResponseBody to all handler methods
  • All methods return data directly (serialized to JSON by default)
  • No view resolution occurs; responses are pure data
  • Ideal for building APIs that serve JSON/XML data to frontend applications or other services

Both annotations:

  • Are scanned by @ComponentScan
  • Can use @RequestMapping and its variants (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc.)
  • Support dependency injection
  • Are singletons by default

The choice depends on your application's architecture:

  • Use @Controller for web apps with server-side rendering
  • Use @RestController for REST APIs and microservices

Spring Boot's auto-configuration sets up content negotiation and JSON serialization automatically when web starters are included.

Code Example
// Traditional MVC Controller - returns views
@Controller
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class UserMvcController {
    
    @GetMapping("/list")
    public String listUsers(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("users", userService.getAllUsers());
        return "users/list";  // Returns view name (users/list.html)
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/api/list")
    @ResponseBody  // Explicitly marks for JSON response
    public List<User> getUsersApi() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();  // Returns JSON data
    }
}

// REST Controller - returns data only
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserRestController {
    
    private final UserService userService;
    
    public UserRestController(UserService userService) {
        this.userService = userService;
    }
    
    @GetMapping
    public List<User> getAllUsers() {
        return userService.getAllUsers();  // Automatically JSON
    }
    
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return userService.findById(id)
            .map(user -> ResponseEntity.ok(user))
            .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<User> createUser(@RequestBody @Valid CreateUserRequest request) {
        User user = userService.createUser(request);
        return ResponseEntity.created(
            ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(user.getId())
                .toUri()
        ).body(user);
    }
}

// Data Transfer Object
public class CreateUserRequest {
    @NotBlank
    private String email;
    @NotBlank
    private String name;
    
    // getters and setters
}

In Thymeleaf template users/list.html:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html xmlns:th="http://www.thymeleaf.org">
<body>
    <h1>Users</h1>
    <ul>
        <li th:each="user : ${users}" th:text="${user.name}"></li>
    </ul>
</body>
</html>

The @RestController automatically configures Jackson for JSON serialization, while @Controller works with view resolvers for template rendering.

configuration

What is the purpose of application.properties (or .yml)?

Quick Answer

It allows you to externalize configuration so you can work with the same application code in different environments.

Detailed Explanation

application.properties (or its YAML equivalent application.yml) is the primary mechanism for externalizing configuration in Spring Boot applications. It allows you to define properties that can be changed without recompiling the code, enabling different configurations for different environments (development, testing, production).

Key features:

  • External Configuration: Properties can be overridden by environment variables, system properties, command-line arguments, or external property files
  • Profile-Specific: You can have application-dev.properties, application-prod.properties, etc., activated by spring.profiles.active
  • Hierarchical Loading: Properties are loaded in a specific order, with later sources overriding earlier ones
  • Type-Safe Binding: Spring Boot automatically binds properties to @ConfigurationProperties classes
  • Validation: Properties can be validated using Bean Validation annotations

Common categories of properties:

  • Server: server.port, server.servlet.context-path
  • Database: spring.datasource.url, spring.datasource.username
  • Logging: logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
  • Security: spring.security.user.name, spring.security.user.password
  • Custom Application: Your own properties like app.email.from

Spring Boot also supports YAML format for more complex hierarchical configurations, and properties can reference each other using ${property.name} syntax.

The file is typically placed in src/main/resources/ and is automatically picked up by Spring Boot's auto-configuration.

Code Example
# Server configuration
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# Database configuration
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

# JPA/Hibernate configuration
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# Logging configuration
logging.level.com.example.myapp=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=INFO
logging.file.name=app.log

# Custom application properties
app.name=My Spring Boot App
app.version=1.0.0
app.email.enabled=true
app.email.from=noreply@myapp.com

# Profile activation
spring.profiles.active=dev

YAML equivalent (application.yml):

server:
  port: 8080
  servlet:
    context-path: /api

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
    driver-class-name: org.h2.Driver
    username: sa
    password: ""
  jpa:
    database-platform: org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop
    show-sql: true

logging:
  level:
    com.example.myapp: DEBUG
    org.springframework.web: INFO
  file:
    name: app.log

app:
  name: My Spring Boot App
  version: 1.0.0
  email:
    enabled: true
    from: noreply@myapp.com

spring:
  profiles:
    active: dev

Using properties in code:

@Service
public class EmailService {
    
    @Value("${app.email.from}")
    private String fromEmail;
    
    @Value("${app.email.enabled:false}")
    private boolean emailEnabled;
    
    // Or using @ConfigurationProperties
}

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
@Component
public class AppProperties {
    private String name;
    private String version;
    private Email email = new Email();
    
    public static class Email {
        private boolean enabled;
        private String from;
        // getters/setters
    }
    // getters/setters
}

Profile-specific files:

  • application-dev.properties (activated with --spring.profiles.active=dev)
  • application-prod.properties

Command line override: java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090 --app.name="Production App"
